countries.name: Australia
countries.tagline: The country that kept phylloxera out of its oldest vineyards, then taught the world to drink Shiraz, Riesling under screwcap and hundred-year-old Tawny.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026): 159 kha of vineyard, 11.3 mhl of wine in 2025, fifth in the world and the largest producer in the Southern Hemisphere. Wine Australia's National Vintage Report 2026 put the 2026 crush at 1.27 million tonnes, the smallest since 2000.

countries.overview:
Australian wine is a story told in two scripts at once. One is industrial and brilliant: irrigated vineyards along the Murray, Darling and Murrumbidgee rivers that turned out clean, sunny, cheap wine in such volume that a kangaroo on a label became a global brand. The other is ancient and stubborn: gnarled, own-rooted Shiraz, Grenache and Mourvèdre in the Barossa and McLaren Vale planted by Silesian farmers and English gentlemen in the 1840s and 1850s, vines older than almost anything left standing in Europe. Both scripts matter, and the second exists because the first colonists' descendants were fanatical about quarantine.

Phylloxera reached Victoria in 1877 and laid waste to Geelong, Bendigo and much of the colony's young industry. South Australia shut its borders to vine material and has kept them shut ever since, policed today by Vinehealth Australia. The result is a living museum: the Langmeil Freedom block of Shiraz (1843), Cirillo's Grenache at Light Pass (1848), Hewitson's Old Garden Mourvèdre (1853), Penfolds' Block 42 Cabernet at Kalimna (1888), plus Tahbilk's 1860 Shiraz in Victoria, a pocket the louse never found. The Barossa Old Vine Charter, drafted by Yalumba in 2007, now registers these vines as Old (35 years plus), Survivor (70), Centenarian (100) and Ancestor (125). Old-vine fruit tends to be lower yielding and more even in ripening, and these vineyards are the reason a Barossa Shiraz can taste of place rather than of sunshine alone.

For most of its first 150 years Australia was a fortified-wine country. Port-style blends, sherry-style flor wines and the extraordinary liqueur Muscats of Rutherglen dominated until the 1960s. The pivot came from inside the biggest company: Max Schubert of Penfolds came home from Bordeaux and Jerez in 1950 and made the first experimental Grange Hermitage in 1951, a Shiraz built to age for decades. Management ordered him to stop in 1957; he kept going in secret. Grange became the national first growth, and the table-wine revolution followed: Hunter Semillon and Shiraz, Coonawarra Cabernet off the terra rossa, Clare and Eden Valley Riesling, and from the late 1960s the doctors' vineyards of Margaret River and the Yarra Valley.

The modern map is set by the Geographical Indication system. Wine Australia registers 28 zones (plus state and super-zone GIs such as South Eastern Australia), 65 regions and 14 subregions. They are lines on a map and nothing more: no rules on grape varieties, yields or winemaking, just the guarantee, enforced through the Label Integrity Program, that at least 85 percent of the wine comes from the place, variety and vintage on the label. That freedom explains why Australian producers can make Fiano in McLaren Vale or Nebbiolo in the Adelaide Hills without asking anyone, and why the more meaningful sub-divisions (the Barossa Grounds, McLaren Vale's districts, Margaret River's Wilyabrup, Tasmania's Tamar and Coal River valleys) are informal.

Climate is the great organiser. Inland, three irrigated regions (Riverland, Murray Darling and Riverina) still crush more than half the national tonnage. Along the southern coast, cold Southern Ocean air, altitude and latitude produce a mosaic of cool sites: Tasmania, with under 800 growing degree days, now supplies much of the country's best sparkling wine and Pinot Noir, while the Mornington Peninsula, Macedon Ranges, Adelaide Hills and Great Southern make Chardonnay and Pinot as taut as anything in the New World. Australia also gave the world a closure: in August 2000, fourteen Clare Valley Riesling producers bottled together under screwcap to escape cork taint, and within a decade most Australian and New Zealand wine followed.

The 2020s have been hard. China imposed anti-dumping duties of 116.2 to 218.4 percent on Australian bottled wine from late 2020, wiping out a market worth more than a billion Australian dollars a year, and lifted them only in March 2024. Red wine demand is falling worldwide, and growers in the warm inland are pulling out vines. The 2026 crush of 1.27 million tonnes was the smallest since 2000, 25 percent below the ten-year average, with reds down 29 percent. The industry that emerges will be smaller, cooler-climate and more site-specific, which is good news for anyone who cares about where wine comes from.

history.title: First Fleet vines at Farm Cove
history.text: Governor Arthur Phillip's First Fleet carried vine cuttings collected at Rio de Janeiro and the Cape of Good Hope, and planted them at Farm Cove on Sydney Harbour. Humidity and disease killed most of them, an early lesson that Sydney's climate was the wrong one.

history.title: Macarthurs and Blaxland
history.text: John Macarthur's family planted vines at Camden Park, and Gregory Blaxland shipped wine to London, where it won a silver medal from the Royal Society of Arts in 1823: the first sign that Australian wine could travel.

history.title: James Busby's cuttings
history.text: James Busby, a Scottish-born teacher of viticulture, toured the vineyards of Spain and France in 1831 and returned to Sydney in 1832 with cuttings of several hundred varieties. Planted at the Sydney Botanic Gardens, Camden Park and in the Hunter Valley, they seeded much of early Australian viticulture, including some of its Shiraz. Busby left for New Zealand in 1833 as British Resident.

history.title: Silesian Lutherans reach the Barossa
history.text: Prussian Lutherans fleeing religious pressure, sponsored by George Fife Angas and led by Pastor August Kavel, settled around Adelaide from 1838 and in the Barossa (Bethany) from 1842. They brought village farming, smallgoods, choirs and a habit of planting vines that their great-great-grandchildren still tend.

history.title: The Freedom vineyard
history.text: Christian Auricht planted Shiraz at what is now Langmeil, Tanunda. Still producing as the Freedom 1843 Shiraz, it is generally cited as the oldest continuously producing Shiraz vineyard in the world.

history.title: Dr Penfold's Grange
history.text: Dr Christopher Rawson Penfold planted vines at his Magill cottage, The Grange, east of Adelaide, to make tonic wines for patients. His wife Mary ran the winery; the company became the biggest in the land.

history.title: Tahbilk's Shiraz
history.text: The Goulburn Vineyard Proprietary planted at Tahbilk on the Goulburn River. A small block of 1860 Shiraz survived phylloxera on its sandy soils and still makes the 1860 Vines Shiraz.

history.title: Phylloxera at Geelong
history.text: Phylloxera was confirmed near Geelong in 1877. Victoria ordered vineyards uprooted, then lost Bendigo and much of the north-east over following decades. South Australia banned imports of vines and later created a Phylloxera Board (now Vinehealth Australia), which is why its old vines survive on their own roots.

history.title: Penola Fruit Colony
history.text: John Riddoch subdivided land at Coonawarra into 10-acre blocks for settlers in 1890 and built a triple-gabled winery in 1891 to process their grapes. The strip of red soil over limestone became Australia's Cabernet heartland; the building is now Wynns Coonawarra Estate.

history.title: Grange Hermitage
history.text: Back from Bordeaux, Max Schubert made the first experimental Grange Hermitage at Magill. Told to stop in 1957, he made the 1957 to 1959 vintages in secret. Grange turned Australia from a fortified-wine nation into a table-wine one.

history.title: The doctors' vineyards
history.text: Agronomist John Gladstones published research in 1965 suggesting Margaret River resembled Bordeaux. Dr Tom Cullity planted Vasse Felix in 1967, followed by Moss Wood, Cullen and Cape Mentelle; in Victoria Bailey Carrodus (Yarra Yering, 1969) and Dr John Middleton (Mount Mary, 1971) revived the Yarra Valley.

history.title: Geographical Indications
history.text: Amendments to the Australian Wine and Brandy Corporation Act created a Geographical Indications Committee, and the first zones and regions were registered from 1994 to 1996, to implement the 1994 wine agreement with the European Union. The Label Integrity Program, started in 1990, audits every claim.

history.title: Clare Valley screwcap
history.text: On 11 August 2000 fourteen Clare Valley wineries, including Grosset, Mount Horrocks, Taylors and Leasingham, announced they would bottle Riesling under screwcap to escape cork taint. The rest of Australia followed within a decade.

history.title: Barossa Old Vine Charter
history.text: Yalumba drafted a register of old vines, adopted by the Barossa's grape and wine association: Old Vine (35 years), Survivor (70), Centenarian (100) and Ancestor (125).

history.title: China tariffs
history.text: China imposed anti-dumping duties of up to 218.4 percent on Australian bottled wine from late 2020, closing what had been the largest export market by value. The duties were removed at the end of March 2024, but the market came back smaller.

history.title: Smallest crush since 2000
history.text: Wine Australia reported a 2026 crush of 1.27 million tonnes, 19 percent below 2025 and 25 percent below the ten-year average, as inland growers left red grapes unpicked or pulled out vines in response to soft demand.

countries.classification:
Australia's Geographical Indications (GIs) are registered by Wine Australia's Geographical Indications Committee and protected under the Wine Australia Act 2013. They nest in a hierarchy: the GI 'Australia', the multi-state super zone 'South Eastern Australia' (all of New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania and parts of Queensland and South Australia), state GIs, then 28 zones (the 'Adelaide' super zone sits across three of them), 65 regions and 14 subregions. A region must be a single tract of land producing at least 500 tonnes a year from five or more vineyards of at least 5 hectares each, and be measurably distinct; a subregion must be substantially more homogeneous still.

The lines say nothing about how wine is made. There are no permitted-variety lists, yield caps or ageing rules. What the law enforces, through the Label Integrity Program, is truth in labelling: if a GI, a variety or a vintage appears on the label, at least 85 percent of the wine must match it; blends must list varieties in descending order. Some boundaries were fought over in court for years (Coonawarra was registered only in 2003, after a long dispute over which red-soil vineyards were in), which shows how much money a name carries.

Other protected terms matter too. The fortified-style terms Cream, Crusted, Ruby, Solera, Tawny and Vintage are 'quality wine terms' with set definitions. After the 2008 wine agreement with the EU, Australia retired European names: 'Tokay' became Topaque, Australian sherry became Apera (from 2011), and 'port' became Tawny or simply fortified. Rutherglen's producers run their own four-step ladder for Muscat and Topaque (Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare). Informal sub-zoning has also grown: the Barossa Grounds study, McLaren Vale's district maps and Langton's Classification of Australian Wine (a market ranking, not a law) are where the finer distinctions live.
countries.climate_soils:
Most Australian vineyards sit between 32 and 38 degrees south, in a band where a Mediterranean pattern of winter rain and dry summers meets the huge thermal mass of an arid continent. Without moderation they would be hot; the art of Australian site selection is finding the moderators. The Southern Ocean cools Margaret River, the Great Southern, the Limestone Coast, the Fleurieu and the Mornington Peninsula; altitude cools the Adelaide Hills, Eden Valley, Orange, Tumbarumba, the Macedon Ranges and the Granite Belt; latitude makes Tasmania the coolest state, with growing degree days below 800.

Wine Australia's own climate figures show the range. Riverland and Murray Darling run around 2,350 to 2,550 growing degree days (October to April) with under 180 mm of growing-season rain, so they are entirely irrigated. Barossa Valley sits at about 1,970 degree days, Coonawarra 1,570, the Yarra Valley 1,440 and the Macedon Ranges 1,390. The Hunter is the anomaly: warm (about 2,200) but wet in summer, with more than 550 mm of rain in the growing season, which explains its early-picked, low-alcohol Semillon.

The soils are some of the oldest on earth. Weathered, low in nutrients and often sandy over clay, they keep vigour in check. Famous exceptions are the terra rossa over limestone at Coonawarra, Padthaway, Wrattonbully and Watervale; the Cambrian greenstone of Heathcote; the ironstone, quartz and slate of Eden Valley; the deep Blewitt Springs sands of McLaren Vale; the gravelly loams over granite of Margaret River; the volcanic basalts of Orange and parts of the Yarra; and Tasmania's dolerite and basalt. Water is the limit everywhere: rights to the Murray and its tributaries, more than any GI, decide where the bulk of Australian wine can be grown.

grapes.name: Shiraz
grapes.note: The national red and the most planted grape. Barossa and McLaren Vale make it dense and chocolatey, Heathcote and the Grampians peppery, the Hunter medium-bodied and earthy, Canberra and the Yarra Rhône-like and often co-fermented with Viognier. Some of the world's oldest Shiraz vines are in the Barossa (1843) and at Tahbilk (1860).

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Classic in Coonawarra, Margaret River (Wilyabrup), the Yarra Valley and Clare; often blended with Shiraz in the uniquely Australian Cabernet-Shiraz style.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Swung from the oaky 1980s style to lean, struck-match wines from Margaret River (Leeuwin, the Gingin clone), Yarra, Mornington, Adelaide Hills, Beechworth and Tasmania; also the base of Tasmanian sparkling.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: Bone-dry, lime-scented and long-lived from Clare (Polish Hill, Watervale) and Eden Valley, with newer cool sites in the Great Southern, Henty and Tasmania. The variety that drove the screwcap switch.

grapes.name: Semillon
grapes.note: The Hunter's signature: picked early at 10 to 11 percent alcohol, unoaked, and transformed by ten years in bottle into toast and honey. Also blended with Sauvignon Blanc in Margaret River and made botrytised in the Riverina (De Bortoli Noble One).

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.note: Once dismissed as fortified fodder, now prized from old bush vines in McLaren Vale (Blewitt Springs) and the Barossa, made lighter and more perfumed.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Tasmania, Mornington Peninsula, Yarra Valley, Macedon Ranges, Gippsland (Bass Phillip) and the Adelaide Hills.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre (Mataro)
grapes.note: Old Barossa plantings (Hewitson's 1853 Old Garden) and the GSM blend with Grenache and Shiraz.

grapes.name: Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge and Muscadelle
grapes.note: The grapes behind Rutherglen Muscat and Topaque, Australia's great fortified wines.

grapes.name: Mediterranean newcomers
grapes.note: Fiano, Vermentino, Nero d'Avola, Montepulciano, Tempranillo, Touriga Nacional and Prosecco (King Valley): a response to heat, drought and a migrant heritage, especially in McLaren Vale, the Riverland and the King Valley.

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.tagline: One of the world's most southerly wine countries, which turned one grape and one valley into a global style in a single generation.

stats.note: Planted area 44,184 ha in 2025 (New Zealand Winegrowers Vineyard Report 2026; 44,229 ha forecast for 2026); production 3.7 mhl in 2025, the second-largest harvest in the country's history (OIV, May 2026).

countries.overview:
New Zealand wine is young, cool and astonishingly concentrated. Almost three quarters of the country's 44,000 hectares of vines are in a single region, Marlborough, and about 82 percent of its white plantings are a single grape, Sauvignon Blanc. That combination produced one of the most recognisable wine styles on earth: pungent, zesty Sauvignon smelling of passion fruit, gooseberry, lime and cut grass, made in stainless steel and bottled under screwcap. The country exports about four fifths of its wine, worth around NZ$2 billion a year, and Sauvignon Blanc accounts for most of it.

The speed of the change is the story. Fifty years ago New Zealand made mostly fortified 'sherry' and semi-sweet Müller-Thurgau, much of it in West Auckland sheds run by Croatian (Dalmatian) and Lebanese families. Marlborough had no vineyards until Montana planted at Brancott in 1973, against expert advice that it would be too cold and dry. The first Montana Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc came from the 1979 vintage; Hunter's won a major London tasting in 1986; and Cloudy Bay's first release in 1985, with its misty-mountain label, made the style famous among the world's wine drinkers almost overnight.

But New Zealand is more than Sauvignon. Its Pinot Noir, about three quarters of the red vineyard, ranges from the dark, spicy wines of Central Otago (long billed as the world's most southerly commercial wine region, at around 45 degrees south, a title now contested by Patagonian vineyards near Sarmiento) to the fine, savoury Pinots of Martinborough and North Canterbury. Hawke's Bay, the second-largest region, has warm gravel soils that grow some of the best Syrah and Bordeaux-style blends in the Southern Hemisphere. Chardonnay from Kumeu, Hawke's Bay, Gisborne and Nelson is among the best in the New World. Riesling, Pinot Gris and aromatic whites thrive in Waipara, Nelson and Central Otago, and traditional-method sparkling is growing.

The climate is maritime everywhere. No vineyard is more than about 130 km from the sea, and the westerly winds that cross the Tasman Sea hit the Southern Alps and dump their rain on the West Coast, leaving the eastern side of both islands (where almost all the vineyards are) sunny and relatively dry. Long days, cool nights and high UV light give vivid fruit flavour and high natural acidity; a long, slow ripening season lets aromatics build without the sugar racing ahead.

New Zealand is also a leader in two things the wider wine world cares about. The New Zealand Screwcap Wine Seal Initiative, launched in 2001, made the screwcap the default closure; today almost all New Zealand wine is sealed that way. And Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand, started in the mid-1990s, now certifies members that cover about 98 percent of the vineyard area. The registered Geographical Indications are newer: the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006 came into force in 2017, and IPONZ registered the first 18 wine GIs from 2018, adding North Canterbury (2020) and Bannockburn (2022). They are geographic boundaries only, with an 85 percent origin rule, but they finally give names like Marlborough legal protection worldwide.

The country's challenges are the flip side of its success. Reliance on one grape and one market (the United States, Britain and Australia take most exports) leaves it exposed; frost in 2024 and an oversupply of Sauvignon in 2025 hit prices. Growers are planting more Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir and talking about sub-regional identity, from Marlborough's Awatere Valley to Central Otago's Bendigo, as the next stage of the story.

history.title: Marsden's vines at Kerikeri
history.text: The Anglican missionary Samuel Marsden planted about 100 vine cuttings at the Kerikeri mission in the Bay of Islands in 1819, the first recorded vines in New Zealand.

history.title: Busby's wine at Waitangi
history.text: James Busby, the British Resident and father of Australian viticulture, planted vines at his house at Waitangi, where the Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840. The French explorer Dumont d'Urville tasted his wine there in 1840, the first recorded New Zealand wine.

history.title: Mission Estate
history.text: French Marist missionaries planted vines in Hawke's Bay, settling at Meeanee and later Taradale. Mission Estate, still owned by the Society of Mary, is New Zealand's oldest winery.

history.title: A French miner in Central Otago
history.text: Jean Désiré Feraud, a French gold miner, planted vines at Clyde in Central Otago in 1864; his wine won a prize at a Sydney exhibition in 1881, a century before the region's modern revival.

history.title: Romeo Bragato
history.text: The government invited Romeo Bragato, a Dalmatian-born, Conegliano-trained viticulturist working in Victoria, to assess the colony. He called New Zealand eminently suited to viticulture and warned about phylloxera; as government viticulturist from 1902 he ran the Te Kauwhata research station.

history.title: Dalmatians in West Auckland
history.text: Croatian immigrants from Dalmatia, many of whom came to dig kauri gum, planted small vineyards in Henderson and Kumeu. Babich (1916), Nobilo (1943), Selak, Delegat and the Brajkovich family of Kumeu River built the modern industry from these roots, along with the Lebanese Corban family (1902).

history.title: Prohibition narrowly defeated
history.text: A national referendum voted for prohibition until the votes of soldiers returning from the First World War tipped the result the other way. Licensing laws remained restrictive for decades.

history.title: Montana plants Marlborough
history.text: Frank Yukich's Montana Wines planted the first commercial vineyard in Marlborough at Brancott. Its first Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc came from the 1979 vintage.

history.title: Martinborough's terraces
history.text: A 1979 soil and climate report by Dr Derek Milne compared Martinborough to Burgundy. Neil McCallum (Dry River) and Clive Paton (Ata Rangi) planted in 1979 and 1980, and the village became the first centre of New Zealand Pinot Noir.

history.title: Cloudy Bay
history.text: David Hohnen of Cape Mentelle in Margaret River founded Cloudy Bay in Marlborough, with Kevin Judd as winemaker. Its first Sauvignon Blanc, and its label of misty mountains, made Marlborough a world brand.

history.title: Vine-pull scheme
history.text: With a glut of bulk wine, the government paid growers to pull out about a quarter of the national vineyard, mostly Müller-Thurgau. Replanting with Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir reset the industry.

history.title: Screwcap initiative
history.text: A group of producers launched the New Zealand Screwcap Wine Seal Initiative to escape cork taint and oxidation. Within a few years almost all New Zealand wine was under screwcap.

history.title: First registered GIs
history.text: Under the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006, in force from 2017, IPONZ registered the first New Zealand wine GIs, starting with Marlborough, Hawke's Bay and other regions on 26 February 2018. Bannockburn, registered in 2022, was the most recent.

history.title: Second-largest harvest
history.text: After the frost-hit 2024 vintage, 2025 produced about 3.7 million hectolitres, the second-largest harvest in New Zealand history according to the OIV.

countries.classification:
New Zealand's wine Geographical Indications are registered by the Intellectual Property Office of New Zealand (IPONZ) under the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006, which came into force in July 2017. There are three 'enduring' GIs created by statute (New Zealand, North Island, South Island) and 19 registered wine GIs: Northland, Auckland (with Matakana, Kumeu and Waiheke Island inside it), Gisborne, Hawke's Bay (with Central Hawke's Bay), Wairarapa (with Gladstone and Martinborough), Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury (with North Canterbury, which contains Waipara Valley), Waitaki Valley North Otago and Central Otago (with Bannockburn).

A GI only defines a boundary. To use one on a label, at least 85 percent of the wine must come from the named area (the same 85 percent rule applies to variety and vintage). There are no rules on grape varieties, yields or winemaking. The registration process does require evidence that the area's wines have a quality, reputation or characteristic linked to it, which is why only established places are registered and why informal sub-areas such as Marlborough's Awatere Valley, Hawke's Bay's Gimblett Gravels or Central Otago's Bendigo are not GIs. Gimblett Gravels instead uses a trademark controlled by its winegrowers' association.

Other labelling signals matter more in practice: Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand certification (members cover about 98 percent of vineyard area), organic (BioGro) and biodynamic (Demeter) certification, and in Central Otago and Martinborough the vineyard name.
countries.climate_soils:
New Zealand stretches from about 35 degrees south in Northland to 45 degrees south in Central Otago. Every vineyard is close to the sea, but the mountain spine matters more than the coast: the Southern Alps and the North Island's ranges block the prevailing westerlies, so the eastern regions where vines grow are sunny and dry. Marlborough is one of the sunniest places in the country, Central Otago is semi-continental with hot days, freezing nights and frost, while Auckland and Northland are humid and warm.

The country's soils are young and alluvial. Marlborough's Wairau Valley is a bed of greywacke gravels and silts laid down by the Wairau River, with stony, free-draining soils on the north side (Rapaura) and clay-rich soils in the Southern Valleys; the Awatere Valley is higher, colder and windier. Hawke's Bay has deep alluvial gravels left by the Ngaruroro River, notably the Gimblett Gravels, laid bare when a flood in 1867 changed the river's course. Central Otago has schist and windblown loess over gravels. North Canterbury has limestone at Waikari and Weka Pass, a rarity. Nelson's Moutere Hills are weathered gravel-clay. Martinborough sits on a free-draining river terrace of silt over gravel.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: About 82 percent of white plantings and roughly 70 percent of the national vineyard; Marlborough's pungent, aromatic style is the national calling card.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: About 75 percent of red plantings: dark and spicy in Central Otago, savoury in Martinborough, fine and stony in North Canterbury, fragrant in Marlborough's Southern Valleys.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: About 8 percent of whites, but central to New Zealand's fine-wine image: Kumeu River, Hawke's Bay (Te Mata Elston), Gisborne (Millton) and Nelson (Neudorf Moutere).

grapes.name: Pinot Gris
grapes.note: About 7 percent of whites, the country's third white, often off-dry in Central Otago and Hawke's Bay.

grapes.name: Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Grown mostly in Hawke's Bay's gravels for Bordeaux-style blends such as Te Mata Coleraine.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: About 6 percent of reds, mostly in Hawke's Bay, where Gimblett Gravels Syrah has a peppery, northern-Rhône profile.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: A small share but a high reputation in Waipara, Central Otago, Marlborough and Nelson, from dry to botrytised.

countries.name: South Africa
countries.tagline: Three and a half centuries of Cape wine, from Van Riebeeck's first pressing to Swartland old-vine Chenin, told in mountains, wind and granite.

stats.note: About 86,525 ha of wine grapes (WOSA, 2026); total vineyard including table and drying grapes 109 kha and wine production 10.2 mhl in 2025, seventh in the world (OIV, May 2026). SAWIS counted 2,176 grape producers and 507 cellars crushing grapes in 2025.

countries.overview:
South African wine is the oldest in the New World outside the Americas, and the most complicated. On 2 February 1659, seven years after the Dutch East India Company (VOC) set up a supply station at the Cape, Commander Jan van Riebeeck wrote in his diary: 'Today, praise be to God, wine was pressed for the first time from Cape grapes.' Within thirty years Simon van der Stel had founded Constantia, whose sweet wine became one of the most famous in Europe, and French Huguenot refugees had settled the valley that is still called Franschhoek, 'French corner'. Much of the labour on these farms was enslaved, and the industry's history is bound up with slavery, dispossession and, later, apartheid; the wine story cannot be told honestly without that.

The modern industry has about 86,500 hectares of wine grapes, almost all in the Western Cape within a few hours of Cape Town. It is defined by the meeting of a Mediterranean climate with two oceans and a wall of mountains. The cold Benguela current up the west coast and the south-easterly 'Cape Doctor' wind cool vineyards that would otherwise be hot; the Cape Fold Belt's sandstone and granite mountains, some of the oldest soils on earth, give a mosaic of slopes, aspects and altitudes. Inland, behind the mountains, the Breede River Valley, Olifants River and Klein Karoo are hotter, drier and irrigated.

Chenin Blanc is the signature. Brought from the Loire in the seventeenth century, it is the most planted variety, roughly 18 percent of the vineyard and more than in any other country. For centuries it was the workhorse for brandy and bulk wine; today old bush-vine Chenin from the Swartland, Stellenbosch and the Olifants River makes some of the world's most exciting whites. South Africa also has its own grape, Pinotage, a 1925 cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut (then called Hermitage) by Abraham Perold, and world-class Bordeaux blends, Syrah, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and traditional-method sparkling (Cap Classique). Its sweet wine history, from Vin de Constance to the 'Cape Port' styles of Calitzdorp, is equally rich.

The twentieth century was shaped by the KWV, the growers' co-operative founded in 1918 to fix minimum prices in a glutted market. From 1957 a quota system controlled what could be planted and where; it rewarded volume, kept most wine flowing to distillation, and froze the vineyard in old varieties and co-operative cellars. International sanctions against apartheid cut South African wine off from most export markets in the 1980s. The release of Nelson Mandela in 1990 and the democratic elections of 1994 reopened the world; quotas ended in 1992, the KWV became a company in 1997, and exports grew from a trickle to more than 300 million litres a year.

The past two decades brought a quality revolution. In the Swartland, Eben Sadie (Columella, 2000), Chris and Andrea Mullineux and Adi Badenhorst rediscovered old dry-farmed vineyards of Chenin, Grenache, Cinsault and Palomino; their Swartland Revolution festival (2010 to 2015) put a young, natural-leaning generation on the world stage. Rosa Kruger began mapping old vines, and the Old Vine Project now certifies vineyards over 35 years old with a 'Certified Heritage Vineyard' seal giving the planting year; in 2024 the OIV adopted the same 35-year benchmark for an 'old vine'. Cool sites in the Hemel-en-Aarde, Elgin and Elim have made South Africa a serious source of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

The challenges are real. Land and ownership remain overwhelmingly white, three decades after apartheid; black-owned brands, empowerment schemes and organisations such as the Pinotage Youth Development Academy and the Cape Winemakers Guild's protégé programme are growing but still small. The vineyard is shrinking (from over 100,000 ha in 2009), the 2015 to 2017 drought and 2020 Covid alcohol-sales bans hit hard, and prices remain low for the quality. Yet the 2025 harvest of 10.2 million hectolitres was a full recovery, and few countries offer so much old-vine character for the money.

history.title: Van Riebeeck's first wine
history.text: The VOC's Cape commander Jan van Riebeeck planted vines from 1655 and pressed the first Cape wine on 2 February 1659, recording it in his diary. Vines were grown partly to fight scurvy on the ships' crews.

history.title: Stellenbosch and Constantia
history.text: Commander Simon van der Stel founded Stellenbosch in 1679, the colony's second town, and in 1685 was granted Constantia, where he planted a large vineyard and made wine for the Company and the passing fleets.

history.title: The Huguenots arrive
history.text: About 200 French Protestant refugees, fleeing persecution after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, were settled by the VOC in the Drakenstein and Franschhoek valleys. They brought viticultural knowledge and names (de Villiers, du Toit, Joubert, Malan, le Roux) that still run Cape farms.

history.title: Constantia's golden age
history.text: Hendrik Cloete bought Groot Constantia in 1778 and made an unfortified sweet Muscat wine that became the toast of European courts. Napoleon had it shipped to St Helena during his exile (1815 to 1821); Jane Austen recommended it for a broken heart in Sense and Sensibility (1811), and Baudelaire and Dickens wrote about it.

history.title: Emancipation
history.text: Slavery was abolished in the Cape in 1834 (with a four-year 'apprenticeship'). The 'dop' system of paying farm workers partly in wine, which caused generations of harm, persisted long after and was only outlawed in 1960, though it lingered informally.

history.title: Phylloxera
history.text: Phylloxera was found near Mowbray, Cape Town, in 1886 and spread through the winelands, destroying most vineyards. Replanting on American rootstocks favoured high-yielding varieties such as Cinsaut.

history.title: The KWV
history.text: The Koöperatieve Wijnbouwers Vereniging van Zuid-Afrika (KWV) was founded at Paarl in 1918 to stabilise prices in a glutted market. Statutory powers from 1924 and a quota system from 1957 let it control prices and plantings until the 1990s.

history.title: Pinotage
history.text: Professor Abraham Izak Perold crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut (then called Hermitage) at Welgevallen, Stellenbosch University's experimental farm, in 1925. The first wine was made at Elsenburg in 1941, and a Bellevue Pinotage won the Cape Wine Show in 1959; in 1961 it became the first wine labelled Pinotage.

history.title: First Cap Classique
history.text: Frans Malan of Simonsig made Kaapse Vonkel, the first South African bottle-fermented sparkling wine, from the 1971 vintage. The category is now called Méthode Cap Classique.

history.title: Wine of Origin
history.text: The Wine of Origin scheme came into force in 1973, defining regions, districts and wards and certifying origin, variety and vintage claims. Every certified bottle carries a Wine and Spirit Board seal.

history.title: Reopening to the world
history.text: Nelson Mandela's release in 1990 and the elections of 1994 ended apartheid-era sanctions. Exports rose quickly; the KWV's quota system ended in 1992 and the co-operative became a company in 1997.

history.title: Columella and the Swartland
history.text: Eben Sadie made the first Columella, a Syrah-Mourvèdre blend, in 2000 (about 5,000 bottles), followed by Palladius white in 2002. The Swartland became the centre of a new generation of old-vine, low-intervention wines.

history.title: Swartland Revolution
history.text: Sadie, the Mullineuxs, Adi Badenhorst and Callie Louw (Porseleinberg) launched the Swartland Revolution festival at Riebeek-Kasteel, which ran until 2015 and drew wine writers from around the world.

history.title: Old Vine Project
history.text: Rosa Kruger began cataloguing old vineyards in 2002; the Old Vine Project's Certified Heritage Vineyard seal marks vineyards at least 35 years old with their planting date. In 2024 the OIV adopted 35 years as the global definition of an old vine.

history.title: Drought and lockdowns
history.text: The 2015 to 2017 drought shrank Western Cape harvests and the vineyard, and Covid-era bans on alcohol sales and exports in 2020 cost the industry heavily. The 2025 harvest (10.2 mhl) marked a full recovery.

countries.classification:
The Wine of Origin (WO) scheme, in force since 1973 and administered by the Wine and Spirit Board, certifies three claims on a label: origin, grape variety and vintage. If a variety or vintage is named, at least 85 percent of the wine must be that variety or year; an origin claim requires 100 percent of the grapes from the named area. Every certified bottle carries a numbered seal.

Origins nest in a hierarchy that has grown more complex over time. The February 2026 list starts with the overarching geographical unit Greater Cape (Western, Northern and Eastern Cape) and six other geographical units (KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Limpopo, North West and, oddly, a 'none' unit for the Lanseria ward). Inside the Western Cape are the overarching region Cape Coast (Coastal Region plus Cape South Coast) and the regions Breede River Valley, Klein Karoo and Olifants River; the Northern Cape holds the Karoo-Hoogland region. A newer subregion layer, Cape West Coast, groups Darling, Lutzville Valley, St Helena Bay and the coastal wards. Below these are districts (for example Stellenbosch, Paarl, Swartland, Walker Bay) and, at the smallest scale, wards (Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Piekenierskloof). Some wards sit outside any district (Cederberg, Elim's neighbours Napier and Herbertsdale, Lamberts Bay). In total WOSA counts 32 districts and about 100 wards.

Units are defined mostly by geography rather than by proven style, and like the Australian and New Zealand systems the scheme sets no rules on varieties or yields. Two other labels matter: 'Estate Wine', a term for wine grown, made and bottled on registered contiguous land, and the Old Vine Project's Certified Heritage Vineyard seal, which gives the planting year of vineyards at least 35 years old. The Integrated Production of Wine (IPW) sustainability scheme can be combined with the WO seal. 'Cape Port' and 'Cape Sherry' terms were retired under the EU trade agreement from 2012: fortified styles are now labelled Cape Vintage, Cape Ruby, Cape Tawny and Cape White, and Boberg is a historic designation for fortified wines from Paarl, Franschhoek and Tulbagh.
countries.climate_soils:
The Cape winelands have a Mediterranean climate of wet winters and dry summers, but the details are set by oceans and mountains. The cold Benguela current runs up the Atlantic coast, cooling the west coast (Darling, Lamberts Bay, Bamboes Bay) and bringing fog. The strong south-easterly wind of summer, the 'Cape Doctor', blows off False Bay and Walker Bay, cooling Stellenbosch, Constantia, Elgin and the Hemel-en-Aarde, keeping disease down and thickening grape skins. Away from the sea and behind the mountain ranges, temperatures rise and rainfall falls sharply: from about 1,000 mm a year in Constantia and Stellenbosch to 250 to 400 mm in Robertson, the Klein Karoo and the Olifants River, where irrigation is essential.

Geologically the Cape is ancient. Granite intrusions about 550 million years old underlie Stellenbosch, Paarl and the Paardeberg; Table Mountain sandstone forms the high ranges and the poor, sandy soils of Cederberg and Elgin; Malmesbury shale, even older, weathers to the dark 'schist' soils of the Swartland and Tygerberg; Bokkeveld shale is found in the Hemel-en-Aarde and Klein Karoo. Robertson has unusual lime-rich soils along the Breede River. Mostly low in nutrients and naturally acidic, these soils are good at restraining vigour, and the many slopes, aspects and altitudes (from sea level to Sutherland's vineyards at about 1,500 m) give the Cape far more variety than its latitude (roughly 32 to 35 degrees south) would suggest.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.note: The most planted variety (about 18 percent of the vineyard). Once brandy and bulk fodder, now made in every style from crisp and fruity to barrel-fermented old-vine wines of great depth, and in sweet and sparkling forms.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The leading red grape, especially in Stellenbosch, where Bordeaux blends (Meerlust Rubicon, Kanonkop Paul Sauer, Vergelegen V) are classics.

grapes.name: Colombard
grapes.note: Widely planted inland for brandy, bulk wine and fresh, inexpensive whites.

grapes.name: Shiraz / Syrah
grapes.note: Grown everywhere; peppery and fresh from the Swartland and Hemel-en-Aarde, richer from Stellenbosch and Paarl.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Cool-climate styles from Constantia, Durbanville, Elgin, Elim and the west coast.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.note: South Africa's own cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut (1925). Best from old bush vines (Kanonkop, Beyerskloof, Kaapzicht) and in Cape Blends with Bordeaux varieties.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Fine and mineral from the Hemel-en-Aarde, Elgin and Robertson's limestone.

grapes.name: Cinsault, Grenache, Palomino, Sémillon
grapes.note: Old plantings rediscovered by the new wave; Cinsault (once the main red) now makes light, fragrant wines, and Sémillon Gris survives in old Franschhoek vineyards.

grapes.name: Muscat de Frontignan and Muscat d'Alexandrie
grapes.note: Behind Vin de Constance and the fortified 'Muscadel' wines of Robertson and the Klein Karoo.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional and Tinta Barocca
grapes.note: The base of Calitzdorp's Cape Vintage and Cape Tawny fortified wines.

countries.name: China
countries.tagline: The world's third-largest vineyard and its oldest fermented drink, now remaking itself from the desert edge of the Helan Mountains.

stats.note: OIV (May 2026): 733 kha of vineyard (third in the world, most of it table grapes and raisins) and 2.2 mhl of wine in 2025, down 17.8 percent on 2024 and ranked 18th; China was the fifth-largest producer at its 2012 peak.

countries.overview:
China has the oldest chemical evidence of a fermented drink containing grapes and one of the youngest modern wine industries. At Jiahu, a Neolithic village in Henan, residues in pottery jars from about 7000 BC point to a mixed drink of rice, honey and fruit (hawthorn or wild grape). Grape wine proper arrived along the Silk Road: the Han envoy Zhang Qian travelled to Dayuan (Ferghana, in modern Uzbekistan) in the 130s and 120s BC, and by the end of the century Han envoys had brought grape seeds back to plant near the capital, Chang'an. Under the Tang, after the conquest of Gaochang near Turpan in 641, the court learned a 'method of wine making' and planted the long 'mare's teat' grape; poets such as Wang Han wrote of 'fine grape wine in luminous cups of jade'. Yet for most of Chinese history, grain-based huangjiu and later baijiu dominated, and grape wine stayed exotic.

Modern Chinese wine began in 1892, when Zhang Bishi, a Hakka tycoon from the Dutch East Indies, founded Changyu in the treaty port of Yantai, Shandong, and imported European vines (including the grape later identified as Carmenère and sold as 'Cabernet Gernischt'). The state-led era brought Great Wall (1983, at Shacheng in Hebei, now part of COFCO) and the Sino-French joint venture Dynasty (1980, with Rémy Martin, in Tianjin). These three dominated for decades, often blending imported bulk wine with local juice.

The 2000s and early 2010s saw a boom. Rising wealth made Bordeaux a status symbol, and China briefly became the world's biggest market for red wine; domestic production peaked in 2012, when China was the fifth-largest producer. Provincial governments, above all Ningxia's, poured money into new estates. Helan Qingxue's Jiabeilan 2009 won a Decanter international trophy in 2011, and Ningxia became the face of quality Chinese wine. LVMH's Moët Hennessy set up Chandon in Ningxia (2013) and the high-altitude Ao Yun estate in Yunnan (first vintage 2013), and Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite) planted Long Dai in Shandong.

The years since have been tough. An anti-corruption campaign from 2012 cut banquet and gift spending, consumption fell, and production dropped from more than 13 million hectolitres at its 2012 peak to 2.2 million in 2025. China's vineyard, the third-largest in the world at 733,000 ha, is now overwhelmingly for table grapes and raisins. But the quality end is better than ever: small estates in Ningxia, Xinjiang, Shandong, Hebei and Yunnan make serious Cabernet, Marselan and Chardonnay, and Ningxia hosted the 46th OIV World Congress in October 2026.

Viticulture in much of China is extreme. In the north and west, winters fall to minus 20 to minus 30 degrees C, so vines in Ningxia, Xinjiang, Gansu and Hebei must be buried under soil every November and dug out in April, an enormous labour cost that limits vine age and trunk size. In the east, summer monsoon rain brings rot and mildew. The best regions are those in the dry west with access to irrigation, or high mountain valleys in the south-west where the monsoon is blocked.

history.title: Jiahu fermented drink
history.text: Residues in pottery jars from the Neolithic village of Jiahu in Henan, analysed by Patrick McGovern and colleagues in 2004, revealed a fermented beverage of rice, honey and fruit (hawthorn and/or wild grape): the oldest chemically confirmed alcoholic drink in the world.

history.title: Zhang Qian reaches Ferghana
history.text: The Han envoy Zhang Qian reached Dayuan (Ferghana), whose people made and stored grape wine. Han envoys later brought grape seeds back to plant on imperial land near Chang'an.

history.title: Tang conquest of Gaochang
history.text: After conquering Gaochang, an oasis kingdom near Turpan, the Tang court acquired the 'mare's teat' grape and a method of winemaking. Tang poets such as Wang Han celebrated grape wine 'in luminous cups'.

history.title: Changyu at Yantai
history.text: Zhang Bishi founded Changyu in Yantai, Shandong, importing European vines; his Grand Cellar (1894 onward) still stands beside the sea. Changyu is the oldest and largest Chinese wine company.

history.title: Dynasty and Great Wall
history.text: Rémy Martin and Tianjin created Dynasty, China's first Sino-foreign wine joint venture, in 1980; the state-owned Great Wall winery was founded at Shacheng, Hebei, in 1983. With Changyu they dominated Chinese wine for 30 years.

history.title: Sino-French demonstration vineyard
history.text: A Sino-French demonstration vineyard planted at Donghuayuan in Huailai county, Hebei (now Domaine Franco-Chinois), introduced varieties including Marselan, which became a Chinese specialty.

history.title: Ningxia's Decanter trophy
history.text: Helan Qingxue's Jiabeilan 2009, made by consultant Li Demei, won an international trophy at the Decanter World Wine Awards, launching Ningxia's international reputation.

history.title: Peak and pivot
history.text: Chinese wine production peaked at more than 13 mhl; that year an anti-corruption campaign curbed lavish banquets and gifts, and consumption began a long decline.

history.title: Ningxia classification and Ao Yun
history.text: Ningxia introduced a classification of Helan Mountain East estates (expanded to five tiers in 2016); LVMH's Ao Yun made its first vintage high in Yunnan.

history.title: EU-China GI agreement
history.text: The EU-China agreement on geographical indications came into force on 1 March 2021, protecting Chinese wine names including Helan Mountain East Foothill, Yantai, Shacheng and Huanren Icewine in the EU.

history.title: OIV World Congress in Ningxia
history.text: Ningxia hosted the 46th OIV World Congress of Vine and Wine in Yinchuan from 12 to 18 October 2026, a sign of its status as China's flagship region.

countries.classification:
China's wine GIs are protected under national systems (the former AQSIQ geographical-indication product scheme, now run by the China National Intellectual Property Administration), with production standards for named areas such as 'Helan Mountain East Foothill' (贺兰山东麓葡萄酒), 'Yantai' (烟台葡萄酒), 'Shacheng' (沙城葡萄酒), 'Changli' (昌黎葡萄酒) and 'Huanren Icewine' (桓仁冰酒). Four of them (Helan Mountain East Foothill, Yantai, Shacheng and Huanren Icewine) are protected in Europe under the EU-China agreement in force since March 2021. Boundaries are generally administrative and not published as precise maps, so in this atlas they appear as points.

Ningxia also runs China's only official estate classification. Introduced in 2013, when ten wineries became Fifth Growths, it was expanded in 2016 to five tiers (Fifth to First Growth) and is reviewed every two years by a panel of experts, with First Growths to be re-examined every ten years. By 2021 nine estates had reached Second Growth (including Helan Qingxue, Kanaan, Chateau Hedong, Legacy Peak, Lisi and Chateau Yuquan) and the First Growth tier was still empty. Beyond that, labels rely on producer reputation; much Chinese wine carries no regional claim at all.
countries.climate_soils: China's wine regions sit in two very different climates. The north and west (Ningxia, Xinjiang, Gansu, Inner Mongolia, Hebei's Huailai basin, Shanxi) are continental and dry, with hot summers, abundant sun and very cold winters, so vines are buried each autumn; irrigation from the Yellow River, Tianshan snowmelt or underground water is essential. Soils are typically sandy and gravelly alluvial fans (Helan Mountain East) or loess. The east coast (Shandong's Jiaodong Peninsula, coastal Hebei, Beijing, Tianjin) is warmer in winter but has a summer monsoon that brings humidity and disease just as grapes ripen. The south-west mountains of Yunnan and Sichuan offer a third option: high valleys at 2,000 to 2,600 m, sheltered from the monsoon by the Himalayan rain shadow, where Ao Yun and its neighbours grow Cabernet Sauvignon on river terraces.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The dominant wine grape, the core of Ningxia's and Xinjiang's best reds.

grapes.name: Marselan
grapes.note: A 1961 French cross of Cabernet Sauvignon and Grenache, introduced in 2001, now promoted as a Chinese signature for its colour, softness and mildew resistance.

grapes.name: Cabernet Gernischt (Carmenère)
grapes.note: Imported by Changyu in the 1890s and long thought to be a Cabernet Franc relative; DNA profiling showed it is Carmenère. Common in Shandong.

grapes.name: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Petit Verdot
grapes.note: Widely planted in Ningxia, Hebei and Xinjiang.

grapes.name: Chardonnay, Riesling, Italian Riesling (Welschriesling)
grapes.note: The main whites; Italian Riesling was planted extensively in the 1950s to 1980s.

grapes.name: Vitis amurensis and hybrids (Beibinghong, Shuangyou)
grapes.note: Cold-hardy native and hybrid grapes in Jilin and Liaoning used for 'mountain grape' wines and icewine; Vidal is used at Huanren.

grapes.name: Rose Honey (Mei Gui Mi)
grapes.note: A heritage table-and-wine grape planted by French missionaries in Yunnan in the nineteenth century, still made into wine at Mile.

countries.name: Japan
countries.tagline: A thousand years of the Koshu grape, a rainy climate tamed by pergolas, and a new generation of growers from Yamanashi to Hokkaido.

stats.note: Vineyard: 16,300 ha of grapes in 2024 (MAFF via FAOSTAT), almost all table grapes. Production: National Tax Agency survey published in 2025, covering calendar 2024 at responding wineries: 39,454 kl of wine made in Japan, of which 12,682 kl was 'Japan Wine' from Japanese-grown grapes; most of the rest is made from imported concentrate, above all in Kanagawa. 519 wine-producing premises were in the survey on 1 January 2025. Japan imported 2.3 mhl in 2025 (OIV)

countries.overview:
Japan is a difficult place to grow wine grapes. Most of the country has a humid, monsoon summer with heavy rain in June and July (the tsuyu season) and typhoons in late summer and autumn, just as grapes ripen. Yet grapes have been grown in the Kofu basin of Yamanashi for more than a thousand years, and since the 1990s Japanese winemakers have turned an industry of sweet, blended table wine into one of the most interesting small wine cultures in the world.

The emblem is Koshu, a pink-skinned grape grown in Yamanashi for centuries, traditionally said to have arrived along the Silk Road (legends link it to the monk Gyoki in 718 or to Amemiya Kageyu in 1186). DNA analysis published in 2015 showed it is mostly Vitis vinifera with some ancestry from wild East Asian Vitis species, including Vitis davidii, which may explain its thick skin and tolerance of humidity. Koshu makes delicate, low-alcohol white wine with citrus, white peach and a faint bitterness, increasingly made sur lie, in amphora or with skin contact, and it is a natural partner for Japanese food. Japan's other homegrown grape, Muscat Bailey A, was bred by Kawakami Zenbei at Iwanohara in Niigata (released in 1927) from the American Bailey and Muscat Hamburg, and gives light, candied-strawberry reds.

Modern Japanese wine dates from the Meiji era. Two young men from Yamanashi, Takano Masanari and Tsuchiya Ryuken, were sent to Troyes in 1877 to learn French winemaking, and their company was the root of what became Mercian, now Château Mercian. Kawakami Zenbei founded Iwanohara Vineyard in 1890 and bred more than 10,000 crosses to find grapes suited to Japan. For most of the twentieth century the industry made sweet, fortified 'port wine' (Akadama, from 1907) and wines blended from imported concentrate.

The change came with the 1990s and 2000s: Château Mercian's Kikyogahara Merlot and Grace Wine's Koshu won international attention, the Koshu of Japan export project began in 2009, and in 2018 new labelling rules came into force that reserved the term 'Japan Wine' (nihon wine) for wines made in Japan entirely from Japanese-grown grapes, and allowed a place name only if 85 percent of the grapes came from it. The National Tax Agency designated Yamanashi as Japan's first wine GI in 2013, followed by Hokkaido (2018) and Yamagata, Osaka and Nagano (2021).

The most exciting growth is in the north. Hokkaido, cool and largely free of the rainy season and typhoons, has attracted dozens of small growers around Yoichi and Iwamizawa, led by Takahiko Soga of Domaine Takahiko, and in 2017 Burgundy's Domaine de Montille bought land near Hakodate to make Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Nagano, with its high, dry valleys (Kikyogahara, Chikumagawa), is the other rising region.

history.title: Koshu legends
history.text: Tradition credits the monk Gyoki with planting grapes at Daizenji temple in Katsunuma in 718, or a man called Amemiya Kageyu with finding a wild vine there in 1186. Either way, Koshu grapes have been grown in Yamanashi for centuries, eaten fresh rather than made into wine.

history.title: Portuguese wine
history.text: Francis Xavier and other Jesuit missionaries brought Portuguese red wine (called chintashu, from 'tinto') as gifts for Kyushu's feudal lords.

history.title: Two men go to Troyes
history.text: Takano Masanari and Tsuchiya Ryuken, from Katsunuma, were sent by the newly founded Dai Nihon Yamanashi Budoshu company to Troyes in Champagne to study viticulture and winemaking. Their company's lineage leads to today's Château Mercian.

history.title: Iwanohara Vineyard
history.text: Kawakami Zenbei founded Iwanohara Vineyard in Joetsu, Niigata. Working with snow-cooled cellars, he bred thousands of grape crosses, releasing Muscat Bailey A and Black Queen in 1927.

history.title: Akadama Port Wine
history.text: Shinjiro Torii (founder of Suntory) launched Akadama Port Wine, a sweet fortified wine that became Japan's best-known 'wine' for decades.

history.title: Yamanashi GI
history.text: The National Tax Agency designated Yamanashi as Japan's first wine Geographical Indication on 16 July 2013, requiring Yamanashi-grown grapes of approved varieties and standards.

history.title: Japan Wine labelling rules and Hokkaido GI
history.text: New labelling standards reserved 'Japan Wine' for wine made in Japan from 100 percent Japanese grapes and set an 85 percent rule for place names; Hokkaido became Japan's second wine GI on 28 June 2018.

history.title: Yamagata, Osaka and Nagano GIs
history.text: On 30 June 2021 the National Tax Agency designated three more wine GIs: Yamagata, Osaka and Nagano.

countries.classification:
Japan's wine GIs are designated by the National Tax Agency (NTA), which regulates alcohol. Five wine GIs exist, each covering a whole prefecture: Yamanashi (2013), Hokkaido (2018), and Yamagata, Osaka and Nagano (2021). Each GI has production standards: grapes grown entirely in the prefecture, a list of approved varieties (including vinifera, Koshu, Muscat Bailey A and Yamabudo hybrids in some GIs), minimum sugar levels at harvest, limits on chaptalisation and acidification, and in some cases a tasting panel. Yamanashi's standards, for example, require approved varieties and set minimum natural sugar levels for Koshu and Muscat Bailey A.

Separately, labelling rules in force since October 2018 define 'Japan Wine' (nihon wine) as wine made in Japan from 100 percent Japanese grapes, and allow a place, variety or vintage on the label only if at least 85 percent of the wine meets it. 'Domestically made wine' (kokunai seizo wine) can contain imported juice or concentrate and must say so. This distinction matters because the majority of wine bottled in Japan is still made from imported material.
countries.climate_soils:
Japan stretches from subtropical Okinawa to cool Hokkaido, but most vineyards share a problem: summer humidity and rain. The June to July rainy season and late-summer typhoons bring fungal disease and dilution. Growers respond with high pergolas (tanazukuri), which hold the canopy two metres above the ground for airflow and were originally designed for table grapes; with paper hats on individual bunches; with rain covers over rows; and by choosing thick-skinned varieties. Increasingly, vertical shoot positioning is used in drier sites.

The best regions are naturally drier. The Kofu basin in Yamanashi is ringed by mountains, including Mount Fuji, that block some rain, and has hot summers and well-drained alluvial fans. Nagano's high valleys (500 to 900 m) have Japan's lowest rainfall and big day-night temperature swings. Hokkaido largely escapes both the rainy season and typhoons, with a cool climate suited to Pinot Noir, Kerner and Zweigelt, though winters are snowy and very cold. Soils are mostly volcanic or alluvial.

grapes.name: Koshu
grapes.note: The signature white, mostly vinifera with some wild East Asian Vitis ancestry; about 95 percent of plantings are in Yamanashi.

grapes.name: Muscat Bailey A
grapes.note: Bred by Kawakami Zenbei in 1927; the most planted red wine grape, light and fruity.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: Successful in Nagano (Kikyogahara) and Yamanashi.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Widely planted in Nagano, Yamanashi and Hokkaido.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir, Kerner, Zweigelt, Müller-Thurgau
grapes.note: Hokkaido's cool-climate grapes; Pinot Noir is the rising star at Yoichi and Hakodate.

grapes.name: Yamabudo (Vitis coignetiae) and hybrids
grapes.note: Native wild mountain grape and crosses (Yama Sauvignon) used in the north and in Iwate and Hokkaido.

grapes.name: Delaware and Niagara
grapes.note: American table grapes still widely made into sweet and sparkling wine, especially in Yamagata and Osaka.

countries.name: India
countries.tagline: A tropical wine country that prunes twice a year and harvests in the dry winter, led by the Deccan plateau around Nashik.

stats.note: OIV (May 2026): India's total vineyard is about 197 kha, the seventh largest in the world and growing about 4.6 percent a year since 2019, but almost all of it is table grapes and raisins; wine grapes cover only a few thousand hectares.

countries.overview:
India has one of the world's largest and fastest-growing vineyards, but almost all of it grows table grapes and raisins; wine is a tiny, young industry, about two percent of an alcohol market dominated by whisky and beer. Its story is the story of Maharashtra, and especially of Nashik, a pilgrimage city on the Deccan plateau 180 km north-east of Mumbai that now calls itself India's wine capital.

Grapes reached India from Persia in antiquity, and Chanakya's writings in the fourth century BC mention a grape wine called madhu. The Mughals were officially abstinent but some emperors (Babur, Jahangir) loved wine; the Portuguese brought fortified wine to Goa; and under the British, Kashmir and Baramati had vineyards until phylloxera arrived in the 1890s. After independence, prohibition sentiment and policy pushed growers toward table grapes. The modern revival came in the 1980s and 1990s: Chateau Indage at Narayangaon near Pune, with help from Champagne, launched the sparkling Omar Khayyam in the mid-1980s; Kanwal Grover planted French varieties at Nandi Hills near Bangalore in 1988; and Rajeev Samant, back from Silicon Valley, founded Sula Vineyards at Nashik in 1999. Maharashtra's 2001 grape-processing policy cut taxes and licensing hurdles, and dozens of wineries opened.

Viticulture here inverts the usual calendar. Without a cold winter, vines never go dormant. Growers 'back-prune' in April, after harvest, to build canes through the monsoon, then 'forward-prune' in October so the fruit ripens in the dry, sunny winter and is picked from January to March, before the heat. In the far south, vines can crop twice a year. Altitude helps: Nashik's vineyards sit at about 600 m, Nandi Hills at about 900 m. Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel lead, alongside Tempranillo, Viognier and Sangiovese.

Today Sula, a listed company since 2022, sells more than half of India's wine and turned its estate into a tourist destination with an annual festival, SulaFest. Grover Zampa, Fratelli (Akluj, with Italian partners), York and Vallonné make serious wines; Karnataka's Nandi Hills and Bijapur (Vijayapura) are the second centre. 'Nashik Valley Wine' was registered as an Indian Geographical Indication in 2010-11, India's only wine GI.

history.title: Madhu in Chanakya's Arthashastra
history.text: The first known reference to grape wine in India appears in writings attributed to Chanakya, minister to the Mauryan emperor Chandragupta, who describes a grape wine called madhu.

history.title: Chateau Indage and Omar Khayyam
history.text: Shamrao Chougule's Chateau Indage at Narayangaon, near Pune, made India's first modern sparkling wine, Omar Khayyam, with technical help from Champagne. The company later collapsed, but it started the modern industry.

history.title: Grover at Nandi Hills
history.text: Kanwal Grover planted French varieties at Nandi Hills near Bangalore with advice from French consultants; Michel Rolland later advised the estate, which merged with Vallée de Vin (Zampa) in 2012 to form Grover Zampa.

history.title: Sula Vineyards
history.text: Rajeev Samant founded Sula Vineyards near Nashik with Californian winemaker Kerry Damskey, introducing Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc and Zinfandel. Sula became India's largest wine company.

history.title: Maharashtra wine policy
history.text: Maharashtra's grape-processing industry policy reduced excise and licensing barriers for wineries using local grapes, setting off a wave of new wineries around Nashik, Pune and Sangli.

history.title: Nashik Valley Wine GI
history.text: 'Nashik Valley Wine' was registered as a Geographical Indication under India's GI Act, the country's only wine GI.

countries.classification: India's Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, allows registration of product names; 'Nashik Valley Wine' (registered in the 2010-11 year) is the only wine GI. There is no national appellation system with variety or yield rules. Alcohol policy is set state by state, and taxes and distribution rules vary widely, which shapes where wineries locate (Maharashtra and Karnataka offer incentives for local wine).
countries.climate_soils: India's wine regions are tropical or subtropical, between about 13 and 20 degrees north. The monsoon brings most of the year's rain between June and September, so growers time the fruiting season for the dry winter. The Deccan plateau's basalt-derived soils (black cotton soils and red murrum) dominate in Maharashtra and northern Karnataka; Nandi Hills has red lateritic soils on granite. Altitude (about 600 m at Nashik and 900 m at Nandi Hills) keeps night temperatures down.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.note: Sula's first success and still a mainstay of fresh, off-dry whites.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Crisp, tropical-fruited whites from Nashik.

grapes.name: Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The main reds, often blended; Grover Zampa's La Réserve is Cabernet-Shiraz.

grapes.name: Tempranillo, Sangiovese, Zinfandel, Viognier
grapes.note: Varieties suited to heat that several producers have pioneered.

grapes.name: Thompson Seedless
grapes.note: The dominant table and raisin grape, which accounts for most of India's 197,000 ha.

Sommelier India magazine

countries.name: Thailand
countries.tagline: A 'new latitude' wine country where vines crop twice a year and some are harvested by boat.

stats.note: No OIV wine-production figure; Thailand has perhaps a dozen commercial wineries.

countries.overview:
Thailand lies between about 6 and 20 degrees north, far outside the textbook wine belt, yet since the 1990s a handful of wineries have made it the best known of Asia's tropical 'new latitude' wine producers. Grapes first came as a gift: the French embassy of Louis XIV presented King Narai with White Malaga vines in the 1680s. For three centuries they were table fruit.

Two areas lead. Khao Yai, in the hills of Nakhon Ratchasima province about 150 km north-east of Bangkok at 300 to 400 m, is home to GranMonte (founded by Visooth Lohitnavy, whose daughter Nikki trained in Adelaide and became Thailand's first female oenologist) and PB Valley. Hua Hin, on the Gulf coast, is home to Siam Winery's Hua Hin Hills Vineyard, which produces the Monsoon Valley brand and has elephant rides among the vines. Siam Winery, founded in 1986 by Chalerm Yoovidhya of the Red Bull family, also grows grapes in the 'floating vineyards' of the Chao Phraya delta west of Bangkok, raised beds between canals tended and harvested by boat.

Without winter dormancy, vines can be pruned to fruit twice a year. The quality crop ripens in the dry, relatively cool season from December to March; the rainy-season crop is weaker. Chenin Blanc, Shiraz, Colombard and the local Pok Dum grape are the mainstays.

history.title: King Narai's grapes
history.text: The French embassy of Louis XIV presented King Narai of Ayutthaya with White Malaga vines; the grapes were grown as fruit.

history.title: Siam Winery
history.text: Chalerm Yoovidhya founded Siam Winery, later known for the Monsoon Valley brand and its floating vineyards in the Chao Phraya delta.

history.title: Khao Yai estates
history.text: GranMonte and PB Valley built wineries in the hills of Khao Yai, which became Thailand's main fine-wine area and a weekend destination from Bangkok.

countries.classification: No appellation system; Thai wines use brand and estate names. Khao Yai producers have promoted a regional identity informally.
countries.climate_soils: Tropical monsoon climate with a dry season from about November to April; vines are pruned to ripen in it. Khao Yai's elevation of 300 to 400 m and cooler nights help; soils are mostly sandy loam over clay.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.note: The leading white, fresh and fruity.

grapes.name: Shiraz
grapes.note: The main red at Khao Yai and Hua Hin.

grapes.name: Colombard
grapes.note: A heat-tolerant white used by Siam Winery.

grapes.name: Pok Dum
grapes.note: A local black grape, a table variety also made into wine.

further_reading: Asian Wine Review
GranMonte and Siam Winery websites

sources.title: Wikipedia, Thai wine

countries.name: Indonesia
countries.tagline: Bali's north-coast vineyards, eight degrees south of the equator, harvested several times a year.

stats.note: No OIV figure; a few wineries, centred on Bali.

countries.overview:
Indonesia's wine is almost entirely Balinese. In 1994 Ida Bagus Rai Budarsa, whose family made traditional rice and palm drinks, founded Hatten Wines in Sanur and began buying grapes from growers around Singaraja on Bali's dry north coast, an area with a long history of table-grape growing. With no winter, vines there are pruned to produce two or three crops a year, so harvests can happen in almost any month.

Hatten's first wine was a rosé from Alphonse Lavallée (locally called Belgia), still its best-known wine, followed by whites from Muscat Saint-Vallier and the local Probolinggo Biru, and a traditional-method sparkling wine, Tunjung. Sababay Winery, founded in 2010 in Gianyar, works with cooperatives of northern farmers. Other Balinese brands use imported grape juice, so Indonesian labels are worth reading closely. Wine is made mostly for Bali's tourist trade; in a majority-Muslim country, alcohol taxes are very high.

history.title: Hatten Wines
history.text: Ida Bagus Rai Budarsa founded Hatten Wines, Indonesia's first modern winery, using grapes from Bali's north coast.

history.title: Sababay
history.text: Sababay Winery opened in Gianyar, sourcing grapes from cooperatives of north Bali farmers.

countries.climate_soils: Tropical, with a dry season from about April to October on Bali's north coast, which lies in the rain shadow of the central volcanoes; volcanic soils near sea level.

grapes.name: Alphonse Lavallée (Belgia)
grapes.note: A black table grape used for rosé and red.

grapes.name: Muscat Saint-Vallier
grapes.note: A hybrid used for aromatic whites.

grapes.name: Probolinggo Biru
grapes.note: A local Javanese grape.

further_reading: Asian Wine Review
