countries.name: Vietnam
countries.tagline: French colonial vines, highland Da Lat wine and triple-cropping grapes on the hot coast of Ninh Thuận.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 794 ha of grapes in 2024, mostly table grapes around Phan Rang (Ninh Thuận); no OIV wine figure

countries.overview:
French colonists tried vines near Hanoi in the late nineteenth century, but the humid north defeated them and local winemaking turned to fruit wines. Today two areas matter. Ninh Thuận, around Phan Rang on the dry south-central coast, is Vietnam's grape province: its hot, sunny climate lets growers harvest up to three crops a year, mostly Cardinal table grapes and some wine varieties, and the province's first commercial winery operated here. Da Lat, in the Central Highlands at about 1,500 m, gave its name to Vang Đà Lạt (Dalat Wine), Vietnam's most familiar wine brand since 1999, made from grapes and mulberries grown in Lâm Đồng and Ninh Thuận.

In the 1990s Australian winemakers and foreign joint ventures planted international varieties, some on land cleared of wartime mines. Production remains small and mostly for the domestic and tourist markets.

history.title: French plantings
history.text: French colonists planted vines in the Ba Vì area near Hanoi, but the humid climate made vinifera difficult.

history.title: Vang Đà Lạt
history.text: Lâm Đồng's Ladofoods launched Vang Đà Lạt, which became Vietnam's best-known wine brand.

countries.climate_soils: Tropical; Ninh Thuận is one of the driest places in Vietnam, while Da Lat is cool and wet in summer.

grapes.name: Cardinal
grapes.note: The main table grape of Ninh Thuận, also made into wine.

grapes.name: Chambourcin
grapes.note: A disease-resistant hybrid planted for wine.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Vietnamese wine

countries.name: Myanmar
countries.tagline: Two hillside estates in Shan State, above Inle Lake and Taunggyi.

stats.note: Two main wineries; no official statistics.

countries.overview:
Myanmar's wine comes from two estates in the Shan Hills, where altitude tempers the tropical climate. Aythaya Vineyard, near Taunggyi at about 1,300 m, was founded in 1999 by German businessman Bert Morsbach, who imported European vines and made the first vintages in the mid-2000s. Red Mountain Estate, on the hills above Nyaungshwe at the edge of Inle Lake, was planted in the early 2000s and became a stop for tourists visiting the lake. Both grow international varieties, including Shiraz and Sauvignon Blanc. Tourism collapsed after the 2021 coup, and the wineries' fortunes have tracked the country's turmoil.

Both estates face the same tropical constraints: the monsoon brings heavy rain from May to October, so vines are pruned to ripen their main crop in the dry, sunny winter months, when cool nights at altitude help retain acidity. The wines were sold largely to hotels and visitors in Yangon, Bagan and Inle; with international tourism sharply reduced since 2021, both have depended on domestic buyers. Their story is an example of 'new latitude' winemaking, alongside Thailand's and Vietnam's highland vineyards.

history.title: Aythaya
history.text: Bert Morsbach founded Aythaya Vineyard near Taunggyi, Myanmar's first modern winery.

history.title: Red Mountain Estate
history.text: Red Mountain Estate was planted above Inle Lake, becoming a popular tourist winery.

countries.climate_soils: Tropical highland climate at 900 to 1,300 m, with a monsoon from May to October and a dry winter.

grapes.name: Shiraz
grapes.note: The main red at both estates.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Among the whites.

sources.title: Aythaya Wine

countries.name: South Korea
countries.tagline: Campbell Early and wild meoru grapes in the 'wine county' of Yeongdong.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 14,706 ha of grapes in 2023, mostly table and juice grapes such as Campbell Early; wine production is small, mostly from American and native grapes

countries.overview:
Korea's traditional drinks are rice-based, but grapes grow widely, and a small wine industry uses mostly Campbell Early, an American table grape, plus Muscat Bailey A and the native wild grape meoru (Vitis coignetiae). Majuang, launched by Oriental Brewing in 1977, was the first well-known Korean grape wine. Today the centre is Yeongdong County in North Chungcheong, which promotes itself as Korea's wine county, with dozens of small farm wineries and the company Wine Korea; the island of Daebudo, near Ansan, is another Campbell Early area. Monsoon summers and cold winters make vinifera difficult.

Korean winemakers face a short, wet summer monsoon and cold winters, so most vineyards use hardy American or hybrid grapes rather than vinifera. Campbell Early and meoru give sweet or off-dry wines with a grapey, foxy character, and producers also make wines from fruits such as Korean black raspberry (bokbunja). Yeongdong's farm wineries and grape festival draw visitors, and a small number of growers are experimenting with Muscat Bailey A and cold-hardy hybrids. Most wine drunk in Korea is imported.

history.title: Majuang
history.text: Oriental Brewing launched Majuang, the first widely sold Korean grape wine.

history.title: Yeongdong farm wineries
history.text: Yeongdong County supported grape growers to open small farm wineries, becoming the centre of Korean wine.

countries.climate_soils: Continental monsoon climate: hot, wet summers and cold winters.

grapes.name: Campbell Early
grapes.note: The dominant grape, American in origin, used for table and wine.

grapes.name: Meoru (Vitis coignetiae)
grapes.note: Native wild grape used for distinctive dark wines.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Korean wine

countries.name: Taiwan
countries.tagline: A former state monopoly turned farm-winery scene, built on Black Queen and Golden Muscat.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official figure: 2,308 ha of grapes in 2023, almost all table grapes; small wine production and no official wine statistics

countries.overview:
For decades all Taiwanese wine was made by the state Taiwan Tobacco and Liquor Corporation. Liberalisation allowed private winemaking from 2002, and grape farmers in Houli (Taichung) and Erlin (Changhua) opened small wineries using the grapes they had grown under contract: Black Queen and Golden Muscat, Japanese-bred varieties introduced in the 1950s. Taiwan's warm climate lets vines crop twice a year. In 2014 a Taiwanese wine won its first gold medal at an international competition, and Taichung wineries such as Shu Sheng have since won awards abroad.

Taiwan's farm wineries mostly make sweet and off-dry wines from Golden Muscat and fresh, high-acid reds from Black Queen, and some produce fortified and sparkling styles. Growers manage the subtropical climate with practices such as bagging bunches and pruning for a winter crop that ripens in drier weather. The Houli and Erlin areas also host wine-tourism routes and harvest festivals, and local wineries have won medals at competitions in Europe and Asia.

history.title: Black Queen and Golden Muscat
history.text: Japanese-bred grapes were introduced to supply the state monopoly's wine production.

history.title: End of the monopoly
history.text: Private winemaking became legal, and grape farmers began making their own wine.

countries.climate_soils: Subtropical, humid and typhoon-prone; vines are pruned for two crops a year.

grapes.name: Black Queen
grapes.note: A dark, high-acid red bred by Kawakami Zenbei in Japan.

grapes.name: Golden Muscat
grapes.note: Aromatic white used for still and sweet wines.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Taiwanese wine

countries.name: Cambodia
countries.tagline: One family winery near Battambang, below the hilltop temple of Phnom Banan.
countries.overview:
Cambodia's only notable winery, Prasat Phnom Banan, was started by Chan Thai Chhoeung near Battambang in the north-west in the 2000s. It grows Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon along with table grapes and makes red wine, brandy and grape juice, sold mainly to visitors who come to see the Angkorian temple of Phnom Banan nearby. The tropical climate allows more than one crop a year.

The winery's vines are pruned to fruit in the dry season, and its wines are sweet or off-dry reds with a rustic style. Battambang province, Cambodia's rice bowl, has a long history of fruit growing, and grape vines are also grown for the table. Visitors combine the winery with the nearby temple of Phnom Banan, an eleventh-century Angkorian sanctuary on a hilltop. Cambodia otherwise imports nearly all of its wine.

history.title: Prasat Phnom Banan winery
history.text: Chan Thai Chhoeung planted vines near Battambang and opened Cambodia's first winery.

countries.climate_soils: Tropical monsoon climate with a dry season from November to April.

grapes.name: Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The main wine grapes.

countries.name: Namibia
countries.tagline: A few desert-edge wineries in a country better known for its Orange River table grapes.

stats.note: A handful of small wineries; most Namibian grapes are table grapes for export.

countries.overview: Namibia is one of the driest countries on earth and lies largely north of the traditional wine belt, but a few people have made wine there for over a century. German Catholic priests planted vines in Klein Windhoek in the 1890s, making white wine and a schnapps called 'Katholischer' until the 1960s. After independence in 1990, Helmuth Kluge started Kristall Kellerei at Omaruru, growing Colombard and Ruby Cabernet (it now focuses on brandy and fruit wines). In the 1990s Allen Walkden-Davis planted Shiraz at Neuras, a spring-fed oasis near Maltahöhe at the edge of the Namib-Naukluft, which may be the driest vineyard in the world; Thonningii in the Otavi Mountains and Erongo Mountain Winery followed. Large irrigated table-grape farms along the Orange River at Aussenkehr export to Europe.

history.title: Klein Windhoek mission vines
history.text: German Catholic priests planted the first vineyards in Klein Windhoek; production stopped in the late 1960s.

history.title: Kristall Kellerei
history.text: Helmuth Kluge began making wine at Omaruru in the year of independence.

history.title: Neuras
history.text: Allen Walkden-Davis planted Shiraz at the Neuras oasis near Maltahöhe, on the edge of the Namib.

countries.climate_soils: Arid, sunny and hot with cold nights; irrigation from springs and boreholes; vineyards between about 900 and 1,500 m.

grapes.name: Shiraz
grapes.note: The main red at Neuras and Thonningii.

grapes.name: Colombard and Ruby Cabernet
grapes.note: Kristall Kellerei's original grapes.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Namibian wine

countries.name: Zimbabwe
countries.tagline: An industry born of sanctions in the 1960s and shrunk by economic crisis since 2000.

stats.note: Small production; no recent official figures.

countries.overview:
Zimbabwe's wine industry grew after Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence in 1965, when international sanctions cut off imports and local farmers planted vines on the highveld east of Harare. Vineyards around Marondera, Mutare and Odzi supplied a few wineries, of which Mukuyu (Marondera) and Stapleford (part of African Distillers) became the best known, making mostly simple white and fortified wines. Land reform from 2000 and hyperinflation devastated the sector, and output today is small. Summer rainfall and humidity are the main viticultural challenges; altitude (about 1,500 m) keeps nights cool.

Most of Zimbabwe's vineyards are at about 1,500 m, where altitude moderates summer heat but summer rain and humidity bring disease pressure. Wines have mostly been white and sweet or off-dry, with some fortified wine. Vineyards were also planted around Odzi, near Mutare in the eastern highlands. With South African influence and occasional investment, a small number of producers remain active, and imported South African wine dominates the market.

history.title: Sanctions vineyards
history.text: With imports cut off after UDI, Rhodesian farmers planted vines on the highveld and local wineries were built.

history.title: Collapse
history.text: Land reform and hyperinflation sharply reduced the wine industry.

countries.climate_soils: Highveld at about 1,500 m; summer rainfall climate with wet ripening seasons.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc, Colombard, Pinotage
grapes.note: Varieties drawn from South African nurseries.

countries.name: Ethiopia
countries.tagline: Aksumite vines, honey wine and a French-owned estate in the Rift Valley that harvests twice a year.

stats.note: Two main wineries: Awash and Castel's Rift Valley estate.

countries.overview: Ethiopia has an ancient taste for fermented drinks: tej, a honey wine flavoured with gesho leaves, is the national drink, and inscriptions and carvings from the kingdom of Aksum (third and fourth centuries AD) suggest grape wine was known there. Modern grape wine began with the Awash Winery in Addis Ababa, founded in 1956 and long the country's main producer. In the 2000s the French Castel group, invited by the government, planted vineyards in the Central Rift Valley near Ziway (Batu), about 160 km south of the capital at about 1,600 m, and launched its Rift Valley wines in 2014. Near the equator vines do not go dormant, so two harvests a year are possible; the dry season provides the better one.

history.title: Aksumite wine
history.text: Inscriptions of King Ezana and carvings on Aksum's obelisks have been read as evidence of viticulture in the Aksumite kingdom.

history.title: Awash Winery
history.text: Awash Winery was founded in Addis Ababa and became Ethiopia's main wine producer.

history.title: Castel's Rift Valley wines
history.text: Castel's estate near Ziway released its first Rift Valley wines, sold locally and exported, notably to China.

countries.climate_soils: Highland tropical climate; the Rift Valley floor near Ziway has about 650 mm of rain, sandy volcanic soils and average temperatures around 25 degrees C.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
grapes.note: Castel's main reds.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Grown at Ziway.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Ethiopian wine

countries.name: Kenya
countries.tagline: Equatorial vineyards on the shores of Lake Naivasha, high in the Rift Valley.
countries.overview:
Kenya's grape wine is a recent, small-scale story centred on Lake Naivasha in the Rift Valley, about 90 km north-west of Nairobi at about 1,900 m. Altitude moderates the equatorial heat, and the region's horticulture and flower farms supply irrigation know-how. Rift Valley Winery's Leleshwa wines, from vineyards near the lake, are the best known; Kenyans otherwise drink imported wine and locally made fruit wines (the state-founded Kenya Wine Agencies long made papaya-based wine). As on the equator elsewhere, vines can be managed for two crops a year.

Kenya's wine is a niche: high excise and import duties shape the market, and most wine drunk in Kenya is imported from South Africa. The Naivasha vineyards benefit from altitude and Rift Valley sunshine, and are managed for two harvests a year, with the dry-season crop giving the better wine. Kenya Wine Agencies Limited, set up in the 1960s, long made fruit wines, including papaya-based wine, for the domestic market.

history.title: Leleshwa
history.text: Rift Valley Winery began producing Leleshwa wines from vineyards near Lake Naivasha.

history.title: Kenya Wine Agencies
history.text: Kenya Wine Agencies Limited was set up in the 1960s to import and distribute wine and later made fruit wines, including papaya-based wine, for the local market.

countries.climate_soils: Equatorial highland climate at about 1,900 m; volcanic soils.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: International varieties grown near Naivasha.

countries.name: Tanzania
countries.tagline: Semi-arid Dodoma, where missionaries' vines became an industry with two harvests a year.

stats.note: Production concentrated in Dodoma region; no OIV figure.

countries.overview:
Tanzania's wine industry is concentrated around Dodoma, the inland capital, on a semi-arid plateau at about 1,100 m. Catholic missionaries brought vines: Holy Ghost Fathers planted at the Hombolo mission in 1938, and in 1957 Father Irioneo Maggioni at Bihawana began a commercial vineyard from a few cuttings. After independence the government invested in grape growing (a prison farm and the national service camp at Makutupora), founded the Dodoma Wine Company in 1979 and set up the Makutupora Grapevine Research Centre. Distell of South Africa later took over the Dodoma Wine brand through Tanzania Distilleries, and in 2002 an Italian engineer founded the Central Tanzania Wine Company (CETAWICO).

Dodoma's long dry season and warm climate let growers prune for two harvests a year, the main one in the dry season. Chenin Blanc, Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon grow alongside the local Makutupora grape. Tanzania is one of sub-Saharan Africa's larger producers outside South Africa, though output is modest.

history.title: Hombolo mission vines
history.text: Holy Ghost Fathers planted vines at the Hombolo Catholic mission near Dodoma for altar wine.

history.title: Father Maggioni
history.text: Passionist Father Irioneo Maggioni of the Bihawana mission started a commercial vineyard.

history.title: Dodoma Wine Company
history.text: The government founded the Dodoma Wine Company to buy grapes from farmers, with a research centre at Makutupora.

history.title: CETAWICO
history.text: The Central Tanzania Wine Company was founded by an Italian engineer in Dodoma.

countries.climate_soils: Semi-arid plateau (about 550 mm of rain, falling from December to April), warm all year; sandy loams; two harvests possible.

grapes.name: Makutupora
grapes.note: A local grape named after a Dodoma sub-area.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The main international varieties.

countries.name: Madagascar
countries.tagline: Highland vineyards in Betsileo country, planted from colonial-era hybrids.
countries.overview:
Madagascar's wine comes from the central highlands around Fianarantsoa and Ambalavao, in Betsileo country at 1,000 to 1,300 m, where French missionaries and colonists planted vines in the early twentieth century. Most plantings are hybrid varieties chosen for disease resistance in the humid summer, and the wines are mostly sold locally. Producers include the Lazan'i Betsileo cooperative in Fianarantsoa and small estates near Ambalavao such as Clos Nomena and Domaine de Manamisoa. Rain falls in the hot season, so growers rely on altitude and hardy hybrids rather than vinifera.

Wine in Madagascar is mostly consumed locally and made from hybrids such as Couderc, Villard Blanc and Petit Bouschet, chosen for disease resistance. The highland climate, at around 1,000 to 1,300 m, keeps temperatures moderate but brings rain in the hot season, so harvest timing is critical. Tourists travelling the RN7 highland road through Fianarantsoa and Ambalavao are an important market.

history.title: Colonial vines
history.text: French missionaries and colonists planted vineyards in the Betsileo highlands.

history.title: Lazan'i Betsileo
history.text: Local producers around Fianarantsoa organised production, and Lazan'i Betsileo became the best-known brand.

countries.climate_soils: Tropical highland climate with a wet summer; red lateritic soils.

grapes.name: Hybrids (Couderc, Villard Blanc, Petit Bouschet)
grapes.note: Disease-resistant varieties dominate.

regions.name: South Australia
regions.tagline: Half of Australia's wine and nearly all of its oldest vines, protected by a border the phylloxera louse never crossed.
regions.summary:
South Australia crushes roughly half of the national harvest and owns most of its famous names: Barossa Valley, Eden Valley, Clare Valley, McLaren Vale, Adelaide Hills, Coonawarra and the Riverland. It is also Australia's wine capital in an institutional sense, home to Wine Australia, the Australian Wine Research Institute, the University of Adelaide's Waite campus and Roseworthy, where generations of winemakers trained.

What makes the state unique is its quarantine. South Australia never had phylloxera, and strict controls on moving vines, machinery and even grapes across its borders mean that ungrafted vines planted in the 1840s still crop. Those old vineyards, concentrated in the Barossa, McLaren Vale and Langhorne Creek, are the backbone of its fine-wine reputation.
regions.history: Colonised as a free settlement in 1836, South Australia attracted religious dissenters, including the Silesian Lutherans who farmed the Barossa from 1842, and English and Scottish gentlemen such as John Reynell (McLaren Vale, 1838), Dr Christopher Penfold (Magill, 1844), Samuel Smith (Yalumba, 1849) and Joseph Seppelt (1851). The state became the centre of the fortified-wine industry in the late nineteenth century and, after the Second World War, of the table-wine revival led by Penfolds, Hardys, Orlando and Lindemans. Its GI hierarchy groups regions into zones: Barossa, Mount Lofty Ranges, Fleurieu, Limestone Coast, Lower Murray, Far North and The Peninsulas, with the 'Adelaide' super zone wrapping the first three.
regions.terroir: Climates range from the hot, irrigated Riverland (about 2,350 growing degree days and 148 mm of growing-season rain) to the cool, maritime Limestone Coast and the elevated Adelaide Hills and Eden Valley. Gulf St Vincent moderates McLaren Vale and Adelaide; Lake Alexandrina's 'Lake Doctor' breeze cools Langhorne Creek. Soils run from terra rossa over limestone in the south-east to sand, ironstone, schist and ancient quartzite in the Mount Lofty Ranges.
regions.grapes: Shiraz above all, then Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Chardonnay, Riesling and Mourvèdre; Mediterranean varieties such as Fiano, Vermentino, Nero d'Avola and Montepulciano are spreading fastest in McLaren Vale and the Riverland.
regions.styles: Full-bodied Shiraz and Cabernet, old-vine Grenache and GSM blends, bone-dry Riesling, cool-climate Chardonnay and sparkling from the Adelaide Hills, and historic fortifieds (Seppeltsfield's Tawny, Barossa 'Apera').
regions.classification: Zones: Barossa, Mount Lofty Ranges, Fleurieu, Limestone Coast, Lower Murray, Far North, The Peninsulas (plus the Adelaide super zone). Subregions: High Eden, Lenswood, Piccadilly Valley. Informal: the Barossa Grounds and the Barossa Old Vine Charter, McLaren Vale's district maps, Clare's Polish Hill River and Watervale.

regions.name: Victoria
regions.tagline: The gold-rush colony that phylloxera humbled, now the most varied wine state in Australia, from Rutherglen Muscat to Macedon sparkling.
regions.summary:
Victoria has more wine regions than any other state (21) and the widest stylistic range: thick, ancient Rutherglen Muscat, peppery Heathcote and Grampians Shiraz, Yarra Valley Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, Mornington Peninsula Pinot, Macedon Ranges sparkling, King Valley Prosecco, Beechworth's Giaconda Chardonnay and the irrigated volume of the Murray Darling.

In the 1880s Victoria was briefly Australia's largest producer and its wines took medals in Paris and Bordeaux. Phylloxera, found near Geelong in 1877, and the economic depression of the 1890s ended that boom. The modern revival is a story of individuals: doctors, engineers and refugees from city careers who replanted the Yarra, Mornington, Geelong and Macedon from the 1960s onwards.
regions.history: Swiss settlers led by Paul and Hubert de Castella and Guillaume de Pury planted the Yarra Valley from the 1840s to 1860s; Henry and Joseph Best planted Great Western in the 1860s; Rutherglen boomed on gold-rush money from 1858; Tahbilk was founded in 1860. Phylloxera spread from Geelong through Bendigo to the north-east, and by the 1920s Victorian table wine had nearly vanished, leaving fortifieds in Rutherglen and Glenrowan. Revivals came with Brown Brothers (Milawa), Balgownie (Bendigo, 1969), Yarra Yering (1969), Mount Mary (1971) and Domaine Chandon's arrival in 1986.
regions.terroir: Bass Strait and Port Phillip Bay cool the southern regions; the Great Dividing Range lifts the Macedon Ranges, Strathbogie Ranges, Upper Goulburn and Alpine Valleys above 500 m. North of the Divide, heat builds toward Rutherglen and the Murray. Soils are diverse: Cambrian greenstone at Heathcote, granite at Beechworth and Strathbogie, volcanic red earths in parts of the Yarra and Mornington, sandy loams at Tahbilk that kept phylloxera at bay.
regions.grapes: Shiraz, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris; Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge and Muscadelle in Rutherglen; Marsanne at Tahbilk; Italian varieties in the King Valley.
regions.styles: Fortified Muscat and Topaque, cool-climate Pinot and Chardonnay, sparkling (including the historic sparkling Shiraz of Great Western), peppery Shiraz, Prosecco.
regions.classification: Zones: Port Phillip, Central Victoria, North East Victoria, North West Victoria, Western Victoria and Gippsland (Gippsland has no registered regions). Subregions: Great Western (Grampians) and Nagambie Lakes (Goulburn Valley). Rutherglen Muscat has its own four-tier classification.

Wine Australia Open Data Hub, Wine Geographical Indications Australia (feature service with registration year, vine area, climate and crush 2020-2026)

regions.name: New South Wales
regions.tagline: Where Australian wine began, and where the Hunter still makes the country's most singular white.
regions.summary: New South Wales holds the first vineyards of the colony and the second-largest crush, thanks to the irrigated Riverina around Griffith. Its fine-wine centre is the Hunter Valley, three hours north of Sydney, whose Semillon and medium-bodied Shiraz are unlike anything else in Australia. Up on the tablelands and western slopes of the Great Dividing Range, Orange, Mudgee, Hilltops, Tumbarumba and the Canberra District offer cooler, higher sites.
regions.history: From Farm Cove (1788) and Camden Park (1820s) the industry moved to the Hunter, where James Busby's Kirkton estate, George Wyndham's Dalwood (1828), Henry Lindeman's Cavendish (1843) and the Tyrrells (1858) planted. Maurice O'Shea's work at Mount Pleasant from the 1920s to 1956 set the Hunter's style. The Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, opened in 1912, created the Riverina, where Italian families and the McWilliam, De Bortoli and Casella companies built volume brands such as [yellow tail].
regions.terroir: The Hunter is subtropical, hot and humid, with summer rain and cloud cover that temper the heat. The Central Ranges and Southern New South Wales regions climb to 600 to 1,400 m on basalt and granite; Orange's GI only covers land above 600 m. The Riverina is flat, hot and irrigated from the Murrumbidgee.
regions.grapes: Semillon, Shiraz and Chardonnay in the Hunter; Shiraz, Cabernet, Chardonnay and Riesling in the ranges; Semillon (including botrytised), Shiraz, Chardonnay and Durif in the Riverina.
regions.styles: Early-picked, long-lived Hunter Semillon; earthy Hunter Shiraz; Canberra Shiraz-Viognier; cool-climate Chardonnay and sparkling base from Tumbarumba and Orange; botrytis Semillon from the Riverina.
regions.classification: Zones: Hunter Valley, Central Ranges, Southern New South Wales, Big Rivers, South Coast, Northern Rivers, Northern Slopes and Western Plains. Subregions: Pokolbin, Broke Fordwich and Upper Hunter Valley (all within the Hunter region).

regions.name: Western Australia
regions.tagline: Small in volume, huge in reputation: Margaret River Cabernet and Chardonnay, and the cool granite country of the Great Southern.
regions.summary: Western Australia makes only around 3 to 4 percent of Australia's wine but a far larger share of its fine wine. Margaret River, planted on the advice of a scientist in the late 1960s, is one of the world's great places for Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay. Further south and east, the Great Southern is a vast, thinly planted region of granite hills and karri forest whose Riesling, Shiraz and Cabernet are cool, precise and underpriced.
regions.history: Vines arrived with Perth's first settlers in 1829; Olive Farm (1830), Houghton (1836) and Sandalford (1840) on the Swan River made the colony's wine for more than a century, including Jack Mann's Houghton White Burgundy (1937). The south-west was opened by research: Harold Olmo's 1956 report on the Great Southern and John Gladstones' 1965 paper on Margaret River, after which doctors and farmers planted Forest Hill (1966), Vasse Felix (1967), Plantagenet (1968), Moss Wood (1969), Cullen and Cape Mentelle (early 1970s) and Leeuwin (1974).
regions.terroir: A Mediterranean climate with a strong maritime influence: Margaret River is surrounded by ocean on three sides, with almost no frost and very little summer rain (about 210 mm October to April). The Great Southern is cooler (about 1,735 growing degree days) and continental at Frankland River, maritime at Albany and Denmark. Soils are ancient: lateritic gravels over granite and gneiss in Margaret River, granite-derived loams around the Porongurup Range.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Shiraz, Riesling, Merlot, Chenin Blanc (Swan Valley) and Verdelho.
regions.styles: Structured Cabernet and Bordeaux blends, mineral Chardonnay, Semillon-Sauvignon Blanc blends, peppery Great Southern Shiraz, dry Riesling; fortified Verdelho and 'Liqueur' wines in the Swan Valley.
regions.classification: Zones: Greater Perth, South West Australia, Central Western Australia, West Australian South East Coastal and Eastern Plains, Inland and North of Western Australia. Subregions: Swan Valley, and Albany, Denmark, Frankland River, Mount Barker and Porongurup in the Great Southern. Margaret River's six 'Gladstones' subregions (Yallingup, Carbunup, Wilyabrup, Treeton, Wallcliffe, Karridale) are informal.
appellations: Eastern Plains, Inland and North of Western Australia

regions.name: Tasmania
regions.tagline: One GI, seven valleys and Australia's coolest climate: the island that became the country's sparkling and Pinot Noir engine.
regions.summary:
Tasmania is a single GI (it is simultaneously a state, zone and region) with about 1,700 hectares of vines, under 1 percent of Australian wine by volume but a much larger share by value. With fewer than 800 growing degree days on Wine Australia's measure, it is the coolest place in Australia to ripen grapes, and its traditional-method sparkling wine (Jansz, Arras, Clover Hill, House of Arras) and Pinot Noir are the most sought after in the country. Big mainland companies buy Tasmanian fruit for their best fizz.

Wine Tasmania promotes seven informal areas: Tamar Valley, Pipers River, North West, East Coast, Coal River Valley, Derwent Valley and Huon Valley/D'Entrecasteaux Channel. None is a registered GI, but the differences between them (Pipers River's maritime cool, the warm, dry rain shadow of the Coal River and East Coast) are real.
regions.history: Tasmanian cuttings helped found Victoria's and South Australia's vineyards in the 1830s, but the island's own industry faded by the 1860s. The revival began with Jean Miguet's La Provence (1956, now Providence) near Launceston and Claudio Alcorso's Moorilla (1958) on the Derwent. Andrew Pirie's Pipers Brook (1974) proved the north-east; Louis Roederer's partnership at Jansz (1985) and Ed Carr's House of Arras made the island famous for sparkling.
regions.terroir: Cool, maritime and windy, with long autumns. The north (Tamar and Pipers River) is wetter; the south-east (Coal River and Derwent valleys) and East Coast lie in a rain shadow and are among the driest parts of the state. Soils include basalt-derived red earths at Pipers River, dolerite and sandstone in the south, and alluvial gravels.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir (about half the vineyard), Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris and Riesling.
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (often long lees-aged), Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling.
regions.classification: Single GI 'Tasmania' (registered 1994 on Wine Australia's data). Informal sub-areas are used on labels as place names only where they are not misleading.

regions.name: Queensland
regions.tagline: A tropical state whose wine lives up on the granite, a kilometre above sea level.
regions.summary: Queensland's wine is concentrated in the Granite Belt around Stanthorpe, on the New South Wales border, where altitudes of 600 to 1,300 m give one of the coolest climates in mainland Australia despite a latitude of 28 to 29 degrees south. The South Burnett, north-west of Brisbane, is the other registered region. The state's GI 'Queensland' also functions as a zone.
regions.history: Italian immigrants planted table grapes and some wine grapes around Ballandean in the 1920s and 1930s; Ballandean Estate traces its vines to 1932. A boutique industry grew from the 1960s and 1970s, and the Granite Belt's 'Strange Birds' trail now promotes uncommon varieties.
regions.terroir: Granite-derived sandy soils, frost risk in spring and summer rain from the subtropics.
regions.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Verdelho, Semillon and many alternative varieties (Fiano, Vermentino, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Saperavi).
regions.styles: Medium-bodied reds and fresh whites.
regions.classification: Zone/State GI Queensland; regions Granite Belt and South Burnett.

Wine Australia Open Data Hub, Wine Geographical Indications Australia (feature service with registration year, vine area, climate and crush 2020-2026)

regions.name: North Island
regions.tagline: The warmer island: Hawke's Bay reds, Kumeu Chardonnay, Martinborough Pinot and the vineyards where New Zealand wine began.
regions.summary: The North Island has about 7,500 ha of vines, about 17 percent of the national total in 2025, but most of the country's wine history and its warmest regions. Hawke's Bay, the largest, grows Bordeaux varieties and Syrah in gravel; Gisborne is the Chardonnay capital; Auckland and its sub-regions (Kumeu, Matakana, Waiheke Island) have the oldest family wineries; and the Wairarapa, at the southern tip, holds Martinborough, an early home of New Zealand Pinot Noir.
regions.history: Samuel Marsden planted the first vines at Kerikeri in 1819, James Busby made the first recorded wine at Waitangi in the 1830s, and French missionaries founded Mission Estate in Hawke's Bay in 1851. West Auckland was the centre of the twentieth-century industry, built by Dalmatian and Lebanese immigrant families.
regions.terroir: Warmer and more humid than the South Island, especially in Northland and Auckland. Hawke's Bay and Gisborne, on the east coast, are sheltered by ranges. Soils range from Auckland's heavy clays to Hawke's Bay's free-draining gravels and Martinborough's river terraces.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris.
regions.styles: Bordeaux blends and Syrah, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, aromatic whites.
regions.classification: Enduring GI 'North Island'; registered GIs Northland, Auckland (Matakana, Kumeu, Waiheke Island), Gisborne, Hawke's Bay (Central Hawke's Bay), Wairarapa (Gladstone, Martinborough).

regions.name: South Island
regions.tagline: Four fifths of New Zealand's vines, from the Sauvignon flats of Marlborough to the schist hills of Central Otago.
regions.summary: The South Island has about 36,700 ha of vines, about 83 percent of the national vineyard in 2025, almost all on the dry east side of the Southern Alps. Marlborough alone has 32,000 ha. Further south, Nelson, North Canterbury, Waitaki Valley and Central Otago are smaller, cooler and more varied, and produce much of the country's best Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Riesling.
regions.history: Viticulture began with French settlers at Akaroa (1840) and gold-rush miners in Central Otago (1860s), but the modern South Island industry dates from the 1970s: Montana's Marlborough plantings (1973), Neudorf in Nelson (1978), St Helena and Pegasus Bay in Canterbury, and Rippon and Gibbston Valley in Central Otago.
regions.terroir: Cooler than the North Island, with very high sunshine hours and large day-night temperature swings. Soils include Marlborough's alluvial gravels, Nelson's Moutere clays, North Canterbury's limestone and Central Otago's schist and loess.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Riesling.
regions.styles: Aromatic Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, dry to sweet Riesling, sparkling.
regions.classification: Enduring GI 'South Island'; registered GIs Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury (North Canterbury, Waipara Valley), Waitaki Valley North Otago, Central Otago (Bannockburn).

regions.name: Coastal Region
regions.tagline: Stellenbosch, Paarl, Swartland and Constantia: the historic heart of Cape wine, within an hour of Cape Town.
regions.summary: The Coastal Region holds most of South Africa's famous names: the districts of Cape Town (with Constantia and Durbanville), Stellenbosch, Paarl, Franschhoek, Wellington, Swartland, Tulbagh, Darling and Lutzville Valley. It is defined by proximity to the Atlantic and False Bay, whose cool air and the summer south-easter moderate a warm Mediterranean climate.
regions.history: Every chapter of Cape wine history begins here: Van Riebeeck's garden in Cape Town (1659), Constantia (1685), the Huguenot farms of Franschhoek and Drakenstein (1688), the KWV at Paarl (1918), Pinotage at Stellenbosch (1925) and the Swartland Revolution (2010).
regions.terroir: Granite and sandstone mountains (Simonsberg, Helderberg, Paardeberg, Drakenstein) with shale and sandstone-derived soils on the lower slopes; rainfall from about 1,000 mm near False Bay to under 450 mm in the Swartland.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chenin Blanc, Shiraz, Pinotage, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Cinsault, Grenache.
regions.styles: Bordeaux blends, Cape Blends with Pinotage, old-vine Chenin and Rhône blends, Cap Classique, Vin de Constance.
regions.classification: Region within the overarching Cape Coast region; districts Cape Town, Darling, Franschhoek, Lutzville Valley, Paarl, Stellenbosch, Swartland, Tulbagh, Wellington; Cape West Coast subregion overlaps its western part.

sources.title: WOSA / Wine and Spirit Board, Production areas defined in terms of the Wine of Origin scheme (February 2026, PDF)

regions.name: Cape South Coast
regions.tagline: The cool southern rim of Africa, where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay found a home.
regions.summary: Stretching east from Elgin along the coast to Plettenberg Bay, the Cape South Coast region contains South Africa's coolest wine country: Elgin, Walker Bay (with the Hemel-en-Aarde wards), Cape Agulhas (Elim), Overberg, Swellendam, Still Bay, Lower Duivenhoks River and Plettenberg Bay. Most of its vineyards are less than 50 years old.
regions.history: Apart from scattered farms, wine came late: Tim Hamilton Russell planted in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley in 1975, Elgin's apple farmers turned to vines from the late 1980s, and the Elim and Plettenberg Bay vineyards date from the late 1990s and 2000s.
regions.terroir: Strong maritime influence, persistent sea winds and cool, cloudy summers; soils of Bokkeveld shale, Table Mountain sandstone and decomposed granite.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Chenin Blanc, Sémillon.
regions.styles: Burgundy-style Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, cool Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, Cap Classique.
regions.classification: Region within the overarching Cape Coast region; districts Cape Agulhas, Elgin, Lower Duivenhoks River, Overberg, Plettenberg Bay, Swellendam, Walker Bay, Still Bay; wards outside districts: Herbertsdale, Napier.

sources.title: WOSA / Wine and Spirit Board, Production areas defined in terms of the Wine of Origin scheme (February 2026, PDF)
Wines of South Africa, Winelands of South Africa (winegrowing areas)

regions.name: Breede River Valley
regions.tagline: The broad, irrigated engine of Cape wine and brandy, with Robertson's limestone as its fine-wine jewel.
regions.summary: East of the Du Toitskloof and Hex River mountains, the Breede River Valley region (Breedekloof, Worcester and Robertson districts) grows a large share of South Africa's grapes for wine, brandy and grape juice. Its co-operative cellars were the backbone of the quota era; today they bottle good-value wines, and Robertson's estates make some of the country's best Chardonnay and Cap Classique.
regions.history: Settled in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as stock and grain country, the valley grew with irrigation schemes in the twentieth century. Worcester is South Africa's brandy capital, and Robertson's De Wetshof and Graham Beck put the district on the fine-wine map in the 1970s to 1990s.
regions.terroir: Hot, dry summers (300 to 400 mm of rain in Robertson) moderated by south-easterly winds funnelling up the valley; alluvial soils along the river and lime-rich soils in Robertson.
regions.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Colombard, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Muscadel.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, Chardonnay, Cap Classique, brandy base, fortified Muscadel.
regions.classification: Region with districts Breedekloof (wards Goudini, Slanghoek), Robertson (14 wards) and Worcester (7 wards).

sources.title: WOSA / Wine and Spirit Board, Production areas defined in terms of the Wine of Origin scheme (February 2026, PDF)
Wines of South Africa, Winelands of South Africa (winegrowing areas)

regions.name: Klein Karoo
regions.tagline: Ostrich farms, mountain passes and South Africa's finest port-style wines.
regions.summary: A long, semi-arid valley between the Langeberg and Swartberg ranges along Route 62, from Montagu to the Langkloof. Vines grow in kloofs and river valleys. The region is best known for Calitzdorp's fortified wines in the Portuguese style and for Muscadel, but cooler, higher wards (Tradouw Highlands, Upper Langkloof, Outeniqua, Koo Plateau) make fine table wines.
regions.history: Calitzdorp's Nel family (Boplaas and De Krans) planted Touriga Nacional and Tinta Barocca and built the Cape's reputation for 'Cape Port'; the term was retired in 2012 under the EU agreement in favour of Cape Vintage, Cape Ruby and Cape Tawny.
regions.terroir: Hot days, cold nights and very low rainfall; Bokkeveld shale and alluvium, with Table Mountain sandstone in the ranges.
regions.grapes: Muscat, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Barocca, Souzão, Chenin Blanc, Colombard, Shiraz.
regions.styles: Cape Vintage, Cape Tawny, Cape Ruby, Muscadel, potstill brandy.
regions.classification: Region with districts Calitzdorp (ward Groenfontein) and Langeberg-Garcia; wards outside districts Cango Valley, Koo Plateau, Montagu, Outeniqua, Tradouw, Tradouw Highlands, Upper Langkloof.

regions.name: Olifants River
regions.tagline: From the high sandstone of Piekenierskloof to the huge co-operatives of Vredendal.
regions.summary: The Olifants River valley runs north from the Piekenierskloof Pass past Citrusdal and Clanwilliam to the Atlantic near Lutzville. It is citrus and rooibos country with large irrigated vineyards in the lower valley (Vredendal, Spruitdrift) and old, dry-farmed bush vines in the mountains (Piekenierskloof, Skurfberg) that new-wave winemakers prize for Grenache, Chenin and Palomino.
regions.history: Irrigation from the Clanwilliam Dam (1930s) created the lower valley's large cellars; Namaqua Wines at Vredendal is among the biggest in the country.
regions.terroir: Warm and dry, with sandy soils from Table Mountain sandstone in the mountains and red clay loams on the valley floor.
regions.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Colombard, Grenache, Pinotage, Shiraz, Palomino.
regions.styles: Value whites and reds; old-vine Grenache and Chenin from the mountains.
regions.classification: Region with districts Citrusdal Mountain (ward Piekenierskloof) and Citrusdal Valley; wards Spruitdrift and Vredendal.

regions.name: Cape West Coast
regions.tagline: Fog, cold Atlantic air and some of the Cape's most windswept vineyards.
regions.summary: A subregion created after a 2019 proposal to group the vineyards nearest the Atlantic: the Darling and Lutzville Valley districts, St Helena Bay (in Swartland) and the wards of Bamboes Bay and Lamberts Bay. The cold Benguela current and morning fog make these some of the coolest sites in the Western Cape for their latitude.
regions.history: Mostly planted since the 1990s; Fryer's Cove at Bamboes Bay and Groote Post at Darling were pioneers of cool west coast Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.terroir: Sandy and granite-derived soils, strong sea winds, low rainfall and fog.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Pinotage, Shiraz.
regions.styles: Crisp, saline whites; fresh reds.
regions.classification: Subregion of the Coastal Region (and listed under it on the February 2026 schedule).

sources.title: WOSA / Wine and Spirit Board, Production areas defined in terms of the Wine of Origin scheme (February 2026, PDF)

regions.name: Northern Cape
regions.tagline: Desert vineyards on the Orange River and the highest vines in South Africa at Sutherland.
regions.summary: The Northern Cape geographical unit includes the irrigated vineyards along the Orange River around Upington (the Central Orange River district), the Douglas and Hartswater areas, and the Karoo-Hoogland region, whose Sutherland-Karoo district grows grapes near South Africa's coldest town at about 1,500 m.
regions.history: Irrigation along the Orange River from the early twentieth century created a large table-grape and raisin industry; wine cellars such as Orange River Cellars grew from it.
regions.terroir: Hot, arid and irrigated along the river; cold and high on the Karoo plateau.
regions.grapes: Colombard, Chenin Blanc, Muscat d'Alexandrie, Pinotage, Shiraz.
regions.styles: Everyday whites, sweet Muscat, some reds.
regions.classification: Geographical unit within Greater Cape; region Karoo-Hoogland (district Sutherland-Karoo); districts Central Orange River and Douglas; wards Hartswater and Prieska.

sources.title: WOSA / Wine and Spirit Board, Production areas defined in terms of the Wine of Origin scheme (February 2026, PDF)
Wines of South Africa, Winelands of South Africa (winegrowing areas)

regions.name: Ningxia
regions.tagline: A desert strip between the Yellow River and the Helan Mountains that became China's showcase for fine wine.
regions.summary: Ningxia's vineyards run for about 200 km along the alluvial fans at the eastern foot of the Helan Mountains, between the mountains and the Yellow River, from Shizuishan in the north through Yinchuan, Yongning and Qingtongxia to Hongsipu. With about 40,400 ha (606,000 mu) of vines and 131 wineries in 2026, the Helan Mountain East Foothill area claims nearly 40 percent of China's estate vineyard. Its Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Marselan reds and its Chardonnay whites have won hundreds of international medals since Helan Qingxue's 2011 Decanter trophy.
regions.history: Changyu and Great Wall planted grapes here in the 1980s and shipped them east for winemaking. The provincial government turned arid land into a wine zone from the late 1990s, and boutique wineries (Helan Qingxue, Silver Heights, Kanaan, Domaine Pushang, Chateau Yuanshi) emerged in the 2000s. Moët Hennessy's Chandon Ningxia (2013) and Pernod Ricard's Helan Mountain winery followed, and the region launched China's only estate classification in 2013. It hosted the OIV World Congress in October 2026.
regions.terroir: A high (about 1,100 to 1,200 m), arid, continental climate with about 200 mm of annual rain, 3,000 hours of sunshine, hot summer days and very cold winters (minus 20 degrees C or lower), so every vine is buried in November. Soils are gravelly, sandy alluvial fans washed down from the Helan Mountains; irrigation comes from the Yellow River.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Marselan, Cabernet Gernischt, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling.
regions.styles: Bordeaux-style reds, Marselan, Chardonnay, traditional-method sparkling (Chandon).
regions.classification: National GI Helan Mountain East Foothill (protected in the EU); Ningxia's five-tier winery classification (2013, expanded 2016, reviewed every two years).

regions.name: Xinjiang
regions.tagline: China's largest wine-grape province, oasis vineyards on the old Silk Road between the Tianshan and the deserts.
regions.summary: Xinjiang, in China's far west, has the country's largest area of vineyards, most of them for table grapes and raisins (Turpan is famous for both). Wine vineyards cluster in three areas: the northern foothills of the Tianshan around Changji, Manas and Shihezi; the Yanqi Basin by Bosten Lake near Korla (Hoxud and Yanqi counties); and the Turpan depression, one of the hottest and lowest places in Asia. CITIC Guoan's Suntime, Tiansai, Chateau Zhongfei and Xinjiang Changyu (Baron Balboa) are notable producers.
regions.history: Grapes have grown in Xinjiang's oases for over 2,000 years; the Tang learned winemaking from Gaochang near Turpan in 641. Large state farms planted wine grapes from the 1970s; boutique estates such as Tiansai (Yanqi, 2010) and Puchang (Turpan) arrived in the 2010s.
regions.terroir: Extreme continental desert climate with very hot summers, freezing winters (vines buried) and less than 100 mm of rain in places; irrigation from Tianshan snowmelt via canals and karez (qanat) tunnels. Sandy and gravelly soils.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Marselan, Syrah, Chardonnay, Riesling, Saperavi.
regions.styles: Ripe, sun-drenched reds; some sweet and fortified wines.
regions.classification: No EU-protected wine GI; Yanqi and Tianshan North are promoted as producing areas; Turpan and Hoxud were proposed as national GIs in 2015.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Shandong
regions.tagline: The cradle of modern Chinese wine, on a monsoon-lashed peninsula between two seas.
regions.summary: Shandong's Jiaodong Peninsula, around Yantai, Penglai and Qingdao, is where China's modern wine industry began with Changyu in 1892. It remains a major production centre, with hundreds of wineries and the headquarters of Changyu, although many big companies also process grapes and imported bulk wine here. Penglai's hills, near the coast, have attracted Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Long Dai, first vintage 2017) and boutique estates.
regions.history: Zhang Bishi's Changyu (1892), the Grand Cellar beneath Yantai (1894 to 1905), Huadong winery near Qingdao (1985, an early producer of Chardonnay), and later Long Dai and Chateau Changyu-Castel.
regions.terroir: Maritime-influenced and milder in winter, so vines need not be buried; but the summer monsoon brings heavy rain in July and August, making disease control the main challenge. Granitic and sandy soils on hillsides near Penglai.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Gernischt, Merlot, Marselan, Chardonnay, Petit Manseng, Italian Riesling.
regions.styles: Light to medium reds, whites, some sweet Petit Manseng.
regions.classification: National GI Yantai (protected in the EU); Penglai is promoted as a sub-zone.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Hebei
regions.tagline: Two very different wine areas: the dry Huailai basin beyond the Great Wall, and the coastal Changli hills.
regions.summary: Hebei's Huailai County (with Shacheng, Great Wall's home) lies in the Sanggan River valley north-west of Beijing, behind the Great Wall, where a dry, windy, sunny climate suits red grapes and Dragon's Eye (Longyan) table grapes have grown for centuries. Huailai is also home of the Sino-French demonstration vineyard (2001, now Domaine Franco-Chinois) that introduced Marselan. Changli, on the Bohai coast near Qinhuangdao, is the other major area. Grace Vineyard's sister estate and Chateau Sungod (Huailai) are among its boutique producers.
regions.history: Great Wall winery was founded at Shacheng in 1983 and made China's first dry white in 1979 as a state research project. Changli's Huaxia Great Wall winery (1988) and the Sino-French vineyard made Hebei a centre of experimentation.
regions.terroir: Huailai: continental, dry (about 400 mm of rain) and cold in winter, vines buried. Changli: maritime, milder, monsoon rain in summer.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Marselan, Chardonnay, Longyan (Dragon's Eye).
regions.styles: Reds and dry whites; Longyan whites.
regions.classification: National GIs Shacheng (protected in the EU) and Changli.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Yunnan
regions.tagline: Vineyards at 2,000 to 2,600 m in Tibetan valleys under the Meili Snow Mountains.
regions.summary: In north-west Yunnan, along the upper Mekong (Lancang) and Jinsha (upper Yangtze) rivers in Deqin and Shangri-La counties, small terraced vineyards sit between 2,000 and 2,600 m. French Catholic missionaries planted vines at Cizhong church in the nineteenth century; LVMH's Ao Yun, after a four-year search by Australian winemaker Tony Jordan, released its first Cabernet blend (2013) in 2016, and Shangri-La Winery and smaller estates followed. Further south, Mile and Mengzi grow the old Rose Honey grape.
regions.history: Missionaries at Cizhong kept vines for mass wine until their expulsion in 1952; Catholic villagers continued to tend them. The government encouraged villagers to plant vines in the 1990s, and Moët Hennessy contracted 320 small plots in 2012 for Ao Yun.
regions.terroir: High altitude, dry valleys in the rain shadow of the Himalayas, strong UV, cool nights; river-gravel and schist soils. Different villages ripen weeks apart because of altitude and sun exposure.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Syrah, Petit Verdot, Chardonnay, Rose Honey.
regions.styles: Structured high-altitude reds.
regions.classification: No national wine GI; Deqin and Shangri-La are promoted as producing areas.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Gansu
regions.tagline: Vineyards along the Hexi Corridor, the Silk Road route between desert and the Qilian Mountains.
regions.summary: The Hexi Corridor runs for 1,000 km through Gansu between the Qilian Mountains and the Gobi, through Wuwei, Zhangye and Jiayuguan. Grapes were grown at Liangzhou (Wuwei) in the Tang dynasty, whose wine the poets praised. Today Mogao, Ziyuan and Qilian wineries farm vines buried every winter.
regions.history: Liangzhou grape wine was famed in the Tang; modern plantings date from the 1980s and 1990s.
regions.terroir: Arid, continental, high (1,400 to 1,800 m); snowmelt irrigation; loess and gravel.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling.
regions.styles: Reds, whites and some icewine-style sweet wines.
regions.classification: No EU-protected GI.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Shanxi
regions.tagline: Loess plateau country, home of Grace Vineyard, one of China's first boutique estates.
regions.summary: Grace Vineyard at Taigu, founded by Hong Kong businessman C.K. Chan in 1997, was one of the first Chinese estates to win international attention for quality, with wines such as Chairman's Reserve; his daughter Judy Leissner ran it for many years. Taiyuan was famous for grape wine in the Tang dynasty.
regions.history: Taiyuan's 'mare's teat' grape wine was a Tang dynasty luxury; Grace Vineyard revived the area's reputation from 1997.
regions.terroir: Continental loess plateau at about 800 m; vines buried in winter.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Bordeaux-style reds.
regions.classification: No EU-protected GI.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Beijing
regions.tagline: Capital-region wineries in the Yanqing and Fangshan hills.
regions.summary: Vineyards in Yanqing, north-west of the city beyond the Great Wall, and in Fangshan to the south-west support a cluster of chateaux aimed at Beijing's market and tourists, including Bodega Langes and Chateau Changyu AFIP in Miyun.
regions.history: Small plantings since the 1990s and a government push for 'wine chateau' tourism in the 2000s.
regions.terroir: Continental, monsoon summer rain, cold winters.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Reds.
regions.classification: No EU-protected GI.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Liaoning
regions.tagline: Icewine on Hanlong Lake, near the North Korean border.
regions.summary: In Huanren County, Liaoning, the area around Hanlong Lake has cold winters but enough sun to ripen Vidal, and since the early 2000s Changyu and others have made icewine from grapes frozen on the vine. Huanren Icewine is a GI protected in the EU.
regions.history: Vidal was introduced from Canada; Changyu built its Golden Icewine Valley at Huanren.
regions.terroir: Cold continental climate; lake moderates temperatures; vines buried or protected.
regions.grapes: Vidal, Beibinghong.
regions.styles: Icewine.
regions.classification: National GI Huanren Icewine (protected in the EU).

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Yamanashi
regions.tagline: The Kofu basin under Mount Fuji, home of Koshu and of a third of Japan's wineries.
regions.summary: Yamanashi has about 80 wineries, around a third of Japan's, and about 40 percent of domestic wine production; it grows about 95 percent of the country's Koshu. The heart is the eastern Kofu basin around Katsunuma, Enzan and Yamanashi city (now merged into Koshu city), where vineyards on alluvial fans climb the slopes among peach orchards.
regions.history: Grapes were grown here from at least the medieval period, and the first commercial wineries were founded in the 1870s. Château Mercian, Grace Wine (Chuo Budoshu, 1923), Lumière, Marufuji and Haramo are among the historic houses.
regions.terroir: A basin ringed by mountains with hot, humid summers but relatively low rainfall for Japan; well-drained alluvial gravels and volcanic soils.
regions.grapes: Koshu, Muscat Bailey A, Merlot, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.styles: Delicate dry Koshu (including sur lie, sparkling and orange), light reds, Bordeaux blends.
regions.classification: NTA GI Yamanashi (2013), covering the whole prefecture.

sources.title: National Tax Agency of Japan, Geographical Indications (designations for wine: Yamanashi 2013, Hokkaido 2018, Yamagata, Osaka and Nagano 2021)

regions.name: Nagano
regions.tagline: Japan's high, dry wine valleys, where Merlot found a home on the Kikyogahara plateau.
regions.summary: Nagano (historically Shinshu) has high valleys at 500 to 900 m with the lowest rainfall in Japan and large day-night temperature swings. Its Kikyogahara plateau at Shiojiri made Château Mercian's Merlot famous, and the Chikumagawa valley near Ueda and Tomi hosts dozens of new small wineries, encouraged by the prefecture's 'Shinshu Wine Valley' plan.
regions.history: Concord and Niagara were grown at Kikyogahara from the late nineteenth century; Mercian switched growers to Merlot in 1976. Mercian's Mariko vineyard at Ueda (2003) and Villa d'Est (Tamamura Toyoo, 2003) helped launch the Chikumagawa boom.
regions.terroir: Inland, high and continental; volcanic and alluvial soils; cold winters.
regions.grapes: Merlot, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Concord, Niagara.
regions.styles: Structured reds and fresh whites.
regions.classification: NTA GI Nagano (2021).

sources.title: National Tax Agency of Japan, Geographical Indications (designations for wine: Yamanashi 2013, Hokkaido 2018, Yamagata, Osaka and Nagano 2021)

regions.name: Hokkaido
regions.tagline: Snowy, cool and largely free of typhoons: Japan's new frontier for Pinot Noir.
regions.summary: Hokkaido, Japan's northern island, has the country's largest wine-grape area by some measures and its fastest-growing number of wineries, more than 60. Yoichi, near Otaru, is the centre of a Pinot Noir and natural-wine boom led by Takahiko Soga; Iwamizawa (Sorachi), Ikeda (Tokachi wine, a municipal winery since 1963) and Hakodate are the other centres.
regions.history: Ikeda town founded Japan's first municipally run winery in 1963 to use wild yamabudo grapes. German varieties (Kerner, Müller-Thurgau, Zweigelt) were planted from the 1980s; Pinot Noir arrived in force from the 2000s; Domaine de Montille of Burgundy bought land near Hakodate in 2017.
regions.terroir: Cool, with about 1,000 growing degree days in Yoichi; no rainy season to speak of and few typhoons; heavy snow protects vines in winter. Volcanic and alluvial soils.
regions.grapes: Kerner, Pinot Noir, Zweigelt, Müller-Thurgau, Chardonnay, Yamabudo hybrids.
regions.styles: Light, fresh whites; delicate Pinot Noir; sparkling.
regions.classification: NTA GI Hokkaido (2018).

sources.title: National Tax Agency of Japan, Geographical Indications (designations for wine: Yamanashi 2013, Hokkaido 2018, Yamagata, Osaka and Nagano 2021)

regions.name: Yamagata
regions.tagline: Fruit country in Tohoku with a century-old wine tradition.
regions.summary: Yamagata in northern Honshu is a fruit-growing prefecture (cherries, grapes) with about 15 wineries; Takahata Winery and the old Sakai Winery (1892) at Akayu are well known. Delaware and other American grapes are traditional, alongside Chardonnay and Merlot.
regions.history: Grapes were planted in the Okitama basin in the nineteenth century; Sakai Winery dates from 1892.
regions.terroir: Basins with snowy winters and warm summers.
regions.grapes: Delaware, Chardonnay, Merlot, Muscat Bailey A, Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, sparkling Delaware, light reds.
regions.classification: NTA GI Yamagata (2021).

sources.title: National Tax Agency of Japan, Geographical Indications (designations for wine: Yamanashi 2013, Hokkaido 2018, Yamagata, Osaka and Nagano 2021)

regions.name: Osaka
regions.tagline: Hillside Delaware vineyards on the edge of a megacity, once Japan's largest grape region.
regions.summary: In the 1930s Osaka prefecture had more grape vineyards than anywhere else in Japan, on the slopes of the Ikoma and Kongo ranges around Kashiwara and Habikino. Katashimo Winery (founded 1914) is western Japan's oldest operating winery and still makes Delaware, Muscat Bailey A and other wines.
regions.history: Grape growing spread in the Meiji and Taisho eras; urbanisation shrank it after the Second World War.
regions.terroir: Warm, humid, hillside vineyards near the city.
regions.grapes: Delaware, Muscat Bailey A, Koshu, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Light whites and reds, sparkling Delaware.
regions.classification: NTA GI Osaka (2021).

sources.title: National Tax Agency of Japan, Geographical Indications (designations for wine: Yamanashi 2013, Hokkaido 2018, Yamagata, Osaka and Nagano 2021)

regions.name: Niigata
regions.tagline: Snow country, where Kawakami Zenbei bred Japan's own red grapes.
regions.summary: Niigata, on the Sea of Japan coast, is best known for sake, but its Iwanohara Vineyard (1890) at Joetsu was where Kawakami Zenbei bred Muscat Bailey A and Black Queen. Newer estates such as Cave d'Occi cluster near the coast at Kakudahama. Niigata has no wine GI.
regions.history: Kawakami used snow from winter to cool his fermentations, storing it in a 'snow room' built in 1898.
regions.terroir: Heavy winter snow, warm humid summers; sandy coastal soils at Kakudahama.
regions.grapes: Muscat Bailey A, Black Queen, Albariño, Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.styles: Light reds and whites.
regions.classification: No GI.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Japanese wine

regions.name: Nashik
regions.tagline: India's wine capital, on the Deccan plateau above the Godavari.
regions.summary: The Nashik district, especially the Dindori and Gangapur Dam areas west of the city, has the largest concentration of Indian wineries: Sula, York, Soma, Grover Zampa's Nashik operation and Vallonné at nearby Igatpuri. Vineyards sit at about 600 m on basalt soils, irrigated from the Godavari's reservoirs.
regions.history: A table-grape centre since the 1960s; Sula's arrival in 1999 and Maharashtra's 2001 policy turned it into a wine region.
regions.terroir: Tropical with a dry winter harvest; basalt-derived soils; altitude about 550 to 700 m.
regions.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Tempranillo.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, rosés, medium-bodied reds, sparkling.
regions.classification: GI Nashik Valley Wine.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Indian wine

regions.name: Karnataka
regions.tagline: Hillside vineyards near Bangalore and on the northern plateau.
regions.summary: Karnataka is India's second wine state, with vineyards at Nandi Hills north of Bangalore (Grover Zampa, at about 900 m) and in the hot north around Bijapur (Vijayapura) and Belgaum. The state created a Karnataka Wine Board to promote local wine.
regions.history: Grover planted at Nandi Hills in 1988.
regions.terroir: Red lateritic and granite soils at Nandi Hills; black soils in the north.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Viognier, Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.styles: Reds and sparkling.
regions.classification: No GI.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Indian wine

regions.name: Pune and Solapur
regions.tagline: Where India's modern wine began, at Narayangaon, and where Italian varieties thrive at Akluj.
regions.summary: South of Nashik, the Pune district (Narayangaon, birthplace of Chateau Indage) and the Sangli-Solapur area (Akluj, home of Fratelli) are Maharashtra's other wine zones, hotter and drier, suited to Sangiovese, Cabernet and Shiraz.
regions.history: Chateau Indage's Omar Khayyam sparkling (1980s); Fratelli founded at Akluj in 2007.
regions.terroir: Semi-arid Deccan plateau, black basalt soils.
regions.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Chenin Blanc.
regions.styles: Reds, sparkling.
regions.classification: No GI.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Indian wine

regions.name: Khao Yai
regions.tagline: Thailand's hill-country wine area, a weekend drive from Bangkok.
regions.summary: Vineyards in the foothills of Khao Yai National Park around Pak Chong, at 300 to 400 m, where GranMonte and PB Valley make Chenin Blanc, Viognier, Shiraz and Syrah-based blends.
regions.history: Planted from the 1990s and 2000s.
regions.terroir: Tropical upland; dry-season harvest.
regions.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Shiraz, Viognier, Tempranillo.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, rosé, medium reds.
regions.classification: None.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Thai wine

regions.name: Hua Hin
regions.tagline: Coastal hill vineyards inland from the royal resort town.
regions.summary: Siam Winery's Hua Hin Hills Vineyard, inland from the resort, produces the Monsoon Valley brand from Colombard, Chenin Blanc, Shiraz and Sangiovese.
regions.history: Planted in the early 2000s; the visitor centre opened in 2008.
regions.terroir: Sandy soils, hot and dry for half the year.
regions.grapes: Colombard, Chenin Blanc, Shiraz, Sangiovese.
regions.styles: Light whites and reds.
regions.classification: None.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Thai wine

appellations.name: South Australia
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Grenache, Riesling, Merlot
appellations.summary: The state GI covers every vineyard in South Australia and appears on blends drawn from several regions, such as multi-regional Shiraz from the big companies. South Australia crushes roughly half of Australia's grapes, and as a phylloxera-free state with tight quarantine on vine material it holds most of the country's pre-1900 plantings.
appellations.terroir: From the hot, irrigated Riverland to the cool Limestone Coast and the elevated Mount Lofty Ranges; the common thread is winter rainfall and dry summers.
appellations.nerd_note: Vinehealth Australia (originally the Phylloxera Board of South Australia, created under an 1899 act) still controls the movement of vines, used machinery and even grape bins into the state.

appellations.name: Adelaide
appellations.summary: A 'super zone' wrapping the Mount Lofty Ranges, Fleurieu and Barossa zones, created so that wines blended across the hills and plains near the city can carry a place name more specific than South Australia. It is used mainly for multi-regional blends; its value is that it guarantees the fruit is from the cooler, older vineyards near the capital rather than the irrigated Riverland.
appellations.terroir: Includes everything from Barossa's valley floor to the Adelaide Hills at 700 m and the coastal Fleurieu.
appellations.nerd_note: Adelaide is the only super zone inside a single state; South Eastern Australia, the other super zone, straddles five.

appellations.name: Barossa
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Riesling, Semillon
appellations.summary: The Barossa zone joins the warm valley floor of the Barossa Valley with the cooler, higher Eden Valley to the east. Wines labelled simply 'Barossa' are usually blends across both, a historic practice: Barossa winemakers have long balanced the density of valley-floor Shiraz with the acidity and perfume of Eden Valley fruit. The two regions share a history of Silesian settlement, Lutheran churches and family growers whose names (Hoffmann, Kalleske, Lindner, Henschke) recur on labels and vineyard registers.
appellations.terroir: A single zone of about 1,690 square kilometres with 13,500 ha of vines, rising from about 110 m on the North Para River to over 600 m on the Barossa Range.
appellations.nerd_note: The Barossa Old Vine Charter applies across the zone, so an Ancestor vineyard (125 years or older) can be in either the valley or Eden Valley.

appellations.name: Barossa Valley
appellations.grapes: Shiraz (about half the vineyard), Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Mourvèdre (Mataro), Semillon, Riesling
appellations.summary:
The Barossa Valley is the heartland of Australian Shiraz and holds some of the oldest producing vines on earth. A shallow valley 25 km long, drained by the North Para River 60 km north-east of Adelaide, it was settled from 1842 by Lutheran farmers from Prussian Silesia, who called it 'Neu-Schlesien'. They planted mixed farms with a few rows of vines; when the fortified-wine boom came in the late nineteenth century the vines became the crop. Because South Australia kept phylloxera out, many of those own-rooted, dry-grown bush vines still crop: Langmeil's Freedom Shiraz (1843), Cirillo's Grenache at Light Pass (1848), Turkey Flat's Shiraz at Bethany, Hewitson's Old Garden Mourvèdre (1853) and Penfolds' Block 42 Cabernet at Kalimna (1888).

For decades this fruit went into fortified wine and then into anonymous blends; in the 1980s, with a government vine-pull scheme paying growers to grub up old vines, much was lost. Peter Lehmann, who guaranteed to buy growers' grapes during the crisis, Robert O'Callaghan at Rockford and Charlie Melton saved what remained, and in the 1990s American critics fell for the ripe, dense, chocolate-and-blackberry style. Since the 2010s the style has moved toward earlier picking, less new oak and more whole-bunch Grenache and Mataro, without losing the region's generosity.

The Barossa Old Vine Charter registers vines by age (Old 35+, Survivor 70+, Centenarian 100+, Ancestor 125+). The Barossa Grounds project grouped the valley's soils and climates into broad zones (commonly called the Northern Grounds around Moppa, Ebenezer and Greenock, which give the darkest, most tannic Shiraz; the Central Grounds around Marananga, Seppeltsfield and Tanunda; the warmer, sandier Southern Grounds around Rowland Flat and Lyndoch; and the cooler Eastern Edge and Western Ridge), which producers now cite on labels as informal sub-districts.
appellations.terroir: Warm and dry: Wine Australia records about 1,970 growing degree days and 209 mm of growing-season rain, so most of the oldest vines are dry-grown and rely on deep soils that hold winter rain. Soils change over short distances, from red-brown clay loams and ironstone in the north and west (Marananga, Greenock, Ebenezer) to deep sand over clay at Light Pass and Vine Vale and grey sandy loams in the south. Altitude runs from about 110 m on the valley floor to almost 600 m on the western ridge.
appellations.nerd_note: Penfolds' Block 42 at Kalimna, planted around 1888, is thought to be the oldest continuously producing Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard in the world; it is bottled alone only in exceptional years.

appellations.name: Eden Valley
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Viognier
appellations.summary:
Eden Valley is the high, cool eastern half of the Barossa: rolling granite and schist country at 400 to 600 m, with gum trees, sheep paddocks and widely spaced vineyards. It makes two of Australia's greatest wines. Its Riesling is fine, floral and lime-scented, more delicate than Clare's and capable of decades in bottle (Pewsey Vale, Heggies, Henschke Julius, Mesh). And its old Shiraz, above all Henschke's Hill of Grace and Mount Edelstone, shows that Australian Shiraz can be about perfume, spice and silk rather than weight.

Settlement began in the 1840s: Joseph Gilbert planted Pewsey Vale in 1847, and Johann Christian Henschke, a Silesian, started making wine at Keyneton in 1868. The Hill of Grace vineyard, named after the Gnadenberg (Hill of Grace) Lutheran church opposite, holds Shiraz planted in the 1860s; Cyril Henschke first bottled it alone with the 1958 vintage, a pioneering single-vineyard release. Yalumba revived Eden Valley Riesling and planted Viognier there in 1980, one of the first serious plantings in the New World.
appellations.terroir: About 1,800 growing degree days on Wine Australia's measure, but cold nights and wind make it feel cooler than the figure. Soils are thin and stony, derived from weathered granite, schist, ironstone and quartz, giving low yields. Altitude runs from about 220 m to over 630 m.
appellations.nerd_note: The 'Grandfathers' in Hill of Grace are Shiraz vines planted in the 1860s by Nicolaus Stanitzki; Henschke propagates new plantings from them using its own massal selection.

appellations.name: High Eden
appellations.summary: The highest part of Eden Valley, registered as a subregion in 2001, around the Barossa Range above Springton and Flaxman Valley. It was championed by David Wynn, who left the family's Wynns business to plant Mountadam here in 1972 and made one of Australia's early cool-climate Chardonnays. Riesling is tight and slow to open; Chardonnay and sparkling base are crisp.
appellations.terroir: Altitudes up to about 630 m, on quartzite, schist and sandy soils, cooler and windier than the rest of Eden Valley.
appellations.nerd_note: At 46 square kilometres, High Eden is one of the smallest registered GIs in Australia.

appellations.name: Mount Lofty Ranges
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: The zone that follows the Mount Lofty Ranges north and south of Adelaide, grouping three very different regions: the cool Adelaide Hills, the warm Clare Valley 100 km north, and the flat Adelaide Plains. It is rarely seen on labels; its regions do the work.
appellations.terroir: Elevations rise to over 700 m in the Adelaide Hills; the ranges catch more rain than the plains and the Barossa.
appellations.nerd_note: The Clare Valley sits in this zone, not in the Barossa zone, even though Clare and Barossa are often discussed together.

appellations.name: Adelaide Hills
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Pinot Gris, Grüner Veltliner, Nebbiolo
appellations.summary:
A long, narrow region of hills, orchards and stringybark forest running about 70 km along the Mount Lofty Ranges east of Adelaide. Vineyards sit at roughly 300 to 700 m, which makes it one of the coolest regions in mainland South Australia, and it has become the state's centre for Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, cool-climate Shiraz and traditional-method sparkling.

German settlers planted vines at Hahndorf and Lobethal in the nineteenth century, but by the 1930s the Hills were orchard country. The modern era began with Brian Croser's Petaluma, whose Piccadilly Valley Chardonnay (from 1976 onward) and Croser sparkling proved the site, followed by Henschke at Lenswood, Stephen George's Ashton Hills (Pinot Noir) and Shaw + Smith, whose 1989 Sauvignon Blanc became a benchmark. In the 2000s and 2010s the Basket Range area became the heart of Australia's natural-wine movement, with Lucy Margaux, BK Wines, Ochota Barrels and Commune of Buttons making skin-contact whites, light reds and pét-nats.
appellations.terroir: About 1,710 growing degree days on Wine Australia's data, with 740 mm of annual rain, more than the Barossa or McLaren Vale. Soils are mostly ancient sandstones, schist, quartzite and siltstone, often weathered to grey-brown loam over clay. The northern end (Gumeracha, Birdwood) is warmer; the central Piccadilly Valley and Lenswood are the coolest and wettest.
appellations.nerd_note: Hahndorf Hill planted Grüner Veltliner in 2006 from Austrian clones imported through quarantine, and the Hills now grow most of Australia's Grüner.

appellations.name: Lenswood
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling
appellations.summary: A high, apple-growing valley in the central Adelaide Hills, registered in 1998 as one of Australia's first subregions. Henschke's Lenswood vineyard (Croft Chardonnay, Giles Pinot Noir), Knappstein Lenswood and Pike & Joyce showed its Chardonnay and Pinot have the acidity for long ageing.
appellations.terroir: Steep slopes at roughly 400 to 560 m, on podzolic soils over sandstone and schist; cooler and wetter than most of the Hills.
appellations.nerd_note: Lenswood is only about 39 square kilometres, among the smallest GIs in Australia.

appellations.name: Piccadilly Valley
appellations.summary: A small, cool valley beneath Mount Lofty, registered in 2000. Brian Croser planted Petaluma's Tiers vineyard here in 1979, and the Tiers Chardonnay (now under Croser's Tapanappa label) is one of Australia's most precise. It is also prime country for sparkling base wine.
appellations.terroir: Among the highest and wettest vineyards in the Hills, at about 500 to 700 m, on brown loam over clay and sandstone.
appellations.nerd_note: At about 42 square kilometres with 221 ha of vines, Piccadilly Valley produces less than a single big Riverland vineyard but some of the country's most expensive Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Clare Valley
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Semillon, Malbec
appellations.summary:
