The Clare Valley, 120 km north of Adelaide, is not one valley but a series of narrow north-south valleys on a plateau between about 300 and 500 m, and it is Australia's most famous source of dry Riesling. Clare Riesling is bone dry, smells of lime juice and lime blossom when young, and turns to toast, honey and kerosene over ten to twenty years. The region also makes structured Shiraz and Cabernet, from estates such as Wendouree and Jim Barry, that need years to soften.

Settlement was varied: the Austrian Jesuits founded Sevenhill in 1851 to make altar wine (they still do), Polish immigrants settled the Polish Hill River valley from 1856, and English and Cornish miners worked the copper mines at nearby Burra. Two sub-areas define Clare Riesling. Watervale, in the south, has red-brown loam over limestone and gives more floral, generous, earlier-drinking wines; Polish Hill, in a side valley to the east, has hard slate and shale and gives austere, tightly wound wines that need time.

Clare also changed how the world closes bottles. In August 2000, fourteen producers including Grosset, Mount Horrocks, Taylors, Leasingham, Mitchell and Knappstein announced they would bottle Riesling together under screwcap, with bottles from Saverglass and caps from Pechiney, because cork taint was ruining at least one bottle in twenty. It worked: aromatic Riesling ages slowly and predictably under screwcap, and within a decade most of Australia and New Zealand had switched.
appellations.terroir: Wine Australia records about 1,950 growing degree days, warmer than its reputation suggests, but cool nights, altitude and afternoon breezes preserve acidity. Soils are a patchwork: terra rossa and red loam over limestone at Watervale and Auburn, slate and shale at Polish Hill, sandy loam around Sevenhill and Penwortham.
appellations.nerd_note: Jim Barry's Florita vineyard at Watervale was bought from Leo Buring in 1986; John Vickery's Leo Buring Rieslings made from it in the 1960s and 1970s are among the oldest Australian Rieslings still drinking well.

appellations.name: Adelaide Plains
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Colombard, Nero d'Avola
appellations.summary: Flat, hot market-garden country north of Adelaide around Virginia and Angle Vale, registered in 2002. Much of the fruit goes into blends, but Primo Estate (Joe Grilli, who first made Colombard famous here and created the amarone-style Joseph Moda) and Ceravolo show the region can make characterful wine.
appellations.terroir: About 2,250 growing degree days and under 400 mm of annual rain; flat alluvial soils near Gulf St Vincent, irrigated.
appellations.nerd_note: Primo Estate's Joseph Moda Cabernet Merlot uses partially dried grapes, an Australian take on the Veneto's appassimento.

appellations.name: Fleurieu
appellations.summary: The zone covering the Fleurieu Peninsula south of Adelaide and Kangaroo Island. It includes McLaren Vale, Langhorne Creek, Currency Creek, Southern Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island, and together these crush around 15,000 hectares' worth of fruit, much of it red.
appellations.terroir: Strong maritime influence from Gulf St Vincent, the Southern Ocean and Lake Alexandrina.
appellations.nerd_note: Langhorne Creek's high yields make the Fleurieu one of the biggest-volume zones outside the irrigated inland.

appellations.name: McLaren Vale
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Mourvèdre, Fiano, Nero d'Avola, Vermentino, Tempranillo
appellations.summary:
McLaren Vale is a Mediterranean pocket between the Mount Lofty Ranges and Gulf St Vincent, 40 minutes south of Adelaide, and it makes some of Australia's most interesting warm-climate reds. It was planted almost as soon as South Australia was settled: John Reynell put in vines at Reynella in 1838, and Thomas Hardy, who bought Tintara in 1876, built the business that became the country's biggest wine company. Old dry-grown Shiraz and Grenache survive across the region, many over 80 years old.

The style of the region changed after 2000. Shiraz remains the main grape, but Grenache from the deep sands of Blewitt Springs, picked earlier and made with whole bunches, has become its signature: pale, perfumed and fine, from producers such as Yangarra, SC Pannell, Bekkers, Ox Hardy and Clarendon Hills. Hot, dry summers and limited water have pushed growers toward Mediterranean varieties: Coriole was among the first to plant Sangiovese and Fiano, and Fiano, Vermentino, Nero d'Avola, Montepulciano and Tempranillo are spreading. The region also leads Australia in organic and biodynamic certification.

McLaren Vale's growers mapped their geology in 2010 and found around 40 rock and soil units, ranging from recent sands to rocks more than 500 million years old. The region now uses an informal district map with names such as Blewitt Springs, Clarendon, Kangarilla, McLaren Flat, Seaview, Willunga and Sellicks Foothills, so drinkers can tell a sandy, perfumed Blewitt Springs Grenache from a dense, ironstone-grown Seaview Shiraz.
appellations.terroir: About 1,940 growing degree days and only 211 mm of growing-season rain. Afternoon sea breezes off Gulf St Vincent moderate the heat. Soils vary sharply: deep, white-grey sands over clay at Blewitt Springs, ironstone and red clay at Seaview, terra rossa and limestone in the south around Willunga, and older siltstones and quartzites near the hills at Clarendon (up to about 400 m).
appellations.nerd_note: d'Arenberg still uses open fermenters and basket presses for its reds, foot-treading the fruit; in 2017 it opened the d'Arenberg Cube, a five-storey glass Rubik's-cube-shaped cellar door.

appellations.name: Langhorne Creek
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Malbec, Chardonnay
appellations.summary:
A flat, quiet region on the floodplains of the Bremer and Angas rivers near Lake Alexandrina, and one of Australia's great unsung sources of soft, fleshy red. It has about 6,100 ha of vines, more than McLaren Vale's area of land would suggest, and much of its fruit disappears into famous blends: Wolf Blass's Black Label and many big-company Cabernet Shiraz blends rely on it.

Frank Potts founded Bleasdale here in 1850 and the family still runs it; Potts cut red gum from the riverbanks to build a huge lever press that still stands. Growers historically flooded their vineyards in winter by diverting the rivers, and the 'Lake Doctor', an afternoon breeze off Lake Alexandrina, cools ripening fruit. Saltram's Metala vineyard dates from 1891.
appellations.terroir: Low-lying (under 65 m), with deep alluvial sandy loams over clay. About 1,970 growing degree days but only 389 mm of annual rain, so water from the lake and rivers matters.
appellations.nerd_note: Bleasdale's red gum lever press, built in 1892 from a single tree trunk, worked until 1960 and is still on site.

appellations.name: Currency Creek
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: A small region near Goolwa and the Murray Mouth, registered in 2001, with vineyards planted mostly since the 1990s. Its maritime climate and sandy soils give fruit-forward reds and fresh whites, much of it sold to larger wineries.
appellations.terroir: Close to Lake Alexandrina and the Southern Ocean; about 1,870 growing degree days and 460 mm of rain.
appellations.nerd_note: The region's name comes from a creek named in 1837 after the cutter 'Currency Lass'.

appellations.name: Kangaroo Island
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Australia's third-largest island, 13 km off the Fleurieu Peninsula, has about 144 ha of vines spread among small family producers. The bushfires of December 2019 and January 2020 burnt about half the island and damaged several vineyards.
appellations.terroir: Cool and maritime (about 1,625 growing degree days), with laterite and ironstone soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The Islander Estate was founded by Jacques Lurton of the Bordeaux family.

appellations.name: Southern Fleurieu
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: The hilly tip of the Fleurieu Peninsula, from Mount Compass to Cape Jervis and Victor Harbor, registered in 2001. Cooler and wetter than McLaren Vale next door, it suits Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and medium-bodied reds.
appellations.terroir: About 1,640 growing degree days and 700 mm of annual rain, with Southern Ocean winds.
appellations.nerd_note: Salomon Estate's founder Bert Salomon is an Austrian winemaker who works vintages in both hemispheres.

appellations.name: Limestone Coast
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: The flat south-east corner of South Australia, a former seabed of limestone ridges and swamps that runs from Padthaway to Mount Gambier. Its regions (Coonawarra, Wrattonbully, Padthaway, Mount Benson, Robe and Mount Gambier) share cool maritime air and soils of terra rossa or sand over limestone, and together grow about 15,400 ha of vines.
appellations.terroir: Low relief, high water tables and a cool climate moderated by the Southern Ocean.
appellations.nerd_note: 'Limestone Coast' on a label often means a blend from Coonawarra, Wrattonbully and Padthaway.

appellations.name: Coonawarra
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon (more than half the vineyard), Shiraz, Merlot, Chardonnay
appellations.summary:
Coonawarra is Australia's most famous Cabernet Sauvignon region, and its fame rests on a strip of soil. A narrow band of bright red terra rossa over soft white limestone, about 15 km long and rarely more than 2 km wide, runs north from Penola across flat country otherwise covered by black, poorly drained clays. Vines on the red strip ripen Cabernet with intense blackcurrant fruit, a mint and eucalyptus lift and firm but fine tannins.

The district was invented by John Riddoch, a Scottish pastoralist who in 1890 subdivided part of his property into small blocks for his Penola Fruit Colony and in 1891 built a stone winery with three gables. Bill Redman made the wine from 1901 and kept Coonawarra going through the lean decades; in 1951 the Wynn family bought Riddoch's winery and launched Wynns Coonawarra Estate, whose triple-gabled label is still the region's emblem. Mildara, Lindemans, Penfolds and others followed in the 1960s and 1970s.

Because the soil made the name, the boundary became a decade-long legal fight in the 1990s and early 2000s, as growers on black soil, those just outside and those on the terra rossa argued over what Coonawarra meant. The final boundary (registered in 2003) is broader than the red strip, so the best producers name the soil and the vineyard. The region's water table is high, so vines need little irrigation and suffer little from drought, but spring frost is a real risk.
appellations.terroir: Cool for its latitude: Wine Australia records about 1,570 growing degree days and a mean January temperature near 20.6 degrees C. Terra rossa (iron-rich red clay loam 20 to 50 cm deep) sits on calcrete and porous limestone; outside the strip are rendzina black soils and sandy flats. Altitude barely varies (about 50 to 130 m).
appellations.nerd_note: Wynns made its first Black Label Cabernet Sauvignon in 1954; the flagship John Riddoch Cabernet, named after the founder, followed with the 1982 vintage.

appellations.name: Wrattonbully
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo
appellations.summary: Wrattonbully sits just north of Coonawarra and shares its terra rossa over limestone, but its land is more undulating and less prone to frost, and it ripens grapes a little earlier. Most vineyards date from the 1990s, many owned by big companies whose fruit goes into Coonawarra-style blends. Brian Croser's Tapanappa makes its Whalebone Vineyard Cabernet Shiraz here from vines planted in 1974, named for a 35-million-year-old whale skeleton found in a cave beneath it.
appellations.terroir: About 1,650 growing degree days; terra rossa and sandy loam over limestone, at 75 to 150 m, with caves and sinkholes in the karst below.
appellations.nerd_note: The Naracoorte Caves, a World Heritage fossil site, lie at the region's edge in the same limestone.

appellations.name: Padthaway
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Planted from the 1960s by Seppelt and Lindemans, who were looking for cheap land with good water and a cool climate, Padthaway (originally called Keppoch) became a major source of Chardonnay for national brands; Hardys' Eileen Hardy Chardonnay long relied on it. Today it supplies Shiraz and Cabernet too, with a few local labels.
appellations.terroir: Terra rossa and sandy loams over limestone, on a low ridge; about 1,700 growing degree days and 480 mm of rain, warmer than Coonawarra.
appellations.nerd_note: Padthaway Estate operates in a former homestead built in 1882 and was one of the first to make traditional-method sparkling in the region.

appellations.name: Mount Benson
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A coastal region near Kingston SE, planted from the late 1980s, notable for investment from the Rhône: Michel Chapoutier planted biodynamic Shiraz here in the late 1990s. The climate is cool and windy, giving peppery Shiraz.
appellations.terroir: Terra rossa and sand over limestone within sight of the ocean; about 1,520 growing degree days.
appellations.nerd_note: Chapoutier's Mount Benson vineyard was one of the first biodynamic plantings in South Australia.

appellations.name: Robe
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A cool coastal region around the fishing town of Robe, registered in 2006. Large vineyards supply fruit to Treasury Wine Estates and others; local sparkling and Pinot show the climate.
appellations.terroir: One of the coolest Limestone Coast regions (about 1,485 growing degree days), on limestone ridges and sand.
appellations.nerd_note: Robe was a landing point for thousands of Chinese gold seekers in the 1850s, who walked from here to the Victorian goldfields to avoid a landing tax.

appellations.name: Mount Gambier
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Riesling
appellations.summary: South Australia's coolest region, around the extinct volcano and Blue Lake at Mount Gambier, registered in 2010. Small vineyards make crisp whites, Pinot Noir and sparkling base.
appellations.terroir: About 1,450 growing degree days, volcanic and limestone soils, frequent cloud and wind.
appellations.nerd_note: The Blue Lake in the volcano's crater turns cobalt blue every November.

appellations.name: Lower Murray
appellations.summary: The zone covering South Australia's stretch of the Murray River, whose only region is the Riverland. It is the largest wine-producing zone in the state by volume. In 2026 the Riverland alone crushed about 389,000 tonnes, close to a third of Australia's harvest, so the zone's fortunes are a barometer of the bulk-wine market.
appellations.terroir: Hot, dry and irrigated from the Murray.

appellations.name: Riverland
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, Colombard, Petit Verdot, Nero d'Avola, Montepulciano, Fiano
appellations.summary:
The Riverland, along the Murray around Renmark, Berri, Loxton and Waikerie, is Australia's largest wine region by tonnage, with about 21,800 ha of vines. In 2026 it crushed about 389,000 tonnes, roughly 30 percent of the national total, even in a short year. The Canadian Chaffey brothers began irrigation at Renmark in 1887, and soldier-settler blocks after both world wars filled it with family growers. Its fruit makes cask, bulk and branded wine for the world.

The Riverland is also where Australia is rethinking warm-climate wine. Growers such as Ashley Ratcliff (Ricca Terra), 919 Wines, Bassham and Delinquente have planted Nero d'Avola, Montepulciano, Fiano, Vermentino and Touriga Nacional, varieties that hold acidity in the heat and need less water. The falling demand for cheap red since 2020 has hit the region hardest: many growers have left grapes unpicked or pulled out vines.
appellations.terroir: Hot and dry: about 2,350 growing degree days, 148 mm of growing-season rain and 254 mm a year. Every vine depends on Murray water allocations. Sandy loams over limestone (mallee country).
appellations.nerd_note: Angove's, founded in 1886 near Adelaide, moved to Renmark in 1910 and later invented one of the first commercial wine casks with a tap in the 1960s.

appellations.name: Far North
appellations.summary: A vast zone covering the north of South Australia, from the Flinders Ranges to the deserts, whose only region is the Southern Flinders Ranges. Almost all of its 858,000 square kilometres are desert with no vines.

appellations.name: Southern Flinders Ranges
appellations.summary: Small vineyards in the hills around Wirrabara, Port Pirie and Laura, registered in 2003, mostly making full, warm-climate reds and some Riesling for local producers. It is the northernmost wine region in South Australia, and its cooler hill sites near Wirrabara and Bundaleer Forest show that altitude can offset the heat of the plains below.
appellations.terroir: Warm (about 2,220 growing degree days) but with cooler pockets at altitude up to about 950 m.

appellations.name: The Peninsulas
appellations.summary: A zone covering the Eyre and Yorke peninsulas west of Adelaide, with about 70 ha of scattered vineyards, notably around Boston Bay near Port Lincoln and on Yorke Peninsula. It has no registered regions.
appellations.terroir: Maritime, on limestone and sand.

appellations.name: Victoria
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscat
appellations.summary: The state GI for Victoria, used for blends across its 21 regions. Victoria has more registered regions than any other state, reflecting a climate range from the hot Murray to the cold Macedon Ranges, and the family-scale, region-driven industry that rebuilt itself after phylloxera.
appellations.terroir: Cool maritime south, alpine centre and north-east, hot irrigated north-west.
appellations.nerd_note: In the 1880s Victoria produced more wine than New South Wales and South Australia combined; phylloxera and the 1890s depression ended that.

appellations.name: Port Phillip
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: The zone around Melbourne and Port Phillip Bay, containing the Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula, Geelong, Macedon Ranges and Sunbury. It is Victoria's cool-climate core and the centre of Australian Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
appellations.terroir: Bay and Bass Strait moderate the coastal regions; the Great Dividing Range lifts Macedon.

appellations.name: Yarra Valley
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc, Nebbiolo
appellations.summary:
The Yarra Valley, an hour east of Melbourne, was Victoria's first wine region and is its most celebrated. Swiss settlers planted it from the 1840s: Paul de Castella at Yering Station, his brother Hubert at St Hubert's and Guillaume de Pury at Yeringberg. In 1889 a Yering wine won a grand prix at the Paris Exposition. Then fashion, phylloxera fears and the dairy industry wiped it out; the last vintage at Yeringberg in its first life was 1921.

Doctors and scientists brought it back. Dr Reg Egan replanted Wantirna Estate in 1963, Dr Bailey Carrodus founded Yarra Yering in 1969 and Dr John Middleton Mount Mary in 1971, both making Bordeaux and Burgundy styles of rare finesse. Moët & Chandon chose the valley for Domaine Chandon in 1986, and since the 2000s producers such as Giant Steps, Oakridge, Mac Forbes, Yarra Yering under Sarah Crowe, and Timo Mayer have made it Australia's best-known source of elegant Pinot Noir and tight, struck-match Chardonnay, as well as perfumed, medium-bodied Shiraz and Cabernet.

The region is split by geology and altitude. The lower, warmer valley floor and northern slopes (Coldstream, Dixons Creek, Gruyere) suit Cabernet and Shiraz on grey sandy clay loams; the Upper Yarra (Hoddles Creek, Seville, Woori Yallock), on deep red volcanic soils at up to about 400 m, is cooler and wetter and makes taut Chardonnay and Pinot. Wine Australia records about 1,440 growing degree days, among the coolest of mainland Australia's major regions.
appellations.terroir: Rainfall around 1,080 mm a year and 550 mm in the growing season, high for Australia. Grey sandy loams over clay and sandstone on the valley floor and northern hillsides; red volcanic krasnozem in the Upper Yarra. Bushfires (2009) and smoke taint (2020) are recurring risks.
appellations.nerd_note: Mount Mary's Quintet is a blend of all five Bordeaux reds, and until 2008 the estate sold almost entirely by mailing list; Dr Middleton refused to enter wine shows.

appellations.name: Mornington Peninsula
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Shiraz
appellations.summary: A boot-shaped peninsula between Port Phillip Bay and Western Port, an hour south of Melbourne, surrounded by water on three sides. Vines arrived in the 1880s, but the modern industry dates from the 1970s, when Baillieu Myer (Elgee Park, 1972) and Nat and Rosalie White (Main Ridge, 1975) planted. Today about 200 small vineyards make Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris (often labelled Pinot Grigio in a nod to the peninsula's Italian heritage) with a tense, saline freshness. Producers such as Paringa Estate, Kooyong, Stonier, Yabby Lake, Ten Minutes by Tractor, Eldridge and Moorooduc have built an international reputation for Pinot that varies vineyard by vineyard.
appellations.terroir: Maritime and cool (about 1,560 growing degree days). Red Hill and Main Ridge, at 150 to 300 m on deep red volcanic soils, are the coolest; Moorooduc and Tuerong, lower and on sandier soils over clay, are warmer and riper. Strong winds at flowering reduce yields.
appellations.nerd_note: Kathleen Quealy and Kevin McCarthy at T'Gallant made Pinot Grigio fashionable in Australia in the 1990s.

appellations.name: Geelong
appellations.summary: Geelong was one of Australia's biggest wine districts in the 1860s and 1870s, planted by Swiss vignerons, and it was where phylloxera was found in 1877: the government ordered the vines uprooted, and the region vanished for 90 years. Revived from 1966 by Daryl and Nini Sefton at Idyll, it now makes some of Victoria's most distinctive Pinot, Chardonnay and Shiraz, from Gary Farr's By Farr and Bannockburn on the Moorabool Valley's limestone and basalt, and from the Bellarine Peninsula and Surf Coast.
appellations.terroir: Dry and windy (518 mm a year), with about 1,570 growing degree days. Three sub-areas: the Moorabool Valley (volcanic basalt and limestone), the Bellarine Peninsula (maritime) and the Surf Coast.
appellations.nerd_note: Bannockburn's Serré Pinot Noir comes from a close-planted block of about 9,000 vines per hectare, rare in Australia, planted on Burgundian lines in 1984.

appellations.name: Macedon Ranges
appellations.summary: The coldest wine region on mainland Australia by Wine Australia's measure (about 1,390 growing degree days), high on the Great Dividing Range north-west of Melbourne around Kyneton, Gisborne, Lancefield and Woodend. It is marginal country, where a cold spring can cut a crop in half, but its traditional-method sparkling and taut Pinot and Chardonnay are among Australia's most elegant. Bindi (Michael Dhillon), Curly Flat, Hanging Rock and Granite Hills are the reference producers.
appellations.terroir: Altitudes of about 300 to 800 m; granite, sandstone and volcanic soils; windy, with frost risk.
appellations.nerd_note: Hanging Rock Winery's 'Macedon' non-vintage sparkling uses a solera-style reserve system started in the late 1980s.

appellations.name: Sunbury
appellations.summary: A small region just north-west of Melbourne airport, with a nineteenth-century heritage: Craiglee's bluestone winery was built in 1864, and its 1872 Hermitage was still being opened in the twentieth century. Today Craiglee and Galli Estate make peppery Shiraz and Chardonnay.
appellations.terroir: Dry (about 530 mm), windy plains with volcanic soils.
appellations.nerd_note: Goona Warra, also at Sunbury, has a bluestone winery from 1863.

appellations.name: Central Victoria
appellations.summary: The zone of central Victorian goldfields and river country, containing Bendigo, Heathcote, Goulburn Valley (with Nagambie Lakes), Strathbogie Ranges and Upper Goulburn. Its regions share a gold-rush history: most nineteenth-century vineyards here were planted with mining wealth and destroyed by phylloxera, and the modern industry began again in the 1960s and 1970s.

appellations.name: Heathcote
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Fiano
appellations.summary: Heathcote's fame rests on a band of deep red soil derived from Cambrian greenstone, volcanic rock about 500 million years old, that runs north-south along the Mount Camel Range for about 60 km. On it Shiraz is dense yet fresh, with dark fruit, spice and fine tannin. Ron and Elva Laughton planted Jasper Hill in 1975 and their dry-grown, own-rooted Georgia's Paddock and Emily's Paddock Shiraz made the region famous; Wild Duck Creek, Paul Wilson and Tellurian followed. The GI was registered in 2002 after a dispute with Bendigo over the boundary.
appellations.terroir: About 1,880 growing degree days and only 521 mm of annual rain. Altitude 110 to 600 m. The Cambrian red soils hold water well, allowing dry-farming.
appellations.nerd_note: Jasper Hill's Emily's Paddock is co-planted with a little Cabernet Franc, which goes into the Shiraz.

appellations.name: Bendigo
appellations.summary: Gold-rush Bendigo had more than 100 vineyards by 1880 until phylloxera arrived in 1893 and the government ordered vineyards destroyed. Stuart Anderson revived it at Balgownie in 1969, and the region now makes rich, minty Shiraz and Cabernet from small family producers.
appellations.terroir: Warm and dry (about 1,880 growing degree days, 496 mm of rain), on gravelly quartz soils over clay.

appellations.name: Goulburn Valley
appellations.summary: The Goulburn River valley in north-central Victoria, from Seymour to Shepparton. Its heart is the Nagambie Lakes subregion, where Tahbilk has made wine since 1860; elsewhere irrigated orchards dominate. The broader region outside Nagambie Lakes is mostly irrigated orchard and dairy country, with vineyards that supply fruit for larger wineries.
appellations.terroir: Warm (about 2,100 growing degree days) and dry, on alluvial soils.

appellations.name: Nagambie Lakes
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Marsanne, Cabernet Sauvignon, Viognier, Roussanne
appellations.summary: A subregion registered in 2001, defined by the lagoons and billabongs of the Goulburn River near Nagambie, the only Australian GI defined by its water bodies. It holds Tahbilk, whose 1860 Shiraz block survived phylloxera on sandy soils, and whose Marsanne vineyard (planted from 1927) is one of the largest and oldest in the world. Mitchelton, founded in 1969 with a tower overlooking the river, is the other landmark.
appellations.terroir: Wine Australia's description points to the influence of the lakes and the region's red sandy loams with ironstone gravel; the water moderates temperatures at night.
appellations.nerd_note: Tahbilk's Marsanne is unoaked and built to age: at ten years old it tastes of honeysuckle and lanolin.

appellations.name: Strathbogie Ranges
appellations.summary: A granite plateau between the Goulburn Valley and the Upper Goulburn at roughly 150 to 1,000 m, registered in 2002, supplying cool-climate Riesling, Chardonnay and sparkling base as well as some fine Shiraz.
appellations.terroir: Granite-derived sandy soils; about 1,620 growing degree days.

appellations.name: Upper Goulburn
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Hilly country around Mansfield, Alexandra and Lake Eildon at the foot of the Victorian Alps, registered in 2003. Delatite, founded by the Ritchie family in 1968, is its best-known estate, with aromatic whites and biodynamic farming.
appellations.terroir: Elevations up to about 1,000 m, cool (about 1,540 growing degree days).

appellations.name: North East Victoria
appellations.grapes: Muscat, Muscadelle, Shiraz, Durif, Prosecco, Sangiovese
appellations.summary: The zone of the Ovens and King valleys, the Victorian Alps and the Murray around Rutherglen: Rutherglen, Glenrowan, Beechworth, King Valley and Alpine Valleys. The zone is the home of Rutherglen Muscat and Topaque and of the Italian families of the King Valley, and it climbs from the Murray plains to alpine vineyards at almost 1,000 m.

appellations.name: Rutherglen
appellations.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge ('Rutherglen Brown Muscat'), Muscadelle, Durif, Shiraz
appellations.summary:
Rutherglen, on the Murray River in north-east Victoria, makes one of the world's great fortified wines, and it does so from grapes ripened to raisins on the vine. Gold was found here in 1860; the gold ran out within a decade, but many miners stayed and planted vines, and by the 1880s the region was exporting to London. Phylloxera arrived in 1899 and the region shrank, but a handful of families (Chambers, Morris, Campbell, Sutherland Smith at All Saints, Stanton & Killeen) kept their soleras of fortified wine going, some for more than 140 years.

Rutherglen Muscat is made from a dark-skinned clone of Muscat à Petits Grains, left on the vine until the berries shrivel and reach 17 to 20 degrees Baumé. Fermentation is stopped early with grape spirit, and the wine then ages for years in old casks stacked in hot iron sheds, where heat concentrates it and the 'angels' share' takes about half the volume over 20 years. The result is dark brown, viscous and tastes of raisin, toffee, coffee and rose petal. Topaque, made the same way from Muscadelle, was called Tokay until EU agreements retired the name in 2010; it tastes of malt, tea leaf and butterscotch.

The producers' Muscat of Rutherglen network classifies these wines on four tiers by richness and age: Rutherglen (an average age of about 3 to 5 years), Classic (6 to 10), Grand (11 to 19) and Rare (more than 20 years). Only a few hundred bottles of the Rare wines are released each year; Chambers Rosewood and Morris have barrels from the 1890s and earlier in their blends. The region also makes dense, inky Durif, a red grape that found its best Australian home here.
appellations.terroir: Warm and continental (about 2,080 growing degree days), with hot days, cool nights and a long dry autumn that lets fruit shrivel safely on the vine. Soils are red loams and alluvial sands along the Murray; vineyards sit at about 120 to 590 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Bill Chambers' blends of Rare Muscat include wine from casks started by his great-grandfather; the oldest material in the Chambers solera is thought to date to the 1890s.

appellations.name: Glenrowan
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Durif, Muscat, Muscadelle, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Ned Kelly's last stand took place at Glenrowan in 1880, and Baileys of Glenrowan, founded in 1870, still makes thick, dry-grown Shiraz and fortified Muscat and Topaque on the red granite soils of the Warby Ranges.
appellations.terroir: Warm (about 2,020 growing degree days), on deep red loam derived from granite.
appellations.nerd_note: Baileys' 1920s Block Shiraz is still dry-grown.

appellations.name: Beechworth
appellations.summary: A gold-rush town in the foothills of the Victorian Alps that became a cult wine region thanks to Rick Kinzbrunner, who planted Giaconda at Everton Upper in 1982. Giaconda's Chardonnay, fermented with wild yeast and aged in a granite cave cellar, is one of Australia's most sought-after whites, and Kinzbrunner's Nebbiolo and Shiraz are equally serious. Sorrenberg (1985), Castagna (biodynamic Syrah and Sangiovese), Savaterre and A. Rodda followed.
appellations.terroir: About 1,720 growing degree days. Altitudes from about 200 to 1,000 m, on granite and on sandy, quartz-rich soils over decomposed granite; cool nights.
appellations.nerd_note: Giaconda blasted its cellar into the granite hillside so the wines age at a natural cool temperature.

appellations.name: King Valley
appellations.grapes: Prosecco (Glera), Pinot Grigio, Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Chardonnay, Riesling
appellations.summary: A narrow valley rising into the Alps from Milawa, settled after the Second World War by Italian families who grew tobacco. When tobacco collapsed in the 1990s they planted vines, and the Pizzini, Dal Zotto and Brown families made the King Valley Australia's Prosecco capital. Otto Dal Zotto planted the first Prosecco vines in 1999. Since an EU challenge, Australia has defended 'Prosecco' as a grape variety name. Brown Brothers, founded at Milawa in 1889, is the region's oldest producer.
appellations.terroir: Vineyards from about 150 m at Milawa to over 800 m at Whitlands; about 1,710 growing degree days, wetter (970 mm) than most.
appellations.nerd_note: Brown Brothers runs a small 'Kindergarten' winery where it has trialled more than 100 grape varieties.

appellations.name: Alpine Valleys
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Tempranillo, Prosecco, Shiraz, Saperavi
appellations.summary: The Ovens, Kiewa, Buckland and Buffalo river valleys around Bright and Myrtleford, registered in 1999, with vineyards up to about 1,000 m among former tobacco and hop farms. Producers such as Billy Button, Mayford and Gapsted experiment widely.
appellations.terroir: About 1,580 growing degree days; alluvial soils; cold winters.

appellations.name: North West Victoria
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: The Victorian bank of the Murray, from Swan Hill to Mildura. Its regions, Murray Darling and Swan Hill, cross the river into New South Wales. Almost all of its fruit is irrigated from the Murray and goes into branded and bulk wine, much of it labelled South Eastern Australia.
appellations.terroir: Hot and irrigated.

appellations.name: Murray Darling
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Colombard
appellations.summary: One of the three great irrigated regions, straddling the Murray around Mildura, Robinvale and Wentworth in both Victoria and New South Wales, with about 13,500 ha of vines. In 2026 it crushed about 237,000 tonnes. The Chaffey brothers began irrigation at Mildura in 1887. Lindeman's Karadoc winery made the region's best-known export, Bin 65 Chardonnay, launched in 1985; at its peak several million cases a year were sold.
appellations.terroir: About 2,550 growing degree days and 284 mm of rain a year: entirely irrigated. Sandy red mallee soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The GI is registered in both Victoria and New South Wales because it crosses the state line along the river.

appellations.name: Swan Hill
appellations.summary: An irrigated Murray River region around Swan Hill and Robinvale, straddling Victoria and New South Wales, producing about 35,000 to 47,000 tonnes a year for branded and bulk wine. Like the Murray Darling region downstream, it depends entirely on river water allocations, which in drought years can decide the size of the crop.
appellations.terroir: Hot (about 2,360 growing degree days), very dry (329 mm), irrigated.

appellations.name: Western Victoria
appellations.summary: The zone of western Victoria's ranges and plains: Grampians (with Great Western), Pyrenees and Henty. It is one of the coolest parts of the state, and its historic centre is the gold-rush town of Great Western, where wine has been made at Best's and at the cellars that became Seppelt since the 1860s.

appellations.name: Grampians
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Meunier
appellations.summary: The region around the sandstone Grampians ranges, Ararat and Great Western, whose cool, peppery, medium-bodied Shiraz is among Australia's most elegant. Its history is gold-rush: Henry Best planted Concongella in 1866, and Hans Irvine's Great Western winery (later Seppelt) dug kilometres of tunnels ('drives') to age traditional-method sparkling wine from 1868 onward. Mount Langi Ghiran, Best's and The Story make the reference Shiraz today.
appellations.terroir: About 1,540 growing degree days; altitudes up to about 500 m on vineyards; soils of sandy loam over clay and granite-derived gravels.
appellations.nerd_note: Seppelt's Great Western also made sparkling Shiraz, a uniquely Australian style, from the 1890s.

appellations.name: Great Western
appellations.summary: A subregion of the Grampians registered in 2007 around the village of Great Western. Its name had long been used on cheap sparkling wine made elsewhere by Seppelt, and its registration came with legally enforceable conditions on use. It contains Best's Concongella vineyard, planted from 1866, whose Nursery Block holds about 40 varieties, several of them unidentified, and some of the oldest Pinot Meunier and Dolcetto vines in the world.
appellations.terroir: Granite-derived sandy loams over clay, cool and dry.
appellations.nerd_note: Wine Australia notes that the use of 'Great Western' is subject to legally enforceable conditions because of the history of the name on sparkling wine.

appellations.name: Pyrenees
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Rolling hills around Avoca and Moonambel, named after the Pyrenees by the explorer Thomas Mitchell. Rémy Martin planted Chateau Remy (now Blue Pyrenees) for brandy and sparkling in 1963, and Taltarni and Dalwhinnie built the reputation for firm, minty Shiraz and Cabernet.
appellations.terroir: About 1,710 growing degree days; 507 mm of rain; quartz-gravel and clay loams at 200 to 800 m.

appellations.name: Henty
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: A huge, sparsely planted region in Victoria's far south-west near Portland and Hamilton, one of the coolest in mainland Australia (about 1,430 growing degree days). Crawford River's Rieslings (John Thomson, from 1975) are among the country's best, and Seppelt once sourced Drumborg fruit here for sparkling and Riesling.
appellations.terroir: Maritime, windy and cool, on volcanic basalt soils near the coast.

appellations.name: Gippsland
appellations.summary: A zone covering eastern Victoria from Phillip Island to the New South Wales border, with no registered regions and fewer than 200 ha of vines. It is famous for one estate: Bass Phillip, where Phillip Jones planted dense, unirrigated Pinot Noir at Leongatha South from 1979 and made wines that were compared with Burgundy grand crus. Burgundian Jean-Marie Fourrier became a partner in the estate in 2020.
appellations.terroir: South Gippsland is cool and wet, on deep, fertile red soils; East Gippsland is warmer.
appellations.nerd_note: Bass Phillip's Premium Pinot comes from vines planted at about 9,000 per hectare, very dense by Australian standards.

appellations.name: Australia
appellations.summary: The national GI, used for wines blended from anywhere in the country. Most Australian wine sold in casks or at entry-level prices is labelled 'South Eastern Australia' rather than 'Australia', because that super zone already covers the irrigated heartland.

appellations.name: South Eastern Australia
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, Moscato
appellations.summary: The super zone that took Australian wine to the world. It covers all of New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania and the wine-growing parts of Queensland and South Australia, and so includes the three great irrigated regions on the Murray, Darling and Murrumbidgee rivers. It lets companies blend fruit freely from Coonawarra to the Riverina and still name a place. Brands such as Jacob's Creek, [yellow tail], Lindeman's Bin 65 and Hardys Stamp built their export volume under this label.
appellations.terroir: Too large to have a single terroir; it exists for blending.
appellations.nerd_note: South Eastern Australia was registered in 1996; its boundary in South Australia and Queensland was drawn to exclude deserts and the tropical north.

appellations.name: Western Australia
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon
appellations.summary: The state GI for Western Australia. The state is outside the South Eastern Australia super zone, so its blends cannot carry that name; Western Australian wineries use this GI or their region.
contains: Eastern Plains, Inland and North of Western Australia

appellations.name: New South Wales
appellations.summary: The state GI for New South Wales, including the irrigated Riverina and the Hunter. New South Wales crushes the second-largest share of Australia's grapes, most of it from the Riverina around Griffith, and it holds the country's first vineyards (Farm Cove, 1788, and Camden Park).

appellations.name: Hunter Valley
appellations.summary: The zone containing the Hunter region and its subregions. 'Hunter Valley' is the zone's registered name, while the region inside it is simply 'Hunter'; on labels both are used. Its history goes back to James Busby's and George Wyndham's plantings around 1830, and it is the only zone in New South Wales with registered subregions.
appellations.nerd_note: The zone 'Hunter Valley' and the region 'Hunter' have almost identical boundaries.

appellations.name: Hunter
appellations.summary:
The Hunter is Australia's oldest continuously producing wine region and its most counter-intuitive one. It is too hot, too humid and too wet at harvest for classic viticulture, yet it makes a white that exists nowhere else: Hunter Semillon, picked early at about 10 to 11 percent alcohol, fermented in stainless steel without oak, and bottled lean and lemony. Over ten to twenty years in bottle it develops toast, honey and lanolin flavours that taste as if it had been oaked. Its medium-bodied, earthy Shiraz, once called 'Hunter River Burgundy', is equally individual.

James Busby planted at Kirkton near Branxton around 1830; George Wyndham's Dalwood (1828), Henry Lindeman's Cavendish (1843) and Edward Tyrrell's Ashmans (1858) followed. Maurice O'Shea at Mount Pleasant (1921 to 1956) made the region's greatest mid-century wines, and his sons-in-spirit at Lindemans, Tyrrell's, Drayton's and McWilliam's kept the style alive. Since the 1970s, Lake's Folly (Max Lake's Cabernet, 1963), Brokenwood (Graveyard Shiraz) and the Tyrrells' Vat 1 Semillon and Vat 47 Chardonnay (Australia's first commercial Chardonnay varietal, 1971) have built its modern reputation.

Summer rain and humid cloud cover make the Hunter warm but not baking: the cloud reduces sunshine, and harvest comes early, usually January, to beat the rain. Old, unirrigated vineyards on the red clay of the Brokenback Range (Pokolbin) give the Shiraz; sandy alluvial flats along the creeks give the best Semillon.
appellations.terroir: About 2,215 growing degree days but 556 mm of growing-season rain and frequent cloud. Two soil types matter: friable sandy alluvial flats (Semillon) and red-brown volcanic and limestone-derived clay loams on the slopes of the Brokenback Range (Shiraz).
appellations.nerd_note: Tyrrell's 4 Acres Shiraz comes from vines planted in 1879; the Old Patch block dates to 1867.

appellations.name: Pokolbin
appellations.summary: The historic heart of the Lower Hunter, registered as a subregion in 2010, under the Brokenback Range west of Cessnock. Almost every famous Hunter name is here: Tyrrell's, Mount Pleasant, Lake's Folly, Brokenwood, Drayton's and Tulloch.
appellations.terroir: Red volcanic and limestone-derived clay loams on the slopes, sandy alluvial flats near the creeks; about 1,355 ha of vines in 173 square kilometres.
appellations.nerd_note: Mount Pleasant's Lovedale vineyard, planted by O'Shea in 1946, gives one of the Hunter's longest-lived Semillons.

appellations.name: Broke Fordwich
appellations.summary: A subregion of the Lower Hunter around Broke, west of Pokolbin, registered in 1997, known for Semillon from sandy creek flats (Wollombi Brook) and for Hunter Semillon from producers such as Margan.
appellations.terroir: Sandy alluvial soils and some volcanic clay; slightly drier than Pokolbin.

appellations.name: Upper Hunter Valley
appellations.summary: The upper reaches of the Hunter around Denman and Muswellbrook, registered in 2010. Rosemount Estate, founded at Denman in 1969, made its Roxburgh Chardonnay here; the area is drier and warmer than the Lower Hunter.
appellations.terroir: Black and red clay and limestone soils; irrigated in many places.

appellations.name: Central Ranges
appellations.summary: The zone on the western slopes and tablelands of the Great Dividing Range, containing Mudgee, Orange and Cowra. The zone's regions climb from about 300 m at Cowra to more than 1,000 m on the slopes of Mount Canobolas at Orange, giving a range of climates for Chardonnay, Shiraz and Cabernet.

appellations.name: Mudgee
appellations.summary: Mudgee was planted by German settlers in 1858 and was one of Australia's first regions to adopt a quality-control appellation (a voluntary scheme in 1979). Its Aboriginal name means 'nest in the hills'. Huntington Estate, Lowe and Robert Stein make generous Cabernet and Shiraz; Craigmoor's Chardonnay plantings were among Australia's oldest.
appellations.terroir: Altitudes from about 450 to 1,100 m on the western slopes; warm days and cool nights; red loams over clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Mudgee is thought to have provided one of the clones from which much Australian Chardonnay descends (the 'Mudgee clone').

appellations.name: Orange
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Orange is defined by altitude: the GI covers only land above 600 m on the slopes of Mount Canobolas, an extinct volcano reaching 1,395 m. That makes it one of Australia's coolest regions, with crisp Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, elegant Shiraz and Pinot Noir. Philip Shaw, Ross Hill, Printhie, Bloodwood (one of the first, 1983) and See Saw lead.
appellations.terroir: Basalt-derived red volcanic soils near the mountain, shale and limestone lower down; about 1,620 growing degree days.
appellations.nerd_note: The 600 m contour line is written into the GI definition.

appellations.name: Cowra
appellations.summary: Lower and warmer than Orange, Cowra made its name in the 1970s and 1980s supplying Chardonnay to Petaluma and Rothbury; today its fruit goes mostly into blends. Its warm climate and granite soils give ripe, peachy Chardonnay.
appellations.terroir: About 2,250 growing degree days; granite-derived sandy soils along the Lachlan River.
appellations.nerd_note: Petaluma's first Chardonnay (1977) used Cowra fruit before Brian Croser planted the Piccadilly Valley.

appellations.name: Southern New South Wales
appellations.summary: The zone containing Canberra District, Hilltops, Tumbarumba and Gundagai. It stretches from the Canberra District's cool, high plateau to Tumbarumba in the Snowy Mountains foothills, and much of its fruit goes to sparkling and premium Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Canberra District
appellations.summary: A cool, high region around the national capital, most of whose vineyards lie across the border in New South Wales, around Murrumbateman, because land in the Australian Capital Territory is leasehold. Scientists from the CSIRO founded it: John Kirk at Clonakilla (1971) and Edgar Riek at Lake George (1971). Tim Kirk's Clonakilla Shiraz Viognier, co-fermented in the Côte-Rôtie manner since 1992, is one of Australia's most admired wines, and the region's Riesling is fine and dry.
appellations.terroir: About 1,650 growing degree days; elevations of 500 to 850 m; continental with frosty winters and dry summers; granite and shale soils.
appellations.nerd_note: Ken Helm organises the annual Canberra International Riesling Challenge.

appellations.name: Hilltops
appellations.summary: Around Young, in cherry country, at 450 to 700 m. A Croatian immigrant, Nichole Jasprizza, planted vines in the 1860s. Today Grove Estate, Freeman and Moppity make firm Shiraz, Cabernet and Nebbiolo.
appellations.terroir: Granite and basalt soils; about 1,975 growing degree days.
appellations.nerd_note: Freeman Vineyards grows Rondinella and Corvina and makes an amarone-style wine.

appellations.name: Tumbarumba
appellations.summary: High in the western foothills of the Snowy Mountains at 300 to 800 m, Tumbarumba grows some of Australia's finest Chardonnay and sparkling base for big companies. It was badly hit by the 2019 to 2020 bushfires.
appellations.terroir: About 1,720 growing degree days; granite and basalt soils; cold nights and frost risk.
appellations.nerd_note: Penfolds' Yattarna Chardonnay has included Tumbarumba fruit.

appellations.name: Gundagai
appellations.summary: A broad region around Gundagai on the Murrumbidgee, registered in 2002, mostly growing fruit for larger wineries. Its warm western parts grow Shiraz and Cabernet for blends, while higher eastern sites near Tumut are cooler.
appellations.terroir: Warm (about 2,070 growing degree days).

appellations.name: Big Rivers
appellations.summary: The irrigation zone of inland New South Wales, containing the Riverina, Perricoota, and the New South Wales parts of Murray Darling and Swan Hill. It crushes about a fifth of Australia's grapes.
appellations.terroir: Hot, dry and irrigated.

appellations.name: Riverina
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Semillon, Cabernet Sauvignon, Durif, Pinot Grigio
appellations.summary: The Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area around Griffith and Leeton, opened in 1912 and settled largely by Italian families, crushes about 235,000 to 300,000 tonnes a year. Casella's [yellow tail], launched in 2001, became the best-selling imported wine brand in the United States within a few years. The region's one great wine is a sweet one: De Bortoli's Noble One botrytis Semillon, first made in 1982, showed that the morning humidity around Griffith could produce noble rot in autumn.
appellations.terroir: About 2,545 growing degree days, 420 mm of annual rain; flat red loams irrigated from the Murrumbidgee.
appellations.nerd_note: De Bortoli Noble One is Australia's most successful sweet table wine; the first 1982 vintage was made from Semillon left on the vine after a sales slump.

appellations.name: Perricoota
appellations.summary: A small irrigated region near Moama on the Murray, opposite Echuca, registered in 1999. Its warm, flat vineyards along the Murray grow Shiraz, Cabernet and Chardonnay, much of it sold to larger wineries.
appellations.terroir: Warm (about 2,225 growing degree days).

appellations.name: South Coast
appellations.summary: The coastal zone south of Sydney, containing Shoalhaven Coast and Southern Highlands. It covers the humid coastal strip and the cooler Southern Highlands behind it, both close enough to Sydney for cellar-door tourism.

appellations.name: Shoalhaven Coast
appellations.summary: A humid coastal region around Nowra and Berry, where disease-resistant Chambourcin is a local specialty because summer rain brings mildew. Its small producers sell mostly to visitors from Sydney, and humid summers make disease control the main viticultural task.
appellations.terroir: About 1,220 mm of annual rain.
appellations.nerd_note: Coolangatta Estate stands on the convict-built estate founded by Alexander Berry in the 1820s, now restored as a winery and resort.

appellations.name: Southern Highlands
appellations.summary: A cool, wet plateau around Bowral and Moss Vale at 500 to 900 m, two hours south of Sydney, registered in 2002, mostly cellar-door producers. Rain and spring frost are the main risks; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine make the most of the cool climate.
appellations.terroir: About 1,640 growing degree days, 940 mm of rain.

appellations.name: Northern Rivers
appellations.summary: Subtropical north coast of New South Wales; its only region is Hastings River. Summer rain and humidity make viticulture difficult, which is why disease-resistant hybrids such as Chambourcin are common.

appellations.name: Hastings River
appellations.summary: A tiny subtropical region around Port Macquarie with about 13 ha of vines, where Cassegrain pioneered Chambourcin in Australia in the 1980s. Its annual rainfall of about 1,450 mm is among the highest of any Australian wine region.
appellations.terroir: About 1,450 mm of annual rain.

appellations.name: Northern Slopes
appellations.summary: The northern tablelands and slopes of New South Wales; its only region is New England Australia. Its vineyards are scattered across a cool, high tableland, often above 1,000 m.

appellations.name: New England Australia
appellations.summary: A high plateau around Armidale, Tenterfield and Inverell, registered in 2008, with vineyards at up to about 1,300 m. The suffix 'Australia' distinguishes it from New England in the United States.
appellations.terroir: About 1,760 growing degree days; granite and basalt.

appellations.name: Western Plains
appellations.summary: A vast zone covering western New South Wales, with almost no vineyards and no regions. The zone exists so that every part of the state is covered by a GI.

appellations.name: South West Australia
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon
appellations.summary: The zone covering Western Australia's fine-wine heartland: Margaret River, Great Southern, Geographe, Pemberton, Manjimup and Blackwood Valley, with about 9,900 ha of vines. Margaret River alone grows more than half of the zone's vines and crushed about 28,000 tonnes in 2024 and 2025.
appellations.terroir: Maritime, Mediterranean.

appellations.name: Margaret River
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Shiraz, Merlot
appellations.summary:
Margaret River is a narrow, wave-beaten cape between the Indian and Southern oceans, 270 km south of Perth, and in barely 50 years it has become one of the world's best regions for Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay. Its existence was predicted on paper. In 1965 the agronomist John Gladstones published an analysis showing that the area's climate resembled Bordeaux in a dry year. Dr Tom Cullity, a Perth cardiologist, planted Vasse Felix in 1967; other doctors followed with Moss Wood (Bill Pannell, 1969) and Cullen (Kevin and Diana Cullen, 1971), then Cape Mentelle (David Hohnen, 1970), Sandalford, Leeuwin Estate (Denis and Tricia Horgan, 1974, with advice from Robert Mondavi) and Voyager.

The Cabernet is the region's signature: ripe, structured and fine-grained, with blackcurrant, bay leaf and a saline freshness, and with remarkable consistency from year to year because the ocean buffers both heat and frost. Chardonnay rivals it: Leeuwin Estate's Art Series Chardonnay, first made in 1980, was the first Australian white to rank with grand cru Burgundy, and the region's distinctive Gingin clone, with its 'hen and chicken' bunches of large and small berries, gives concentrated, pineapple-and-grapefruit wines. Semillon-Sauvignon Blanc blends are the everyday white.

Gladstones later proposed six subregions based on soils and climate: Yallingup, Carbunup, Wilyabrup, Treeton, Wallcliffe and Karridale. They are not registered GIs but are widely used. Wilyabrup, in the north-centre, holds Vasse Felix, Moss Wood, Cullen and Woodlands and is the classic Cabernet district; the southern Wallcliffe and Karridale, cooler and wetter, give finer Chardonnay.
appellations.terroir: Wine Australia records about 1,900 growing degree days and only 213 mm of rain from October to April against 914 mm for the year. Ocean on three sides prevents frost and extreme heat; strong winds at flowering cut yields. Soils are ancient: gravelly and sandy loams derived from granite and gneiss of the Leeuwin Complex, often lateritic, over clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Cullen was certified biodynamic in 2004, and its Diana Madeline Cabernet blend is named after founder Di Cullen.

appellations.name: Great Southern
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Australia's largest wine region by area (about 150 km by 100 km) and one of its least known, the Great Southern covers granite hills, karri forest and coast in the far south-west. Its five subregions (Albany, Denmark, Frankland River, Mount Barker and Porongurup) range from maritime to continental, so the region can make both pristine Riesling and spicy Shiraz. It was the first part of the south-west to be planted for fine wine: after Harold Olmo of UC Davis recommended it in 1956, the state government planted a trial vineyard at Forest Hill near Mount Barker in 1966, and Forest Hill's 1975 Riesling won national trophies.
appellations.terroir: About 1,735 growing degree days, cool and dry in summer. Soils are mostly sandy and gravelly loams over granite, gneiss and laterite.
appellations.nerd_note: Alkoomi, at Frankland River, was planted in 1971 by Merv and Judy Lange on a sheep farm.

appellations.name: Frankland River
appellations.summary: The most inland and continental part of the Great Southern, registered in 2000, among sheep paddocks and jarrah forest. Frankland Estate's Isolation Ridge Riesling and peppery Shiraz from Alkoomi and Ferngrove show its brightness and spice.
appellations.terroir: Lateritic gravels and loams; warm days and cold nights; about 1,320 ha of vines.
appellations.nerd_note: Frankland Estate hosts an international Riesling tasting that has brought Germany's top growers to Western Australia.

appellations.name: Mount Barker
appellations.summary: The first Great Southern subregion (1997) and home of Plantagenet (1968) and Forest Hill (1966), whose early Rieslings and Shiraz established the region. Wines are structured, with peppery Shiraz and long-lived Riesling.
appellations.terroir: Lateritic gravelly loam over granite and gneiss.

appellations.name: Porongurup
appellations.summary: Vineyards on the north-facing slopes of the Porongurup Range, a granite massif 1.1 billion years old, registered in 1999. Castle Rock and Duke's Vineyard make some of Australia's most delicate, mineral Riesling.
appellations.terroir: Karri loam over decomposed granite at 250 to 400 m, above the frost line; about 96 ha of vines.

appellations.name: Albany
appellations.summary: Maritime vineyards around Western Australia's oldest European settlement (1826), registered in 1999, suited to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Albany's ocean breezes and granite-derived soils give some of Western Australia's most delicate Pinot Noir.
appellations.terroir: Sandy gravels over granite; strong ocean influence.
appellations.nerd_note: Wignalls was one of the first to show Western Australian Pinot Noir in the 1980s.

appellations.name: Denmark
appellations.summary: The wettest and coolest corner of the Great Southern, among karri and tingle forests near the coast, registered in 2003; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are the focus. Its high rainfall and cool summers make it the most Burgundian of the Great Southern's subregions.
appellations.terroir: Karri loam; high rainfall.

appellations.name: Geographe
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Tempranillo, Sangiovese
appellations.summary: Coastal plain and hills around Bunbury and the Ferguson Valley, just north of Margaret River, registered in 1999. Warmer than its neighbour, it suits Shiraz, Tempranillo and Italian varieties; Capel Vale (1974) was its pioneer.
appellations.terroir: About 2,030 growing degree days; Tuart sands on the coast, gravelly loams in the hills.

appellations.name: Pemberton
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Merlot
appellations.summary: Karri-forest country around Pemberton, registered in 2006, cooler and wetter than Margaret River; Picardy (founded by Bill Pannell after he sold Moss Wood) made its reputation for Pinot and Chardonnay.
appellations.terroir: About 1,730 growing degree days, 1,095 mm of rain; karri loam and gravel.

appellations.name: Manjimup
appellations.summary: Forest and orchard country north of Pemberton, registered in 2006, also known for truffles. Its vineyards, at about 100 to 350 m, sit between Pemberton's karri forest and the drier Blackwood Valley, and are known for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Merlot.
appellations.terroir: About 1,740 growing degree days; lateritic gravel loams.
appellations.nerd_note: Manjimup produces most of Australia's black Périgord truffles.

appellations.name: Blackwood Valley
appellations.summary: An inland valley around Bridgetown and Boyup Brook, registered in 1998, whose fruit is mostly sold to other regions' wineries. Warmer and drier than Pemberton, it suits Shiraz and Cabernet.
appellations.terroir: About 1,840 growing degree days.

appellations.name: Greater Perth
appellations.summary: The zone around Perth, containing the Swan District (with Swan Valley), Perth Hills and Peel. It is where Western Australian wine began in the 1830s, with Olive Farm, Houghton and Sandalford on the Swan River.
appellations.terroir: Hot and Mediterranean.

appellations.name: Swan District
appellations.summary: The region north and east of Perth along the Swan River, containing the Swan Valley subregion, one of the hottest fine-wine regions in Australia. Its hot, dry summers once made it the centre of Western Australian fortified wine.
appellations.terroir: About 2,570 growing degree days; under 150 mm of rain from October to April.

appellations.name: Swan Valley
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Verdelho, Grenache, Shiraz, Muscat, Pedro Ximénez
appellations.summary: Western Australia's oldest wine district, 25 minutes from Perth's centre, registered as a subregion in 2003. Thomas Waters planted Olive Farm in 1830, and Houghton (1836) became famous for its 'White Burgundy', a Chenin-based blend created by Jack Mann in 1937 that was Australia's best-selling white for decades. Croatian families such as the Kosoviches (Westfield) and Yurisiches settled here in the early twentieth century. Today it makes dry Chenin and Verdelho, fortified 'liqueur' wines and generous reds.
appellations.terroir: Hot (about 2,570 growing degree days) and dry, with deep alluvial loams and sands along the river.
appellations.nerd_note: Houghton's White Burgundy was renamed White Classic after the EU wine agreement retired 'Burgundy' on Australian labels.

appellations.name: Perth Hills
appellations.summary: Small vineyards in the Darling Range east of Perth, registered in 1999, cooler than the Swan Valley below. Its elevated sites, on lateritic gravel, get cool evening breezes and ripen grapes later than the Swan Valley.
appellations.terroir: Lateritic and granitic soils at 150 to 400 m.

appellations.name: Peel
appellations.summary: A coastal region around Mandurah, registered in 2001, with about 50 ha of vines. Its sandy coastal soils suit Chenin Blanc and Shiraz.
appellations.terroir: Tuart sands and gravelly loams.
appellations.nerd_note: Peel Estate held an annual blind 'Shiraz tasting' comparing six-year-old Australian Shiraz, started in the 1980s.

appellations.name: Central Western Australia
appellations.summary: A wheatbelt zone east of Perth with about 40 ha of vines and no regions. Its scattered vineyards are mostly hobby or cellar-door plantings among wheat farms.

appellations.name: West Australian South East Coastal
appellations.summary: A coastal zone around Esperance with almost no vineyards. It exists, like several outback zones, so that every part of Western Australia is covered by a GI.

appellations.name: Eastern Plains, Inland and North of Western Australia
match: Eastern Plains, Inland and North of Western Australia
Eastern Plains - Inland and North of Western Australia
Eastern Plains, Inland And North Of Western Australia
appellations.summary: A catch-all zone covering more than two million square kilometres of desert and tropics, from the Kimberley to the Nullarbor, created so that every part of the state sits in a zone.
appellations.nerd_note: It is by far the largest wine GI in Australia by area, and among the largest in the world.

appellations.name: Tasmania
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling
appellations.summary:
Tasmania is one GI that works as a state, zone and region at once, and it has become the most dynamic fine-wine area in Australia. With fewer than 800 growing degree days on Wine Australia's figures, it is the only part of the country with a climate truly comparable to Champagne or Burgundy, and its 1,700 ha now supply most of Australia's best traditional-method sparkling and a growing share of its best Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Large mainland companies (Accolade, Treasury, Brown Brothers) bought Tasmanian vineyards and wineries from the 1990s to secure cool-climate fruit.

The island's informal areas differ sharply. The north, the Tamar Valley and Pipers River, is cooler and wetter; Pipers River, close to Bass Strait, gives the tightest sparkling base (Jansz, Pipers Brook). The south-east, in the rain shadow of the central highlands, is drier and sunnier: the Coal River Valley around Richmond and Cambridge (Tolpuddle, Domaine A, Frogmore Creek, Pooley) and the Derwent Valley (Stefano Lubiana, Moorilla, Derwent Estate) make riper Pinot and Chardonnay. The East Coast around Swansea and Freycinet is warm by Tasmanian standards, and the Huon Valley and D'Entrecasteaux Channel in the far south are the coolest of all.

Ed Carr's House of Arras, with sparkling wines aged up to a decade or more on lees, and Jansz, the Yalumba-owned house founded with Louis Roederer in 1985, are the sparkling references; Tolpuddle, bought in 2011 by Martin Shaw and Michael Hill Smith of Shaw + Smith, Stefano Lubiana (biodynamic), Dawson James and Sailor Seeks Horse lead for Pinot and Chardonnay.
appellations.terroir: Cool and maritime, with long, slow autumns. Wine Australia records about 790 growing degree days and 585 mm of growing-season rain (the north is wetter, the south-east drier). Soils include red basalt-derived krasnozems at Pipers River, dolerite and sandstone in the south, and alluvial gravels along the Tamar and Derwent.
appellations.nerd_note: Tasmania's oldest wine estate in operation, Providence near Launceston, began in 1956 as La Provence; its French name was changed after a challenge from the French appellation authorities.

appellations.name: Queensland
appellations.summary: Queensland's state GI, which also acts as its zone. It contains the Granite Belt and South Burnett regions; elsewhere small vineyards grow around Mount Tamborine and the Darling Downs.
appellations.terroir: Subtropical; quality vineyards depend on altitude.

appellations.name: Granite Belt
appellations.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Verdelho, Fiano, Tempranillo, Saperavi
appellations.summary: A plateau of granite boulders around Stanthorpe and Ballandean on the New South Wales border, at 600 to 1,300 m, registered in 2002. The altitude makes it cool despite a latitude of 28 to 29 degrees south. Italian migrants grew grapes here from the 1920s; today about 300 ha support boutique wineries, and the 'Strange Birds' trail promotes unusual varieties.
appellations.terroir: Decomposed granite sands; about 1,880 growing degree days; summer rain and spring frost.

appellations.name: South Burnett
appellations.summary: A warm, subtropical region around Kingaroy and Murgon, registered in 2000, with small cellar-door wineries. Its summer rainfall and warmth suit Verdelho, Shiraz and hybrid grapes.
appellations.terroir: About 2,660 growing degree days.

appellations.name: Northern Territory
appellations.summary: A state-level GI covering the Northern Territory, registered for completeness; there is essentially no commercial viticulture apart from a former vineyard near Alice Springs (Chateau Hornsby, 1970s to 2000s).
appellations.nerd_note: Chateau Hornsby at Alice Springs was for decades Australia's most remote winery.

appellations.name: Australian Capital Territory
appellations.summary: A state-level GI for the national capital territory. Most 'Canberra District' wineries are across the border in New South Wales; a handful, such as Mount Majura, are inside the ACT.

appellations.name: New Zealand
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: The national GI, created by statute as an 'enduring' GI and registered in July 2017. It covers any wine of which at least 85 percent comes from New Zealand, typically blends across regions.

appellations.name: North Island
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Merlot, Syrah, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: An enduring GI covering the North Island, used for blends of North Island regions (for example Hawke's Bay and Gisborne fruit). The North Island had about 7,500 ha of vines in 2025, about 17 percent of the national total, led by Hawke's Bay and Gisborne.

appellations.name: South Island
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: An enduring GI covering the South Island, used for blends such as Marlborough and Nelson or Central Otago and Waitaki fruit. The South Island had about 36,700 ha of vines in 2025, about 83 percent of the national total, most of them in Marlborough.

appellations.name: Northland
appellations.summary: New Zealand's northernmost and warmest wine region, and its first: Samuel Marsden planted vines at Kerikeri in 1819 and James Busby made wine at Waitangi in the 1830s. Today about 70 ha of vines support small producers making Syrah, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris in a subtropical, humid climate where no point is more than 50 km from the sea.
appellations.terroir: Warm, humid and wet, with clay soils; disease pressure is the main challenge.
appellations.nerd_note: Karikari Estate on the Karikari Peninsula is one of the northernmost vineyards in the country.

appellations.name: Auckland
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: The Auckland GI covers New Zealand's largest city and its surrounding countryside, with only about 250 ha of vines but many of the country's biggest wine companies' headquarters. It was the heart of twentieth-century New Zealand wine, when Dalmatian, Lebanese and English families made fortified and table wine in Henderson, Kumeu and Huapai. It contains three sub-GIs: Matakana to the north, Kumeu to the north-west and Waiheke Island in the Hauraki Gulf.
appellations.terroir: Warm, humid and wet (more than 1,200 mm of rain a year), on heavy clay soils; vineyards favour slopes and free-draining sites.

appellations.name: Matakana
appellations.grapes: Pinot Gris, Syrah, Merlot, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: A small district about an hour north of Auckland, around the village of Matakana and the Mahurangi coast. The first modern vineyards were planted in the 1960s and 1970s, and today about a dozen boutique producers make Bordeaux blends, Syrah, Pinot Gris and Chardonnay for the weekend visitors from the city.
appellations.terroir: Clay soils over sandstone on rolling hills, with warm, humid summers moderated by sea breezes from both coasts.
appellations.nerd_note: Matakana's vineyards share the district with olive groves and a Saturday farmers' market that draws Aucklanders north.

appellations.name: Kumeu
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Merlot
appellations.summary: Kumeu, with neighbouring Huapai and Waimauku north-west of Auckland, is where Dalmatian families such as the Brajkoviches (Kumeu River), Nobilos and Selaks built wineries from the 1930s and 1940s. Its fame today rests on Chardonnay: Kumeu River, run by Michael Brajkovich (New Zealand's first Master of Wine, 1989) and his family, makes some of the finest Chardonnays in the New World, especially the single-vineyard Maté's and Hunting Hill.
appellations.terroir: Heavy clay soils over sandstone that retain water in a wet climate; humid summers favour early-ripening varieties and careful canopy work.
appellations.nerd_note: Kumeu River's Maté's Vineyard, planted in 1990, is named after Maté Brajkovich, who arrived from Dalmatia and bought the property in 1944.

appellations.name: Waiheke Island
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: A hilly island in the Hauraki Gulf, a 40-minute ferry ride from downtown Auckland, which since the 1980s has become a source of expensive Bordeaux blends and Syrah. Goldwater Estate planted the first modern vineyard in 1978 and Stephen White's Stonyridge (1981) made its Larose blend a cult wine. The island is warmer and drier than mainland Auckland, and now has about 30 wineries alongside its holiday homes.
appellations.terroir: Clay over weathered greywacke on steep slopes; warm and maritime, with lower rainfall than Auckland.
appellations.nerd_note: Destiny Bay sells its Bordeaux blends at prices among the highest in New Zealand.

appellations.name: Gisborne
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Gewürztraminer
appellations.summary: Gisborne, on the East Cape, is one of the first places in the world to see the sun each day and calls itself New Zealand's Chardonnay capital. Its fertile alluvial plains grew much of the country's bulk white in the 1970s and 1980s; today its 1,300 ha supply Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and sparkling base, and a few artisans prove its quality. James and Annie Millton started New Zealand's first certified organic and later biodynamic estate here in 1984; their Clos de Ste Anne Chenin Blanc and Chardonnay are reference wines.
appellations.terroir: Warm, sunny and relatively humid; fertile silty loams on the Poverty Bay flats, with clay-limestone hillsides at Manutuke.
appellations.nerd_note: Matawhero's Gewürztraminer in the 1970s and 1980s, made by Denis Irwin, was one of the first New Zealand wines to win international praise.

appellations.name: Hawke's Bay
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Chardonnay, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary:
Hawke's Bay is New Zealand's second-largest wine region (about 4,600 ha) and its oldest continuously producing one: French Marist missionaries planted vines in 1851 and their Mission Estate still makes wine at Taradale. It is the country's red-wine heartland, making Bordeaux-style blends of Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc and, increasingly, peppery Syrah, as well as rich Chardonnay.

The key to its reds is gravel. The Gimblett Gravels, about 800 ha of stony former riverbed west of Hastings, were exposed when a great flood in 1867 diverted the Ngaruroro River. Once considered worthless (a concrete company wanted to quarry them), they absorb daytime heat and drain freely, ripening Syrah and Cabernet in a cool climate; producers formed the Gimblett Gravels Winegrowers Association and trademarked the name in 2001. The Bridge Pa Triangle to the south, on red metal soils, and the limestone hills around Havelock North (home of Te Mata Estate, founded in 1896) are the other key districts. Te Mata's Coleraine blend, first made in 1982, is New Zealand's most famous red.
appellations.terroir: Sunny and dry for the North Island, sheltered from westerlies by the Ruahine and Kaweka ranges. Soils range from free-draining alluvial gravels (Gimblett Gravels, Bridge Pa) to silt loams and limestone hills.
appellations.nerd_note: Alan Limmer planted Syrah at Stonecroft in the Gimblett Gravels area in 1984 and released its first Syrah from the 1989 vintage, the first modern New Zealand Syrah on the market.

appellations.name: Central Hawke's Bay
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: The southern, cooler part of Hawke's Bay around Waipukurau and Waipawa, registered as its own GI in 2019. It has only a few vineyards, but its limestone hills and cooler climate suit Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and aromatic whites.
appellations.terroir: Cooler and more continental than the Heretaunga Plains, with limestone and clay soils.
appellations.nerd_note: Lime Rock Wines takes its name from the limestone outcrops of its vineyard near Waipawa.

appellations.name: Wairarapa
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Syrah
appellations.summary: The Wairarapa lies an hour north-east of Wellington across the Remutaka Range and holds about 1,190 ha of vines, mostly Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc. It contains two registered sub-GIs, Martinborough and Gladstone, and the area around Masterton (Opaki). Boutique producers dominate; the region makes only about 3 percent of New Zealand's wine but a much larger share of its fine Pinot.
appellations.terroir: A rain shadow behind the Remutaka and Tararua ranges, with strong north-westerly winds that cut yields and keep disease low. Free-draining river-terrace soils over gravel.

appellations.name: Martinborough
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Syrah
appellations.summary: A small village laid out in the shape of a Union Jack in the 1870s, now one of New Zealand's most important Pinot Noir districts. In 1979 a report by soil scientist Dr Derek Milne compared its climate and free-draining terrace soils to Burgundy; Neil McCallum (Dry River) and Clive Paton (Ata Rangi) planted that year and the next, followed by Martinborough Vineyard and Palliser. Their Pinots, savoury, firm and long-lived, set the standard for New Zealand red in the 1990s. Ata Rangi's Pinot Noir, from the 'Abel' clone said to have been smuggled in from Burgundy, is the region's icon.
appellations.terroir: The Martinborough Terrace, an old river terrace of silt over deep, free-draining gravel; dry, windy and cool, with frost risk. The Te Muna Road area to the south-east has similar soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The 'Abel' or 'Gumboot' clone of Pinot Noir is said to have been confiscated from a traveller's gumboot at Auckland airport by customs officer Malcolm Abel, who propagated it.

appellations.name: Gladstone
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Riesling
appellations.summary: A tiny rural district in the Ruamahanga River valley between Martinborough and Masterton, registered in 2019. A handful of family vineyards make Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris and Pinot Noir on gravelly river terraces.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial gravels and silts on terraces of the Ruamahanga River; slightly cooler and wetter than Martinborough.
appellations.nerd_note: Urlar is one of the few Wairarapa estates with organic and biodynamic certification.

appellations.name: Nelson
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling
appellations.summary: Nelson, at the top of the South Island, is one of the sunniest places in New Zealand and a small, artistic wine region of about 970 ha. It has two distinct areas: the Waimea Plains, with stony alluvial soils that give fresh Sauvignon and aromatic whites, and the Moutere Hills, where clay-bound gravels give richer Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
