appellations.grapes: Delaware, Muscat Bailey A, Koshu, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A wine GI designated in 2021 for Osaka prefecture, whose hillside vineyards around Kashiwara and Habikino were Japan's largest grape-growing area in the 1930s. Katashimo Winery, founded in 1914, is the oldest winery in western Japan and makes Delaware, Koshu and Muscat Bailey A.
appellations.terroir: Warm, humid slopes of the Ikoma and Kongo ranges overlooking the city.

appellations.name: Nagano
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Concord, Niagara
appellations.summary: A wine GI designated in 2021 for Nagano prefecture, whose high, dry valleys make it one of Japan's best regions for European varieties. The Kikyogahara plateau at Shiojiri, where Château Mercian persuaded growers to switch from Concord to Merlot in 1976, produces Japan's best-known Merlot. The Chikumagawa valley near Ueda and Tomi (Villa d'Est, Mercian's Mariko vineyard), Azumino and the Kiso valley have dozens of newer wineries.
appellations.terroir: Altitudes of 500 to 900 m, the lowest rainfall in Japan, cold winters and large day-night temperature swings; volcanic and gravelly soils.
appellations.nerd_note: Obuse Winery's Domaine Sogga, run by Akihiko Soga (Takahiko's brother), was one of the first Japanese wineries to farm organically and make wine with wild yeast.

appellations.name: Nashik Valley Wine
appellations.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel
appellations.summary: India's only registered wine Geographical Indication, covering wines made from grapes grown in the Nashik valley of Maharashtra. Nashik, at about 600 m on the Deccan plateau, has more than 30 wineries, led by Sula Vineyards (founded 1999). Its wines are mostly fresh, fruity whites, rosés and medium-bodied reds, picked in the dry winter after the vines are pruned twice a year.
appellations.terroir: Basalt-derived soils; dry winter ripening season (harvest January to March) after the monsoon; irrigation from Godavari reservoirs.
appellations.nerd_note: Indian vineyards are 'double pruned': back-pruning in April builds the vine's wood through the monsoon, and fruit-pruning in October times ripening for the cool, dry winter.

sites.name: Langmeil Freedom 1843 Vineyard
sites.text: Langmeil's winery on the North Para River at Tanunda stands beside the Freedom vineyard, a block of Shiraz planted in 1843 by Christian Auricht, a Silesian settler. It is generally cited as the oldest continuously producing Shiraz vineyard in the world. The Lindner family bought the site in 1996, and the wine, Freedom 1843 Shiraz, comes from about 3.5 acres of gnarled, own-rooted vines.

sites.name: Turkey Flat
sites.text: The Schulz family's Turkey Flat at Bethany, on the southern edge of Tanunda, holds Shiraz planted in 1847 by Johann Fiedler, a Silesian settler, among the oldest vines in the Barossa. The cellar door is in the old butcher's shop and bluestone cottage. Turkey Flat also helped revive Barossa Grenache and Mataro rosé.

sites.name: Seppeltsfield
sites.text: Joseph Seppelt, a Silesian snuff and tobacco merchant, bought land here in 1851 and built a wine village of bluestone cellars. In 1878 his son Benno laid down a barrel of Tawny to be opened in 1978, beginning the Centennial Collection, the world's only unbroken run of single-vintage Tawny since 1878. Each year the 100-year-old Para Vintage Tawny is released (the 1926 in 2026), in 100 ml bottles.
sites.class: Centennial Collection, 100 Year Old Para Vintage Tawny

sites.name: Seppelt Family Mausoleum
sites.text: A Doric-columned mausoleum built in 1927 on a hill above Seppeltsfield, reached along an avenue of about 2,000 date palms planted by Seppelt workers during the Depression of the 1930s. It is one of the most photographed landmarks in Australian wine.

sites.name: Yalumba
sites.text: Founded in 1849 at Angaston by Samuel Smith, an English brewer, Yalumba is Australia's oldest family-owned winery, now run by the fifth generation of the Hill-Smith family. Its blue-marble clock-tower winery dates from 1908, and it is one of the few Australian wineries with its own cooperage. Yalumba drafted the Barossa Old Vine Charter in 2007 and planted Viognier in the Eden Valley in 1980, a pioneering move.

sites.name: Chateau Tanunda
sites.text: Built in 1890 from Bethany bluestone in eleven months, Chateau Tanunda was said to be the largest building in the Southern Hemisphere when finished, a co-operative winery and distillery designed to exploit Europe's phylloxera shortage. Seppelt owned it from 1916 to 1998; the Geber family restored it and its cellars, and it is on the South Australian Heritage Register.

sites.name: Rockford
sites.text: Robert O'Callaghan's Rockford, founded in 1984 in old stone buildings at Krondorf, became the conscience of the Barossa during the 1980s vine-pull years by buying old-vine fruit from growers and making it with 1880s machinery, including a hand-fed basket press. Its Basket Press Shiraz and cellar-door-only Black Shiraz (a sparkling red) are cult wines.

sites.name: Torbreck
sites.text: Founded by David Powell in 1994 at Marananga, in the northern-central Barossa, Torbreck built its reputation on old-vine Shiraz, Grenache and Mataro sourced from family growers, and on Rhône-inspired blends such as RunRig (Shiraz with a little Viognier). It became one of the defining names of the 1990s and 2000s Barossa boom.

sites.name: Penfolds Kalimna (Block 42)
sites.text: Penfolds bought the Kalimna vineyard near Moppa in the northern Barossa in 1945. Its Block 42, planted around 1888, is thought to be the oldest continuously producing Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard in the world, and is bottled separately only in rare years. Kalimna fruit has been a backbone of Grange.

sites.name: Cirillo Old Vines, Light Pass
sites.text: The Cirillo family's Grenache at Light Pass was planted in 1848 on deep sand and still grows on its own roots; it is among the oldest Grenache vines in the world. The family bought the vineyard in 1969, and the wine is named The Vincent after Vincenzo Cirillo.

sites.name: Hewitson Old Garden, Rowland Flat
sites.text: A block of Mourvèdre at Rowland Flat planted in 1853, said to be the oldest Mourvèdre vines in the world. Dean Hewitson bought it in 1998 and has propagated cuttings from it, partly to safeguard the genetic material.

sites.name: Jacob's Creek Visitor Centre
sites.text: Johann Gramp planted the first commercial vineyard in the Barossa beside Jacob's Creek at Rowland Flat in 1847. His company, Orlando, made the first Jacob's Creek red from the 1973 vintage and turned it into one of the best-known Australian wines abroad.

sites.name: Peter Lehmann Wines
sites.text: When an oversupply in the late 1970s left Barossa growers with no buyer, Peter Lehmann, then winemaker at Saltram, kept buying their grapes and founded his own company in 1979. His guarantee helped save many old vineyards from the government-funded vine pull of the 1980s.

sites.name: Henschke, Keyneton
sites.text: Johann Christian Henschke, a Silesian stonemason, began making wine at Keyneton in 1868, and the family's sixth generation now runs it. Cyril Henschke released Hill of Grace as a single-vineyard wine with the 1958 vintage, and Stephen and Prue Henschke turned the estate into a leader of sustainable and biodynamic viticulture.

sites.name: Hill of Grace
sites.text: An eight-hectare vineyard opposite the Gnadenberg (Hill of Grace) Lutheran church near Moculta, planted by Nicolaus Stanitzki in the 1860s. Its oldest Shiraz vines, the 'Grandfathers', are around 160 years old and still own-rooted. Hill of Grace Shiraz is Australia's most famous single-vineyard wine after Grange.

sites.name: Mount Edelstone
sites.text: A 16-hectare Shiraz vineyard near Keyneton, planted in 1912 by Ronald Angas and bought by Cyril Henschke in 1974. Its wine, first made as a single vineyard in 1952, is one of Australia's longest-running single-vineyard Shiraz labels.

sites.name: Pewsey Vale
sites.text: Joseph Gilbert planted Pewsey Vale in the High Eden hills in 1847. Yalumba replanted it in 1961 after decades of grazing, and its terraced Riesling vineyard, at nearly 500 m, now produces The Contours, a Riesling released with five years in bottle.

sites.name: Grosset, Auburn
sites.text: Jeffrey Grosset opened his winery in a former dairy factory in Auburn in 1981. He led the 2000 Clare Valley screwcap initiative and makes two benchmark Rieslings that show the region's split: Polish Hill (slate, austere) and Springvale (red loam over limestone at Watervale).

sites.name: Polish Hill River
sites.text: A side valley east of Sevenhill settled by Polish immigrants from 1856, whose stone church of St Stanislaus Kostka (1871) is now a museum. The valley's hard slate and shale soils produce the leanest, most mineral Clare Rieslings, including Grosset's Polish Hill, first made in 1981.

sites.name: Sevenhill Cellars
sites.text: Austrian Jesuits fleeing persecution founded Sevenhill in 1851 and planted vines to make sacramental wine. It is the oldest winery in the Clare Valley and still run by the Jesuits, with St Aloysius' church (1875) and a crypt beneath it on the property.

sites.name: Wendouree
sites.text: A winery founded in 1895 near Clare whose old, dry-grown Shiraz, Malbec, Cabernet and Mataro are made by Tony Brady and family in the same slate-walled cellar. Wendouree sells almost entirely by mailing list, has no cellar door or website, and its tannic reds need two decades.

sites.name: Jim Barry Wines
sites.text: Jim Barry, the first qualified winemaker to work in the Clare Valley (1947), founded this company in 1959. The Armagh Shiraz, first made in 1985, is its flagship, and in 2016 it released Australia's first commercial Assyrtiko, from cuttings imported from Santorini.

sites.name: Kilikanoon
sites.text: A Clare producer founded at Penwortham in 1997, whose old-vine Shiraz (Oracle, Attunga 1865 from vines planted in 1865) and Mort's Block Riesling from Watervale are regional benchmarks. Its cellar door sits in a stone building among the vines in the centre of the valley.

sites.name: d'Arenberg Cube
sites.text: A five-storey glass building opened in 2017 at d'Arenberg, McLaren Vale, inspired by a Rubik's cube and designed to look as if it is floating above the vines. d'Arenberg was founded by Joseph Osborn in 1912 and is run by Chester Osborn, who still foot-treads and basket-presses reds. The Dead Arm Shiraz is named after a vine disease (Eutypa) that kills one arm of the vine.

sites.name: Clarendon Hills Astralis
sites.text: Roman Bratasiuk's Clarendon Hills sources from old, dry-grown vines in the hills above Clarendon, at the northern edge of McLaren Vale. Astralis Shiraz, first made in 1994 from vines planted in the 1920s, became one of Australia's most expensive wines; the estate also bottles single-vineyard Grenache such as Romas and Blewitt Springs.

sites.name: Hardys Tintara
sites.text: Thomas Hardy, who arrived in South Australia in 1850, bought the Tintara winery in McLaren Vale in 1876 and built the company that became Australia's largest. The old Tintara cellars on the main road still house a cellar door; the Hardy family's vineyards include Sauvignon Blanc planted in the 1870s.

sites.name: Chateau Reynella
sites.text: John Reynell planted vines here in 1838, two years after South Australia was founded, and dug an underground cellar in 1845, one of the first winery buildings in the state. The property, now the headquarters of the Hardys business, holds the Old Cave Cellar.

sites.name: Wirra Wirra
sites.text: Founded in 1894 by Robert Strangways Wigley, a cricket-loving eccentric, and revived in 1969 by Greg and Roger Trott. Its ironstone-walled winery and flagship RSW Shiraz and Church Block blend are McLaren Vale fixtures.

sites.name: Coriole
sites.text: The Lloyd family's Coriole, around an 1860 stone farmhouse, planted Sangiovese in 1985 and Fiano in 2000, early moves that helped make McLaren Vale Australia's laboratory for Mediterranean varieties.

sites.name: Bleasdale
sites.text: Frank Potts founded Bleasdale at Langhorne Creek in 1850 and the family still runs it. Its red gum lever press, built in 1892 from a single tree, worked until 1960; Potts also flooded the vineyards in winter by diverting the Bremer River.

sites.name: Shaw + Smith
sites.text: Founded in 1989 by Michael Hill Smith, Australia's first Master of Wine, and his cousin Martin Shaw. Their Adelaide Hills Sauvignon Blanc became a national benchmark; their M3 Chardonnay and Shiraz followed, and in 2011 they bought Tolpuddle in Tasmania.

sites.name: Penfolds Magill Estate
sites.text: Dr Christopher Rawson Penfold and his wife Mary planted vines at their cottage, The Grange, in 1844. Max Schubert made the first experimental Grange Hermitage here in 1951. Penfolds still makes the Magill Estate Shiraz from the five-hectare suburban vineyard, one of the few urban single-vineyard wines in the world, and the restored Grange cottage is on site.

sites.name: Wynns Coonawarra Estate
sites.text: John Riddoch built this triple-gabled limestone winery in 1891 for his Penola Fruit Colony. The Wynn family bought it in 1951; its gabled facade, drawn by artist Richard Beck, became the emblem of Coonawarra on every Wynns label. It makes the Black Label Cabernet (from 1954) and the John Riddoch Cabernet (from 1982).

sites.name: Yallum Park
sites.text: John Riddoch's homestead near Penola, built in 1880 for the pastoralist who founded the Coonawarra fruit colony in 1890. The Riddochs held huge pastoral runs across the south-east; Yallum Park is now a private heritage house.

sites.name: Majella
sites.text: The Lynn family were Coonawarra sheep farmers who planted vines in 1968 and sold grapes to Wynns before making their own wine from 1991. Majella's The Malleea Cabernet Shiraz is a classic Coonawarra blend.

sites.name: Tahbilk
sites.text: Founded in 1860 on the Goulburn River and owned by the Purbrick family since 1925, Tahbilk is the oldest family-owned winery in Victoria. A small block of Shiraz planted in 1860 survived phylloxera on its sandy soils and makes the 1860 Vines Shiraz; the estate also has one of the world's oldest and largest plantings of Marsanne (from 1927). Its 1860 cellars and tower are classified by the National Trust.

sites.name: Mitchelton
sites.text: Founded in 1969 on the Goulburn River near Nagambie, with a 55-metre observation tower that is a local landmark; Mitchelton helped revive Marsanne and Rhône varieties in Victoria.

sites.name: Best's Great Western, Concongella
sites.text: Henry Best planted Concongella in 1866, and the Thomson family has owned it since 1920. Its Nursery Block, planted in the 1860s, holds about 40 varieties, some still unidentified, and the world's oldest Pinot Meunier and Dolcetto vines; the 1868 slab-and-timber cellars are still in use.

sites.name: Seppelt Great Western drives
sites.text: Miners dug about 3 km of tunnels, called 'drives', into the hillside at Great Western from 1868 for Hans Irvine, who made traditional-method sparkling wine here. Seppelt bought the business in 1918 and used the drives to age 'Great Western' sparkling and the famous sparkling Shiraz. The drives are National Trust classified.

sites.name: Chambers Rosewood
sites.text: The Chambers family has made fortified wine at Rutherglen since 1858. Its Rare Muscat and Rare Muscadelle are blended from soleras that include wine laid down in the 1890s, and are among the most acclaimed fortified wines in the world. The cellar door is a working shed.

sites.name: Morris
sites.text: The Morris family has made wine near Rutherglen since George Francis Morris planted in 1859; by the 1880s his Fairfield winery was said to be one of the largest in the Southern Hemisphere. Mick and David Morris built its reputation for Muscat and Topaque; Old Premium Rare Muscat is the flagship.

sites.name: Campbells
sites.text: John Campbell, a Scottish gold miner, planted vines at Bobbie Burns in 1870, and the family still owns the winery. Campbells makes Muscat and Topaque on the four-tier Rutherglen ladder, with Merchant Prince Rare Muscat at the top, and Bobbie Burns Shiraz.

sites.name: All Saints Estate
sites.text: A turreted red-brick castle at Wahgunyah built in 1880s style by George Sutherland Smith, a Scottish carpenter, modelled on the Castle of Mey. The estate has made fortified wine since 1864 and is now owned by the Brown family (Eileen Brown and her children).

sites.name: Brown Brothers, Milawa
sites.text: John Francis Brown made his first wine at Milawa in 1889, and the family still runs one of Australia's largest family wineries. Brown Brothers pioneered variety trials in its Kindergarten winery and helped popularise Moscato and Prosecco in Australia.

sites.name: Giaconda
sites.text: Rick Kinzbrunner planted Giaconda on a steep granite slope at Everton Upper in 1982. Its Chardonnay, wild-fermented and aged in a cellar blasted into the granite, is one of Australia's most sought-after whites; production is tiny.

sites.name: Bass Phillip
sites.text: Phillip Jones planted close-spaced, unirrigated Pinot Noir at Leongatha South in 1979 on deep red soil and made wines compared with Burgundy. Burgundian Jean-Marie Fourrier and partners bought the estate in 2020.

sites.name: Mount Mary
sites.text: Dr John Middleton, a Melbourne physician, planted Mount Mary at Lilydale in 1971. Its Quintet (all five Bordeaux red varieties) and Triolet (Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Muscadelle) are among Australia's most elegant wines, sold mostly by mailing list.

sites.name: Yarra Yering
sites.text: Dr Bailey Carrodus, a plant physiologist, planted Yarra Yering on a north-facing slope at Gruyere in 1969. His Dry Red No. 1 (Cabernet blend) and Dry Red No. 2 (Shiraz blend) were unlike anything else in Australia; Sarah Crowe has made the wines since 2013.

sites.name: Yeringberg
sites.text: Guillaume de Pury, a Swiss from Neuchâtel, founded Yeringberg in 1863, and his descendants still own it. Wine stopped in 1921 and resumed in 1969 in the original 1885 three-storey gravity winery.

sites.name: Domaine Chandon Australia
sites.text: Moët & Chandon's Australian outpost, founded at Coldstream in 1986 on the old Green Point farm, helped prove that the Yarra Valley could make serious traditional-method sparkling wine.

sites.name: De Bortoli Yarra Valley
sites.text: The Riverina's De Bortoli family bought a Dixons Creek vineyard in 1987, and Steve Webber and Leanne De Bortoli turned it into a leader of lighter, more transparent Yarra Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

sites.name: Paringa Estate
sites.text: Lindsay McCall, a schoolteacher, planted Paringa at Red Hill South in 1985; its Pinot Noir and Shiraz won national trophies and put the Mornington Peninsula on the map.

sites.name: Ten Minutes by Tractor
sites.text: Named after the time it takes to drive a tractor between its original three vineyards, this Mornington Peninsula producer makes single-vineyard Pinot and Chardonnay that show the peninsula's site differences.

sites.name: Bannockburn Vineyards
sites.text: Stuart Hooper planted Bannockburn in the Moorabool Valley in 1974; Gary Farr, its winemaker for 20 years, worked vintages at Domaine Dujac. The close-planted Serré Pinot Noir is its icon.

sites.name: Jasper Hill
sites.text: Ron and Elva Laughton planted Jasper Hill on Heathcote's Cambrian greenstone in 1975, dry-grown and own-rooted. Georgia's Paddock and Emily's Paddock Shiraz made the region's reputation.

sites.name: Balgownie Estate, Bendigo
sites.text: Stuart Anderson, a pharmacist, planted Balgownie at Maiden Gully in 1969, reviving viticulture in Bendigo after phylloxera and government-ordered uprooting had ended it about 70 years earlier. Its Shiraz and Cabernet, firm and minty, made Bendigo a fine-wine name again.

sites.name: Dalwhinnie
sites.text: A Pyrenees estate at Moonambel planted in 1976 in an amphitheatre of hills, known for structured, long-lived Shiraz and Cabernet from dry-grown vines on quartz gravel at around 500 to 600 m. It is one of the region's most consistent producers.

sites.name: Farm Cove
sites.text: The first vines in Australia were planted at Farm Cove on Sydney Harbour in 1788, from cuttings the First Fleet collected at Rio de Janeiro and the Cape. They failed in the humid climate; the site is now part of the Royal Botanic Garden.

sites.name: Elizabeth Farm
sites.text: John and Elizabeth Macarthur's farmhouse at Parramatta (1793), the oldest surviving European building in Australia. The Macarthurs' sons later planted vines at Camden Park and sent wine to London; Elizabeth Farm is now a museum.

sites.name: Dalwood Estate
sites.text: George Wyndham bought Dalwood on the Hunter River in 1828 and planted vines there in 1830, among the first in the valley. Penfolds later owned it; it is now a small estate again.

sites.name: Tyrrell's
sites.text: Edward Tyrrell planted at Ashmans in 1858, and the family's fifth generation runs it. Vat 1 Semillon is the archetypal Hunter Semillon; Vat 47 (1971) was Australia's first commercial varietal Chardonnay, and the Old Patch Shiraz vines date from 1867.

sites.name: Mount Pleasant
sites.text: Maurice O'Shea, trained in France, made wine at Mount Pleasant from 1921 until his death in 1956, and his medium-bodied 'Hunter Burgundy' reds and Semillons are legendary. McWilliam's took full control in 1941, and the estate passed to new private owners in 2021 when McWilliam's was sold up; vines planted in 1880 and 1921 still crop.

sites.name: Lake's Folly
sites.text: Dr Max Lake, a Sydney surgeon, planted Cabernet Sauvignon at Pokolbin in 1963, the first new vineyard in the Hunter for decades and the start of Australia's boutique winery movement.

sites.name: Clonakilla
sites.text: CSIRO scientist John Kirk planted Clonakilla at Murrumbateman in 1971. His son Tim, inspired by Côte-Rôtie, co-fermented Shiraz with a little Viognier from 1992, creating one of Australia's most influential wines.

sites.name: Helm Wines
sites.text: Ken Helm, descended from German vignerons, founded Helm at Murrumbateman in 1973 in a nineteenth-century schoolhouse. He champions dry Riesling, founded the Canberra International Riesling Challenge in 2000, and helped make the Canberra District one of Australia's Riesling regions.

sites.name: Philip Shaw
sites.text: Former Rosemount chief winemaker Philip Shaw planted the Koomooloo vineyard on the slopes of Mount Canobolas in 1989, at about 900 m on volcanic soils. His Chardonnay and Shiraz helped build Orange's cool-climate reputation, and his sons now run the estate.

sites.name: Vasse Felix
sites.text: Dr Tom Cullity, a Perth cardiologist, planted Margaret River's first commercial vineyard here in 1967 after reading John Gladstones' climate research. Vasse Felix is now known for its Heytesbury Chardonnay and Tom Cullity Cabernet.

sites.name: Moss Wood
sites.text: Dr Bill Pannell planted Moss Wood at Wilyabrup in 1969; Keith and Clare Mugford have owned it since 1985. Its Cabernet Sauvignon is one of Australia's most consistent and long-lived.

sites.name: Cullen Wines
sites.text: Kevin and Diana Cullen planted at Wilyabrup in 1971; their daughter Vanya made the estate biodynamic and carbon-neutral. The Diana Madeline Cabernet blend is a Margaret River benchmark.

sites.name: Leeuwin Estate
sites.text: Denis and Tricia Horgan founded Leeuwin in 1974 with advice from Robert Mondavi. Its Art Series Chardonnay, first made in 1980, is often called Australia's finest white wine; the estate's concerts on the lawn have run since 1985.

sites.name: Voyager Estate
sites.text: A white Cape Dutch-style estate on Stevens Road, planted in 1978 and bought by mining magnate Michael Wright in 1991. Voyager is known for Chardonnay and Cabernet from the cooler southern part of Margaret River, and now farms organically.

sites.name: Houghton
sites.text: Founded in 1836 in the Swan Valley and named after Colonel Richard Houghton, one of the original partners. Jack Mann, winemaker from 1930 to 1972, created Houghton White Burgundy (1937), Australia's best-selling white for decades.

sites.name: Sandalford
sites.text: John Septimus Roe, Western Australia's first Surveyor-General, was granted land on the Swan River in 1840; the family began making wine commercially here, and the estate's jetty still serves wine-cruise boats from Perth.

sites.name: Frankland Estate
sites.text: Barrie Smith and Judi Cullam planted vines on their sheep farm at Frankland River in 1988; their Isolation Ridge Riesling and organic farming helped make the Great Southern a Riesling region.

sites.name: Plantagenet
sites.text: Tony Smith, an English-born farmer, planted Plantagenet near Mount Barker in 1968, the first commercial winery in the Great Southern, in a former apple-packing shed.

sites.name: Castle Rock Estate
sites.text: Angelo and Wendy Diletti's vineyards on the north-facing granite slopes of the Porongurup Range were planted in 1981, above the frost line. Their delicate, mineral, long-lived Rieslings and fine Pinot Noir define the subregion's style.

sites.name: Stefano Lubiana
sites.text: Steve and Monique Lubiana moved from South Australia's Riverland to the Derwent Valley in 1990 and built a biodynamic estate making Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and long-aged sparkling.

sites.name: Tolpuddle Vineyard
sites.text: Planted in 1988 in the Coal River Valley near Richmond and named after the Tolpuddle Martyrs, one of whom was transported to Tasmania. Shaw + Smith bought it in 2011, and its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are among Australia's best.

sites.name: Josef Chromy
sites.text: Josef Chromy fled Czechoslovakia in 1950, became a butcher in Launceston, and later invested in Tasmanian wine (Rochecombe, Jansz). His own estate at Relbia, in the Tamar Valley, opened in 2007.

sites.name: Jansz
sites.text: Founded in 1985 at Pipers River as a joint venture with Champagne Louis Roederer and now owned by Yalumba's Hill-Smith family, Jansz showed that Tasmania could make serious traditional-method sparkling wine.

sites.name: Ballandean Estate
sites.text: The Puglisi family's estate in the Granite Belt traces its vines to 1932, when Italian migrants grew grapes on the granite plateau near Stanthorpe; it is Queensland's oldest family-owned winery.

sites.name: Waitangi Treaty Grounds
sites.text: James Busby, British Resident from 1833, planted vines beside his house at Waitangi, where the Treaty of Waitangi was signed on 6 February 1840. The French explorer Dumont d'Urville tasted Busby's wine here that year and described a light, sparkling white: the first recorded New Zealand wine. The house is now part of the Treaty Grounds.

sites.name: Kerikeri Mission Station
sites.text: Samuel Marsden, the Anglican missionary, planted about 100 vine cuttings at the Kerikeri mission in 1819, the first recorded in New Zealand. The mission's Kemp House (1822) is the country's oldest surviving building.

sites.name: Mission Estate
sites.text: French Marist missionaries planted vines in Hawke's Bay in 1851 and moved to this hillside at Taradale in 1880. Mission Estate is New Zealand's oldest winery still under the same ownership, the Society of Mary; its seminary building now houses a restaurant.

sites.name: Church Road
sites.text: Founded in 1897 by Bartholomew Steinmetz, a Luxembourger who had worked at the Mission, and later run by Tom McDonald, whose Cabernet in the 1940s and 1950s was one of New Zealand's first serious reds. Pernod Ricard's Church Road now makes Bordeaux blends and Chardonnay here.

sites.name: Te Mata Estate
sites.text: Founded in 1896 by Bernard Chambers on the limestone hills of Havelock North, Te Mata is New Zealand's oldest winery in continuous production. John Buck and Michael Morris bought it in 1974; their Coleraine, a Cabernet-Merlot blend first made in 1982, is the country's most celebrated red, and Elston is a benchmark Chardonnay.

sites.name: Craggy Range
sites.text: Terry Peabody, an Australian businessman, founded Craggy Range in 1997 with viticulturist Steve Smith MW, at the foot of Te Mata Peak. It farms vineyards in the Gimblett Gravels (Sophia, Le Sol Syrah) and at Te Muna Road in Martinborough.

sites.name: Gimblett Gravels
sites.text: About 800 ha of stony former riverbed west of Hastings, exposed when a great flood in 1867 shifted the Ngaruroro River. The gravels store heat and drain freely, ripening Syrah, Merlot and Cabernet. Its winegrowers trademarked the name in 2001 and only wines with 95 percent Gimblett Gravels fruit may use it.

sites.name: Bridge Pa Triangle
sites.text: A triangle of land south of the Gimblett Gravels around the village of Bridge Pa, on 'red metal' soils (iron-stained gravels) and silt loams. It ripens Merlot and Syrah with a softer, more fragrant profile than the gravels and has organised itself as a wine district.

sites.name: Stonecroft
sites.text: Alan Limmer, a soil scientist, planted Syrah at Stonecroft in 1984 and released New Zealand's first modern Syrah from the 1989 vintage, starting the variety's rise in Hawke's Bay.

sites.name: Trinity Hill
sites.text: Founded in 1993 by John Hancock with London restaurateurs Robert and Robyn Wilson. Trinity Hill was one of the first to plant on Gimblett Road and helped create the Gimblett Gravels district; its Homage Syrah is a benchmark.

sites.name: Babich Wines
sites.text: Josip Babich, a Dalmatian immigrant, made his first wine in 1916 in Northland and moved to Henderson in 1919. The family still runs the business, one of the oldest of the West Auckland Croatian wineries.

sites.name: Kumeu River
sites.text: The Brajkovich family bought this Kumeu property in 1944. Michael Brajkovich, New Zealand's first Master of Wine (1989), transformed it into one of the world's great Chardonnay producers; Maté's Vineyard, planted in 1990, is named after his father.

sites.name: Stonyridge
sites.text: Stephen White planted Stonyridge at Onetangi on Waiheke Island in 1981. Its Larose, a Bordeaux-style blend, became one of New Zealand's most sought-after reds and made the island a wine destination.

sites.name: Man O' War
sites.text: A large estate on the remote eastern end of Waiheke Island, on land named after Captain Cook's search for masts. Its vineyards spread across steep slopes and coves facing the Hauraki Gulf.

sites.name: Millton Vineyards
sites.text: James and Annie Millton founded their estate at Manutuke near Gisborne in 1984; it became New Zealand's first certified organic winery and later biodynamic. Clos de Ste Anne, on a steep clay-limestone hill, gives Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay and Syrah of real distinction.

sites.name: Ata Rangi
sites.text: Clive Paton planted Ata Rangi on a stony former sheep paddock at Martinborough in 1980. Its Pinot Noir, built on the 'Abel' clone, is one of New Zealand's most admired reds; the name means 'new beginning' or 'dawn sky' in Māori.

sites.name: Dry River
sites.text: Neil and Dawn McCallum planted Dry River in 1979 after Derek Milne's report on Martinborough. Their Pinot Noir, Gewürztraminer and Riesling, made to age, became some of New Zealand's most collected wines.

sites.name: Escarpment
sites.text: Larry McKenna, often called the 'Prince of Pinot' for his work at Martinborough Vineyard, founded Escarpment on Te Muna Road in 1999, making single-vineyard Pinot Noirs from old Martinborough sites.

sites.name: Neudorf Vineyards
sites.text: Tim and Judy Finn planted Neudorf in the Moutere Hills of Nelson in 1978. Its Moutere Chardonnay, from clay-gravel soils, is one of New Zealand's finest, and the estate now belongs to a group led by Tim and Judy's daughter and partners.

sites.name: Brancott Estate
sites.text: Montana Wines planted the first commercial vineyard in Marlborough here in 1973. The first Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc followed in 1979. Now owned by Pernod Ricard and renamed Brancott Estate, its hilltop heritage centre overlooks the vineyards where the style was born.

sites.name: Cloudy Bay
sites.text: David Hohnen of Cape Mentelle founded Cloudy Bay in 1985 with winemaker Kevin Judd, naming it after the bay Captain Cook named in 1770. Its Sauvignon Blanc and misty-mountain label made Marlborough famous worldwide; Te Koko, a barrel-fermented Sauvignon, showed another side. LVMH owns it.

sites.name: Wairau Valley
sites.text: The broad, flat heart of Marlborough along the Wairau River. Its northern side around Rapaura has stony, free-draining alluvial soils (called 'stoney' by locals) that give the classic tropical, pungent Sauvignon Blanc.

sites.name: Southern Valleys
sites.text: A series of side valleys south of the Wairau (Brancott, Omaka, Fairhall, Ben Morven, Waihopai), with clay-rich soils that give more textured Sauvignon Blanc and Marlborough's best Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

sites.name: Awatere Valley
sites.text: A higher, windier and cooler valley south-east of the Wairau around Seddon, planted on a large scale only from the late 1990s. Its Sauvignon Blanc is leaner and more herbal, with tomato-leaf and saline notes.

sites.name: Yealands Estate
sites.text: Peter Yealands planted his estate near the coast at Seaview in the Awatere Valley from 2003, terracing hills with bulldozers. It markets itself on sustainability, including grazing miniature sheep in the vines.

sites.name: Pyramid Valley
sites.text: Mike and Claudia Weersing planted Pyramid Valley in 2000 on limestone near Waikari after a long search for the right soil. Their biodynamic, block-named Pinot Noirs and Chardonnays were acclaimed; Brian Sheth and Steve Smith bought the estate in 2017.

sites.name: Bell Hill
sites.text: Marcel Giesen and Sherwyn Veldhuizen planted Bell Hill on an old limestone quarry at Weka Pass in 1997, densely, Burgundy-style. Its tiny production of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay is among New Zealand's most collected.

sites.name: Pegasus Bay
sites.text: The Donaldson family (neurologist Ivan Donaldson and his wife Christine) planted Pegasus Bay in the Waipara Valley in 1985. Its Rieslings, from dry to the botrytised Aria, and its Pinot Noir made Waipara's reputation.

sites.name: Rippon
sites.text: Rolfe and Lois Mills planted Rippon on the shore of Lake Wanaka in 1975, one of the first modern vineyards in Central Otago. Their son Nick Mills, who trained in Burgundy, farms it biodynamically; the view across the lake to the mountains is one of the most photographed in wine.

sites.name: Felton Road
sites.text: Stewart Elms planted Felton Road at Bannockburn in 1991 and 1992; Englishman Nigel Greening bought it in 2000, and Blair Walter has made the wines since the start. Its biodynamic, block-designated Pinot Noir (Block 3, Block 5, Calvert, Cornish Point) is the benchmark for Central Otago.

sites.name: Gibbston Valley Winery
sites.text: Alan Brady, a journalist from Northern Ireland, planted vines in the Kawarau Gorge in 1981 and released Gibbston Valley's first commercial wine in 1987. Its schist cave, dug into the hill in 1995, is a tourist landmark.

sites.name: Chard Farm
sites.text: Rob and Greg Hay planted Chard Farm on a ledge above the Kawarau Gorge in 1987, reached by a cliff-edge road; it is one of the pioneers of Central Otago Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Bendigo
sites.text: A former gold-mining settlement on the eastern side of Lake Dunstan, now one of Central Otago's warmest districts, with north-facing schist terraces planted since the late 1990s. Prophet's Rock, Quartz Reef and Mount Edward have vineyards here.

sites.name: Gibbston
sites.text: The coolest and highest of Central Otago's sub-regions, along the Kawarau Gorge near Queenstown at up to about 420 m, where Pinot Noir is lighter and more perfumed.

sites.name: Cromwell Basin (Lowburn and Pisa)
sites.text: The broad basin around Lake Dunstan and Cromwell, including Lowburn and the Pisa terraces on the west bank, holds the largest share of Central Otago's vines. It is warm and dry, and gives ripe, dark-fruited Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Alexandra
sites.text: The southernmost Central Otago sub-region, around the town of Alexandra in the Clutha Valley, among the driest places in New Zealand, with large daily temperature swings. Grasshopper Rock, Two Paddocks and Black Ridge make wine here.

sites.name: Burn Cottage
sites.text: A Pinot Noir estate at Lowburn in the Cromwell Basin, founded by the American Sauvage family in 2002 and farmed biodynamically from the start. Ted Lemon of Littorai advises on the wines, which are among the most structured and age-worthy from Central Otago.

sites.name: Te Kauwhata Viticultural Research Station
sites.text: The government research station where Romeo Bragato worked as the first government viticulturist from 1902, testing grape varieties and phylloxera-resistant rootstocks. It shaped New Zealand viticulture for most of the twentieth century.

sites.name: Company's Garden
sites.text: The VOC's vegetable garden, laid out in 1652 to supply passing ships, where Jan van Riebeeck planted the colony's first vines from 1655. On 2 February 1659 he wrote in his diary that wine had been pressed from Cape grapes for the first time. The garden is now a public park in central Cape Town.

sites.name: Castle of Good Hope
sites.text: The VOC's pentagonal stone fort, built between 1666 and 1679, the oldest surviving colonial building in South Africa. Wine for the garrison and the Company's ships was stored and traded from here.

sites.name: Groot Constantia
sites.text: Simon van der Stel was granted Constantia in 1685 and planted the Cape's first great vineyard here. After his death in 1712 the estate was split; Hendrik Cloete bought this part in 1778, built the cellar (1791) with a pediment by Anton Anreith, and made the Constantia wine Napoleon drank on St Helena. The government bought it in 1885; it now makes Grand Constance and red and white table wines.

sites.name: Klein Constantia
sites.text: Part of Van der Stel's original estate. Duggie Jooste bought the run-down farm in 1980, replanted Muscat de Frontignan and released the revived Vin de Constance in 1986, recreating the legendary unfortified sweet wine of the eighteenth century. It also makes fine Sauvignon Blanc from slopes high on the Constantiaberg.

sites.name: Buitenverwachting
sites.text: Another portion of Van der Stel's Constantia, its name means 'beyond expectation'. Revived from 1981 by the Mueller family, it makes Sauvignon Blanc, Christine (a Bordeaux blend) and, since 2007, its own Constantia sweet wine, 1769.

sites.name: Steenberg
sites.text: The oldest farm in the Constantia valley, granted in 1682 to Catharina Ras, a widow who arrived at the Cape in 1662 and outlived several husbands. Today it is a hotel, golf estate and winery known for Sauvignon Blanc and Cap Classique.

sites.name: Cape Point Vineyards
sites.text: Vineyards at Noordhoek on the Cape Peninsula's Atlantic side, some only about 1.2 km from the sea. Planted in the 1990s by Sybrand van der Spuy, they make taut, saline Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon (Isliedh).

sites.name: Diemersdal
sites.text: A Durbanville estate farmed by the Louw family for six generations since 1885, dry-farmed on red granite and shale soils. Thys Louw made it a leader in Sauvignon Blanc, including a Sauvignon from 1992 plantings.

sites.name: Kanonkop
sites.text: On the lower slopes of the Simonsberg, Kanonkop takes its name from a hill where a cannon was fired to tell farmers a VOC ship had arrived. Paul Sauer, a cabinet minister, and Jan 'Boland' Coetzee and Beyers Truter built its reputation; its Pinotage, from bush vines planted in 1953, and Paul Sauer Bordeaux blend are South African classics. It makes red wine only.

sites.name: Rustenberg
sites.text: A farm on the Simonsberg slopes first planted in the 1680s; the Barlow family has owned it since 1941. Its gabled Cape Dutch homestead and old cellars sit below the mountain, and under Simon Barlow it became a leading producer of Cabernet and Chardonnay (Five Soldiers).

sites.name: Thelema
sites.text: Gyles and Barbara Webb bought this fruit farm on the Helshoogte Pass in 1983 and made Thelema one of the first post-isolation stars with Cabernet and Merlot from steep, red granite slopes.

sites.name: Tokara
sites.text: A modern estate at the top of the Helshoogte Pass founded by banker GT Ferreira in the 1990s, with vineyards on the Simonsberg and in Elgin; known for its Director's Reserve blends and olive oil.

sites.name: Warwick
sites.text: Stan and Norma Ratcliffe bought Warwick on the northern Simonsberg in 1964; Norma became one of South Africa's first female winemakers and made the Trilogy Bordeaux blend. The Ratcliffe family sold the estate in 2017.

sites.name: Delheim
sites.text: Hans Otto Hoheisen built this estate on the Simonsberg in the 1940s, and Michael 'Spatz' Sperling, who arrived from Germany in 1951, turned it into one of Stellenbosch's best-loved family estates and helped found the Stellenbosch Wine Route in 1971.

sites.name: Meerlust
sites.text: The Myburgh family has owned Meerlust, south of Stellenbosch near False Bay, since 1756; the farm was granted in 1693. Nico Myburgh and winemaker Giorgio Dalla Cia created Rubicon, a Bordeaux blend first made in 1980, which became one of South Africa's defining reds.

sites.name: Vergelegen
sites.text: Governor Willem Adriaan van der Stel, Simon's son, built Vergelegen in 1700 on the slopes of the Hottentots Holland mountains; his abuse of office led to his recall in 1707. Anglo American bought the estate in 1987, and its hilltop winery (opened 1992) makes Vergelegen V and GVB, among the Cape's finest Bordeaux blends. Camphor trees planted around 1700 still stand.

sites.name: Rust en Vrede
sites.text: A small red-wine estate on the Helderberg foothills, owned by the Engelbrecht family since 1977 (rugby player Jannie Engelbrecht). Its 1694 farm buildings and Estate blend of Cabernet, Shiraz and Merlot are Stellenbosch classics.

sites.name: Spier
sites.text: One of the oldest farms in Stellenbosch, first granted in 1692, with a 1767 wine cellar among South Africa's oldest. Today it is a large winery, hotel and arts centre with a focus on sustainability and community development.

sites.name: Lanzerac
sites.text: A gabled Cape Dutch estate at the mouth of the Jonkershoek Valley, dating from 1692. Its name became famous in 1961, when Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery released a Pinotage made from Bellevue grapes under the Lanzerac label, the first wine ever to name Pinotage on its label.

sites.name: Kleine Zalze
sites.text: A Stellenbosch estate farmed since 1695 and revived by the Basson family from 1996. Its Family Reserve Chenin Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc are regular award winners, and its cellar door sits on the De Zalze golf estate.

sites.name: Ken Forrester
sites.text: Ken Forrester, a restaurateur from Johannesburg, bought the 1689 farm Scholtzenhof on the Helderberg in 1993 and became 'Mr Chenin', championing old-vine Chenin Blanc. His FMC (with the Meinert family) showed that barrel-fermented, botrytis-touched Chenin could rank with the world's great whites.

sites.name: Welgevallen Experimental Farm
sites.text: Stellenbosch University's experimental farm, where Professor Abraham Perold crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut (then called Hermitage) in 1925 to create Pinotage. The seedlings were nearly lost when Perold left for the KWV in 1927; a colleague, Charlie Niehaus, rescued them from the overgrown garden.

sites.name: Simonsig
sites.text: The Malan family's estate north of Stellenbosch, where Frans Malan made Kaapse Vonkel from the 1971 vintage, South Africa's first bottle-fermented sparkling wine, beginning the Méthode Cap Classique category.

sites.name: Boschendal
sites.text: Granted in 1685 to the Huguenot Jean le Long and owned for a century by the de Villiers family, Boschendal is one of the Cape's most visited estates. Its 1812 manor house is a showpiece of Cape Dutch architecture, and its farm now combines wine with orchards, livestock and food.

sites.name: Huguenot Monument
sites.text: A monument at the head of Franschhoek, completed in 1948, commemorating the French Protestant refugees who settled here from 1688. The adjacent museum records the families, many of whose descendants still farm Cape vineyards.

sites.name: Boekenhoutskloof
sites.text: A Franschhoek farm founded in 1776 whose name refers to the native Cape beech (boekenhout). Marc Kent built it into one of South Africa's leading producers from the 1990s, with Syrah, Cabernet, Sémillon from vines planted in 1902 and 1942, and the value brands The Chocolate Block and Porcupine Ridge. It also owns Porseleinberg in the Swartland.

sites.name: KWV Cathedral Cellar
sites.text: The KWV, founded in 1918, built its headquarters in Paarl; the Cathedral Cellar (1930) has a vaulted roof and carved vats depicting the history of Cape wine. Its 'emporium' complex also houses some of the largest wine vats in the world.

sites.name: Nederburg
sites.text: Founded in 1791 near Paarl, Nederburg was modernised by German winemaker Günter Brözel from 1956 and hosted the Nederburg Auction, South Africa's main fine-wine auction, from 1975.

sites.name: Fairview
sites.text: Charles Back's family estate on the slopes of Paarl Mountain, famous for its goats (and Goats do Roam wine), cheese and Rhône varieties. Back also founded Spice Route in the Swartland in 1998, an early bet on the district.

sites.name: Sadie Family Wines
sites.text: Eben Sadie's farm and cellar on the Paardeberg, where he makes Columella (Syrah-led, first vintage 2000), Palladius (a white blend from 2002) and the Old Vineyard Series of single-site wines from old vines across the Cape. Sadie became the face of the Swartland's revival.

sites.name: A.A. Badenhorst, Kalmoesfontein
sites.text: Adi Badenhorst and his cousin Hein bought the run-down Kalmoesfontein farm on the Paardeberg in 2008, restoring a 1930s cellar and old bush vines of Chenin, Cinsault and Grenache. The Secateurs range and the Family white and red blends made them stars of the Swartland Revolution.

sites.name: Mullineux, Roundstone
sites.text: Chris and Andrea Mullineux arrived in the Swartland in 2007 and farm the Roundstone vineyard near Riebeek-Kasteel on schist and iron-rich soils. Their Syrah and old-vine Chenin, and single-terroir bottlings showing granite, schist and iron, are benchmarks; Andrea was named Wine Enthusiast's winemaker of the year in 2016.

sites.name: Porseleinberg
sites.text: A farm on the blue-grey schist of the 'porcelain mountain' bought by Boekenhoutskloof in 2009, where Callie Louw farms Syrah organically and ferments it in concrete eggs and foudres. Its Porseleinberg Syrah (first vintage 2010) is one of South Africa's most sought-after reds; the label is printed on a hand-operated press on the farm.

sites.name: Riebeek-Kasteel
sites.text: A Swartland village below the Kasteelberg where the Swartland Revolution festival was held from 2010 to 2015, bringing wine writers and sommeliers from around the world to taste old-vine Chenin, Cinsault and Syrah.

sites.name: Hamilton Russell Vineyards
sites.text: Tim Hamilton Russell, an advertising executive, bought land in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley in 1975 to make Burgundy-style wine, at a time when Pinot Noir and Chardonnay imports were restricted. His son Anthony and wife Olive built the estate's reputation; its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, from stony, clay-rich shale, are South African benchmarks.

sites.name: Bouchard Finlayson
sites.text: Peter Finlayson, who made Hamilton Russell's first wines, founded this estate in 1989 with Burgundian Paul Bouchard. Its Galpin Peak Pinot Noir and Hannibal blend are well known, and its Kaaimansgat Chardonnay comes from high vineyards near Villiersdorp.

sites.name: Newton Johnson
sites.text: The Newton Johnson family's estate in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, founded in 1996, makes some of South Africa's most admired Pinot Noir (Family Vineyards) from granite and shale slopes.

sites.name: Creation
sites.text: Swiss winemaker Jean-Claude Martin and his wife Carolyn planted Creation on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge in 2002 on virgin land, and it has become one of the area's leading Pinot Noir and Chardonnay producers.

sites.name: Alheit Vineyards, Hemelrand
sites.text: Chris and Suzaan Alheit make their wines on the Hemelrand farm at the top of the Hemel-en-Aarde, but source old vines across the Cape. Their Cartology blend of old-vine Chenin and Sémillon (from 2011) and single-vineyard Chenins such as Magnetic North, from the high Skurfberg in Citrusdal Mountain, are among the most acclaimed whites in South Africa.

sites.name: Magnetic North (Skurfberg)
sites.text: A dry-farmed bush-vine Chenin Blanc vineyard on the sandstone of the Skurfberg, high above Clanwilliam in the Citrusdal Mountain district. Chris Alheit's Magnetic North and Eben Sadie's Skurfberg both come from this cold, windy, sandy plateau.

sites.name: Paul Cluver
sites.text: Dr Paul Cluver, a neurosurgeon, planted vines on his family's apple farm in Elgin in 1987 and made Elgin's first wines; the estate is known for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and botrytised Riesling, and for its amphitheatre concerts.

sites.name: Elim Moravian Mission
sites.text: A mission village founded by Moravian missionaries in 1824 near Cape Agulhas. Its thatched cottages and church are a national monument, and the windswept Elim ward around it gives some of the Cape's coolest Sauvignon Blanc.

sites.name: Boplaas
sites.text: The Nel family has farmed at Calitzdorp since 1880. Carel Nel built Boplaas's fame for Cape Vintage and Cape Tawny made from Touriga Nacional and Tinta Barocca, and the family also distills potstill brandy and whisky.

sites.name: De Krans
sites.text: Another Nel family farm in Calitzdorp, known for Cape Vintage Reserve, Cape Tawny and dry Portuguese-variety table wines. Calitzdorp hosts an annual 'Port and Wine Festival'.

sites.name: Graham Beck, Madeba
sites.text: Mining magnate Graham Beck bought the Madeba farm near Robertson in 1983; under Pieter Ferreira ('Bubbles') it became South Africa's leading Cap Classique house, whose sparkling wine was served at Nelson Mandela's inauguration in 1994.

sites.name: Cederberg Private Cellar
sites.text: The Nieuwoudt family's farm at Dwarsrivier in the Cederberg mountains, with vineyards at about 1,000 m among some of the highest in South Africa. Planted from the 1970s, they make crisp Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin and Shiraz.

sites.name: Groote Post
sites.text: A historic dairy farm in the Darling hills that Peter Pentz and his son Nick turned to vines in the 1990s, a few kilometres from the Atlantic. Cool Atlantic air gives its Sauvignon Blanc a reputation for freshness.

sites.name: Saronsberg
sites.text: A Tulbagh estate at the foot of the Saronsberg on the valley's northern edge, bought by Nick van Huyssteen in 2002 and replanted with Rhône varieties. Its Shiraz and Full Circle blend show the valley's warm days and cold-trap nights.

sites.name: Jiahu
sites.text: A Neolithic village in Wuyang County, Henan, occupied from about 7000 to 5700 BC. Chemical analysis of residues in its pottery jars, published by Patrick McGovern and colleagues in 2004, found a fermented drink of rice, honey and fruit, probably including hawthorn and wild grape: the oldest chemically confirmed alcoholic beverage in the world. The site is also famous for bone flutes.

sites.name: Changyu Wine Culture Museum and Grand Cellar
sites.text: Changyu's original site in Yantai, founded by Zhang Bishi in 1892. The Grand Cellar, built from 1894 and finished after being rebuilt three times, lies seven metres underground and less than 100 metres from the sea; it still holds large oak casks. The museum tells the story of the company and of Chinese wine.

sites.name: Chateau Changyu-Castel
sites.text: A French-style chateau built by Changyu with France's Castel group at Beiyujia near Yantai, with about 135 ha of vineyards. Its signature grape is Cabernet Gernischt, the variety Changyu imported in the 1890s that DNA later showed to be Carmenère.

sites.name: Long Dai
sites.text: Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite) chose the Qiushan valley near Penglai for its Chinese estate in 2008, building terraces on granite hillsides. The first vintage of Long Dai, a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Marselan and Cabernet Franc, was 2017.

sites.name: Great Wall Sanggan Estate, Shacheng
sites.text: COFCO's Great Wall, China's largest wine brand, was founded at Shacheng in the Huailai basin in 1983; its Sanggan estate on the Sanggan River makes the company's top reds. The basin, behind the Great Wall north-west of Beijing, is dry, windy and sunny.

sites.name: Silver Heights
sites.text: Emma Gao, who studied in Bordeaux, and her father Gao Lin founded Silver Heights at the foot of the Helan Mountains; their first vintage was 2007. Its The Summit red helped show that Ningxia could make fine, balanced Bordeaux blends, and the estate is a reference for the region.

sites.name: Helan Qingxue
sites.text: A small Ningxia estate whose Jiabeilan 2009, made with consultant Li Demei, won an international trophy at the 2011 Decanter World Wine Awards, putting Ningxia on the international map. It is one of the region's Second Growths.

sites.name: Chateau Changyu Moser XV
sites.text: A large chateau built by Changyu with Austrian winemaker Lenz M. Moser near Yinchuan, opened in 2013. In 2013 its wines were listed by London's Berry Bros. & Rudd, the first Chinese chateau wines carried by the merchant.

sites.name: Kanaan Winery
sites.text: Wang Fang's Kanaan winery in Ningxia's Xixia district, founded in the early 2010s, makes Bordeaux blends and Riesling and was promoted to Second Growth in the regional classification.

sites.name: Chandon Ningxia
sites.text: Moët Hennessy's Chandon opened its Chinese sparkling-wine winery at the foot of the Helan Mountains in 2013, after Australian winemaker Tony Jordan chose Ningxia for its dry climate.

sites.name: Ao Yun
sites.text: LVMH's estate in Deqin County, Yunnan, whose name means 'flying above the clouds'. After Australian winemaker Tony Jordan spent four years searching China for a site, Moët Hennessy signed a joint venture in 2012 and leased 320 small plots across four villages at 2,200 to 2,600 m. The first vintage, 2013, was released in 2016. Each village ripens at a different time because of altitude and sun.

sites.name: Cizhong Catholic Church
sites.text: A church on the upper Mekong in Deqin County, built by French missionaries, where vines (including a variety thought to be Rose Honey) were planted in the nineteenth century for mass wine. After the missionaries were expelled in 1952, Catholic villagers kept the vineyard and still make wine.

sites.name: Grace Vineyard
sites.text: Founded in 1997 by Hong Kong businessman C.K. Chan at Taigu in Shanxi, Grace Vineyard was one of the first Chinese boutique estates to gain international recognition. His daughter Judy Leissner ran it for years; its Chairman's Reserve is a Bordeaux-style blend.

sites.name: Tiansai Vineyards
sites.text: A boutique estate in the Yanqi Basin of Xinjiang, founded in 2010, at about 1,100 m near Bosten Lake. It became one of the best-known Xinjiang wineries, with Cabernet, Marselan and whites.

sites.name: Turpan grape valley
sites.text: Turpan's Grape Valley, in one of the hottest depressions on earth, has grown grapes for more than 2,000 years, irrigated by karez underground canals that carry snowmelt from the Tianshan. The Tang learned their 'method of wine making' from nearby Gaochang in 641.

sites.name: Huanren Icewine (Hanlong Lake)
sites.text: On Hanlong Lake in Huanren County, Liaoning, Changyu and others make icewine from Vidal grapes frozen on the vine. The lake moderates temperatures so that grapes can hang into December without being destroyed.

sites.name: Yinchuan (OIV Congress 2026)
sites.text: Ningxia's capital Yinchuan hosted the 46th OIV World Congress of Vine and Wine in October 2026,. The city is the hub of the Helan Mountain East Foothill wine region, whose vineyards run along the desert edge west of town.

sites.name: Château Mercian Katsunuma Winery
sites.text: Château Mercian traces its roots to Dai Nihon Yamanashi Budoshu, founded in 1877, which sent Takano Masanari and Tsuchiya Ryuken to Champagne to learn winemaking. Its Katsunuma winery and museum, in a restored early twentieth-century wooden winery building, tell the story of Japanese wine; Mercian's Koshu and Kikyogahara Merlot helped start the modern quality era.

sites.name: Grace Wine (Chuo Budoshu)
sites.text: Founded by the Misawa family in Katsunuma in 1923. Shigekazu Misawa and his daughter Ayana, trained in Bordeaux and Stellenbosch, raised Koshu's profile abroad; their Grace Koshu Kayagatake and Akeno Koshu sparkling are benchmarks, and their vineyard at Akeno is trained on vertical trellises rather than pergolas.

sites.name: Daizenji Temple
sites.text: A Buddhist temple in Katsunuma whose main hall dates from 1286. Legend says the monk Gyoki founded it in 718 after a vision of the Buddha holding grapes, and introduced grape growing; the temple's Yakushi Nyorai statue holds a bunch of grapes, and it makes a small amount of Koshu wine.

sites.name: Katsunuma
sites.text: The historic heart of Koshu country in eastern Yamanashi, where pergola vineyards and wineries line the slopes above the Kofu basin. Since 2005 part of Koshu city, it has more than 30 wineries and hosts an autumn harvest festival.

sites.name: Iwanohara Vineyard
sites.text: Founded in 1890 by Kawakami Zenbei, the 'father of Japanese wine grapes', in snowy Joetsu, Niigata. He made more than 10,000 crosses to find grapes for Japan's climate and in 1927 created Muscat Bailey A and Black Queen. His 1898 'snow room', which used winter snow to cool fermentations, still stands.

sites.name: Kikyogahara
sites.text: A high plateau at about 700 m in Shiojiri, Nagano, where Concord and Niagara grew for a century. In 1976 Château Mercian persuaded local growers to plant Merlot, and its Kikyogahara Merlot became one of Japan's first internationally acclaimed reds.

sites.name: Château Mercian Mariko Vineyard
sites.text: A vineyard planted by Mercian in 2003 on former mulberry land at Ueda in the Chikumagawa valley, now with its own winery (2019). It grows Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc and is a showcase of Nagano's potential.

sites.name: Domaine Takahiko
sites.text: Takahiko Soga started his estate at Yoichi, Hokkaido, in 2010 after working at Coco Farm in Tochigi and his family's Obuse Winery. His Nana-Tsu-Mori Pinot Noir, fermented with whole bunches and natural yeast, is the most sought-after Japanese red and made Yoichi a magnet for young growers.

sites.name: Domaine de Montille Hakodate
sites.text: In 2017 the Burgundian family estate Domaine de Montille, led by Étienne de Montille, bought land near Hakodate in southern Hokkaido to grow Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, the first investment by a Burgundy domaine in Japan.

sites.name: Tokachi Wine Castle, Ikeda
sites.text: Ikeda town in Tokachi founded Japan's first municipal winery in 1963, first using the wild yamabudo grape, and later bred cold-hardy varieties such as Kiyomi from it. Its 'wine castle' on a hill above the town houses ageing cellars and a museum, and the town holds an autumn wine festival.

sites.name: Takahata Winery
sites.text: A winery in the Okitama basin of Yamagata, opened in 1990 in the town of Takahata, known for barrel-fermented Chardonnay and sparkling Delaware. The basin's snowy winters and warm summers have supported fruit and grape growing for over a century.

sites.name: Katashimo Winery
sites.text: Founded in Kashiwara in 1914, Katashimo is the oldest operating winery in western Japan and a link to the 1930s, when Osaka was Japan's largest grape-growing region. It still farms hillside Delaware and Koshu and makes a Koshu from old vines on the Ikoma slopes.

sites.name: Sula Vineyards
sites.text: Rajeev Samant, a Stanford graduate who worked at Oracle, founded Sula on his family's land west of Nashik in 1999, naming it after his mother Sulabha. Working with Californian winemaker Kerry Damskey, he introduced Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc and Zinfandel. Sula sells more than half of India's wine, hosts the SulaFest music festival and listed on Indian stock exchanges in 2022.

sites.name: York Winery
sites.text: A family winery by the Gangapur Dam outside Nashik, founded by the Gurnani family in the late 2000s, with an Australian-trained winemaker and views over the reservoir; known for Shiraz and sparkling wine.

sites.name: Grover Zampa, Nandi Hills
sites.text: Kanwal Grover planted French varieties at Raghunathapura in the Nandi Hills north of Bangalore in 1988. Michel Rolland consulted on its wines, notably La Réserve, and the company merged with Nashik's Vallée de Vin (Zampa) in 2012.

sites.name: Fratelli, Akluj
sites.text: Founded in 2007 by Indian brothers and Italian partners, with Tuscan winemaker Piero Masi, at Akluj in the Solapur district. Fratelli made Sangiovese a success in India; its Sette is a premium red.

sites.name: Chateau Indage, Narayangaon
sites.text: The winery near Pune where Shamrao Chougule launched Omar Khayyam, India's first modern sparkling wine, in the 1980s with help from Champagne. It pioneered French varieties in India before going into liquidation in the 2010s.

sites.name: Vallonné Vineyards
sites.text: A boutique winery near Igatpuri, in the Western Ghats foothills west of Nashik, overlooking the Mukane reservoir. It is known for Cabernet, Merlot and Chenin Blanc, and its lakeside setting draws visitors from Mumbai.

sites.name: GranMonte
sites.text: The Lohitnavy family's estate in the Asoke Valley of Khao Yai, planted from 1999. Nikki Lohitnavy, who studied winemaking in Adelaide, became Thailand's first female oenologist; GranMonte's Chenin Blanc and Syrah are among Thailand's most awarded wines.

sites.name: PB Valley Khao Yai Winery
sites.text: A Khao Yai estate founded by Piya Bhirombhakdi of the Singha beer family, one of the first commercial vineyards in the area, known for Shiraz and Chenin Blanc and for its vineyard tours.

sites.name: Hua Hin Hills Vineyard (Monsoon Valley)
sites.text: Siam Winery's vineyard in the hills behind Hua Hin, producing the Monsoon Valley range. Visitors can tour the vines by elephant or bicycle. Grapes are pruned so that the main crop ripens in the dry season.

sites.name: Chao Phraya delta floating vineyards
sites.text: West of Bangkok, Siam Winery grows grapes on raised beds between irrigation canals in the Chao Phraya delta, a traditional system for fruit growing in flood-prone land. The vines are tended and harvested from boats.

sites.name: Hatten Wines
sites.text: Bali's pioneering winery, founded in 1994 by Ida Bagus Rai Budarsa, with its winery and tasting room near Sanur. Its grapes come from growers around Singaraja on the north coast, where vines yield more than once a year; its Aga rosé and Tunjung sparkling are its best known wines.

sites.name: Singaraja vineyards (Buleleng)
sites.text: The dry north coast of Bali around Singaraja, in the rain shadow of the island's volcanoes, has grown table grapes for decades; it supplies Hatten and Sababay, and its vines can be cropped two or three times a year.

sites.name: Phan Rang vineyards (Ninh Thuận)
sites.text: The hot, dry plains around Phan Rang are Vietnam's grape country, where pergola vineyards are pruned to crop up to three times a year. Most grapes are sold fresh, but some go to local wineries.

sites.name: Da Lat
sites.text: A French-built hill station at about 1,500 m in the Central Highlands, whose name was given to Vang Đà Lạt, Vietnam's best-known wine brand since 1999.

sites.name: Aythaya Vineyard
sites.text: Myanmar's first modern winery, founded in 1999 by German businessman Bert Morsbach on a hillside near Taunggyi in Shan State, at about 1,300 m. Vines were imported from Europe, and its wines are sold mostly to hotels and restaurants.

sites.name: Red Mountain Estate
sites.text: A winery on the hills above Nyaungshwe and Inle Lake, planted in the early 2000s, whose terrace tasting room overlooking the lake became a fixture of travel in Myanmar's Shan State.

sites.name: Yeongdong wine county
sites.text: Yeongdong County in North Chungcheong grows much of Korea's Campbell Early grapes and has encouraged farmers to make wine; it hosts a grape and wine festival and dozens of small farm wineries.

sites.name: Daebudo
sites.text: An island linked to the mainland by a sea wall near Ansan, west of Seoul, where Campbell Early grapes grown in sea breezes supply local wineries.

sites.name: Houli
sites.text: A district of Taichung where farmers grew Black Queen and Golden Muscat for the state monopoly; since 2002 several farm wineries have opened here, including Shu Sheng.

sites.name: Erlin
sites.text: A township in Changhua County, one of Taiwan's main wine-grape areas, where small wineries make Black Queen and Golden Muscat wines from two harvests a year.

sites.name: Prasat Phnom Banan Winery
sites.text: Cambodia's first and best-known winery, a family vineyard near Battambang below the eleventh-century temple of Phnom Banan. It grows Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon, and makes red wine, brandy and grape juice, sold mostly to visitors.

sites.name: Kristall Kellerei
sites.text: A small winery and distillery at Omaruru, started by Helmuth Kluge in 1990 with Colombard and Ruby Cabernet. Now best known for brandy and fruit wines, it was a pioneer of post-independence Namibian wine.

sites.name: Neuras
sites.text: A spring-fed oasis farm near Maltahöhe at the edge of the Namib-Naukluft, where Allen Walkden-Davis planted Shiraz in the 1990s. With almost no rain, it is one of the driest vineyards in the world and now belongs to a wildlife conservation foundation.

sites.name: Marondera (Mukuyu Winery)
sites.text: The highveld town east of Harare where Mukuyu, one of Zimbabwe's main wineries, was based; vineyards around Marondera were planted after sanctions in the 1960s cut off wine imports.

sites.name: Castel Rift Valley vineyards, Ziway
sites.text: The French Castel group's estate on the floor of the Central Rift Valley near Lake Ziway and the town of Batu, planted in the 2000s on sandy volcanic soils at about 1,600 m. Its Rift Valley wines, launched in 2014, include Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Chardonnay; vines can be harvested twice a year.

sites.name: Awash Winery, Addis Ababa
sites.text: Founded in 1956, Awash is Ethiopia's oldest commercial winery, known for the semi-sweet red Gouder and the dry red Axumit, and for many years the country's only significant producer.

sites.name: Lake Naivasha vineyards
sites.text: Vineyards near Lake Naivasha, at about 1,900 m in the Rift Valley, produce Kenya's best-known grape wines (Leleshwa); the lake's flower and vegetable farms share the area's water and volcanic soils.

sites.name: Dodoma vineyards
sites.text: The vineyards around Dodoma, Tanzania's capital, including Hombolo, Bihawana and Makutupora, supply the Dodoma Wine and CETAWICO cellars. The dry season allows two harvests a year.

sites.name: Hombolo mission
sites.text: The Catholic mission where Holy Ghost Fathers planted vines in 1938 for sacramental wine, the beginning of Tanzanian viticulture. Hombolo is now a grape-growing village beside a reservoir north-east of Dodoma.

sites.name: Lazan'i Betsileo, Fianarantsoa
sites.text: The best-known Malagasy wine name, from Fianarantsoa in the central highlands, where vines planted in the colonial era grow at about 1,200 m. The wines, mostly from hybrid grapes, are sold across the island.

sites.name: Ambalavao vineyards
sites.text: Small estates around Ambalavao, south of Fianarantsoa, including Clos Nomena and Domaine de Manamisoa, grow hybrid vines in the Betsileo highlands. The town is also known for its zebu market and handmade Antemoro paper.
